Dickinson’s poetry uses short, sharp lines, lean descriptions, and slant or off-rhyme—rhyme that is close rather than exact. Its main subjects include nature and mortality, expressed through a distinctive, elliptical style.

key_facts.text: Only 10 of Dickinson’s nearly 1,800 poems were published during her lifetime.
After her death, her sister Lavinia discovered the poems in Dickinson’s desk.
A first selection appeared in 1890, but its editors altered the poems to fit contemporary poetic conventions.
Thomas H. Johnson’s 1955 complete collection restored the poems closer to Dickinson’s original intention.

overview.text: Abraham, originally called Abram, is a foundational figure of the Abrahamic religions. Judaism regards him as its first Hebrew patriarch and an ancestor of the Jewish people; Christianity views him as a forebear of Jesus and a spiritual ancestor of Christians; and Islam regards him as a prophet in a chain from Adam to Muhammad. He is also associated with the ancestry of Arab peoples through Ishmael and Jewish people through Isaac.

In Genesis, Abraham’s story centers on divine promises of descendants and land. He is called to leave his father’s household for Canaan, and the promises connected with him are inherited by Isaac while Ishmael is promised that he will found a great nation. Most scholars regard the patriarchal age as a later literary tradition rather than a securely identifiable historical era.

key_facts.text: Genesis presents Isaac as Abraham’s son by Sarah and Ishmael as his half-brother, who is also promised a great nation.
Abraham purchases the Cave of the Patriarchs at Hebron as Sarah’s burial place, establishing a connection between his family and the land.
The Genesis account says Abraham marries Keturah and has six additional sons; Isaac receives all of Abraham’s goods, while the other sons receive gifts.
Many scholars argue that Abraham traditions developed orally over centuries before being incorporated into Genesis during the Persian period of Judah.

overview.text: Tennis is a racket sport played in singles or doubles. Players use a strung racket to send a felt-covered hollow rubber ball over or around a net and into the opponent’s court; a point is scored when the opponent cannot make a valid return.

Tennis has millions of recreational players and a worldwide spectator audience. Its four Grand Slam majors—the Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, and US Open—are especially popular and regarded as the pinnacle of competitive tennis. Tennis has also been consistently included in the Summer Olympics since 1988.

key_facts.text: The Australian Open and US Open use hard courts; the French Open uses red clay; Wimbledon uses grass.
Modern tennis rules have changed little since the 1890s, while the tiebreak was adopted in the 1970s.

Original forms of tennis developed in France during the late Middle Ages. Modern lawn tennis emerged in Birmingham, England, in the late 19th century and was connected to games such as croquet and bowls, as well as to real tennis.
Tennis can be played by wheelchair users and by people who are blind or have low vision.
Professional tennis introduced Hawk-Eye electronic review and point challenges in 2006; fully automated electronic line-calling systems have increasingly replaced them.

overview.text: Appalachian Spring is an American ballet created through the collaboration of choreographer Martha Graham and composer Aaron Copland. Commissioned by Elizabeth Sprague Coolidge, it premiered in 1944 and was later arranged by Copland as an orchestral work. The piece connects Graham’s dance tradition with Copland’s accessible American musical style and remains part of the Martha Graham Dance Company’s repertoire.

Set in a nineteenth-century Appalachian settlement in Pennsylvania, the ballet follows a Bride and Husbandman celebrating their marriage with the community, while the possibility of war creates tension. Copland’s score includes a theme and variations on the Shaker tune “Simple Gifts,” one of the work’s central musical associations.

key_facts.text: The ballet was well received at its premiere; Copland won the Pulitzer Prize for Music during its 1945 United States tour.
The original score used a thirteen-piece chamber orchestra, while the well-known orchestral suite omits three of the ballet’s eight episodes.
The production featured costumes by Edythe Gilfond and sets by Isamu Noguchi.

overview.text: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is used in chemistry and biochemistry to estimate the pH of weak-acid solutions. Its common form is pH = pKa + log10([conjugate base]/[weak acid]), connecting acidity with the acid’s dissociation behavior and the concentration ratio of a conjugate pair. A key application is buffer chemistry: the equation estimates buffer pH and helps determine reagent volumes before preparation, which can reduce unnecessary chemical waste.

key_facts.text: The acid-base pair can be represented as HA ⇌ A⁻ + H⁺, where HA is the acid and A⁻ is its conjugate base.
For buffer calculations, the actual concentration ratio may be approximated using the analytical concentrations of the acid and a salt such as MA.
The equation can also describe bases by treating the protonated form of the base as the acid.
An example of this base application is the amine pair RNH₃⁺ ⇌ RNH₂ + H⁺.
Applications include physiological processes such as metabolic acidosis as well as geological phenomena.

overview.text: The Roman Catholic Church, also called the Catholic Church, is a worldwide Christian church organized into 24 autonomous churches: the Latin Church and 23 Eastern Catholic Churches. These communities are divided into dioceses and eparchies led by bishops. Catholic teaching regards bishops as successors of the apostles and the pope, bishop of Rome, as the successor of Saint Peter with a primary pastoral role.

Catholic doctrine draws on Scripture and sacred tradition, interpreted by the church’s teaching authority, the magisterium. Its worship includes the Mass and several liturgical rites. Catholic life also includes religious orders, devotional practices, and social teaching focused on helping poor, sick, and marginalized people.

key_facts.text: The Eucharist is central to Catholic worship and is celebrated in the Mass. Catholics believe consecrated bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.
The Virgin Mary is venerated as the Mother of God; associated Catholic dogmas include the Immaculate Conception, perpetual virginity, and Assumption.
The 16th-century Protestant Reformation produced new Christian traditions and prompted the Catholic Counter-Reformation.
Catholic communities operate educational, medical, and charitable institutions around the world, alongside missions and other forms of global organization.

overview.text: Jörmungandr, also called the Midgard Serpent or World Serpent, is an enormous sea serpent in Norse mythology. It dwells in the sea around Midgard, encircling the Earth and biting its own tail. This circular form is an example of an ouroboros.
Jörmungandr is especially associated with Thor and Ragnarök. Thor is described as the serpent’s archenemy, while Jörmungandr’s release of its tail signals that Ragnarök is beginning.

key_facts.text: Jörmungandr is described as the middle child of Loki and the jötunn Angrboða, alongside Fenrir and Hel.
Odin cast Jörmungandr into the great ocean around Midgard, where it grew large enough to surround the Earth.
The Old Norse name Miðgarðsormr means “worm of Midgard.”
During Ragnarök, Thor and Jörmungandr battle, and both die.

overview.text: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, politician, and philanthropist. He joined the African National Congress (ANC) in 1943, helped establish its Youth League, and became prominent in opposition to apartheid, the system of racial segregation that privileged whites. His activism later included co-founding the militant Umkhonto we Sizwe and leading a sabotage campaign; he was sentenced to life imprisonment at the Rivonia Trial.

After 27 years in prison, including time on Robben Island, Mandela was released in 1990. He and F. W. de Klerk negotiated an end to apartheid, and Mandela became South Africa’s first Black head of state after the ANC won the 1994 multiracial election. His government emphasized racial reconciliation and created the Truth and Reconciliation Commission to investigate past human-rights abuses.

key_facts.text: Mandela was Xhosa and was born into the Thembu royal family in Mvezo; he studied law and worked as a lawyer in Johannesburg.
He served as ANC president from 1991 to 1997, including during the transition away from apartheid.
Mandela declined a second presidential term and was succeeded in 1999 by his deputy, Thabo Mbeki.
Mandela was often referred to in South Africa by his Xhosa clan name, Madiba, and was described as the “Father of the Nation.”
Mandela’s political legacy combines African nationalism, opposition to racial injustice, democracy, and reconciliation, although he remained controversial to both right-wing and radical-left critics.

overview.text: Guernica is a large 1937 oil painting by Spanish artist Pablo Picasso. Using gray, black, and white, it portrays suffering caused by violence and chaos through images including a gored horse, bull, screaming women, a dead baby, a dismembered soldier, and flames.

Picasso painted it in Paris in response to the April 26, 1937 bombing of Guernica, a town in Spain’s Basque Country, during the Spanish Civil War. Its antiwar subject and powerful imagery helped draw worldwide attention to that conflict.

key_facts.text: The painting was first exhibited at the Spanish pavilion of the 1937 Paris International Exposition.
A subsequent international tour raised money for Spanish war relief.
Its canvas is about 3.49 meters high and 7.76 meters wide, giving the work a monumental scale.
Guernica is exhibited at the Museo Reina Sofía in Madrid.

overview.text: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only astronomical object known to harbor life. It is an ocean world with liquid surface water covering most of its surface. Slowly moving tectonic plates shape mountains, volcanoes, and earthquakes, while a liquid outer core generates a magnetosphere that helps deflect solar wind and cosmic radiation.

Earth’s atmosphere is composed mainly of nitrogen and oxygen. Water vapor and other greenhouse gases help retain solar energy, allowing liquid surface water and water vapor to persist; regional differences in heating drive atmospheric and ocean currents, climate regions, and weather.

key_facts.text: Earth orbits the Sun in about 365.25 days and rotates in about 23 hours 56 minutes; its tilted axis produces seasons.
The Moon is Earth’s one permanent natural satellite. Its gravity helps stabilize Earth’s axis, causes tides, and gradually slows Earth’s rotation.
Among the four rocky planets, Earth is the largest and most massive, and it is the Solar System’s densest planet.
Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, and life developed during its first billion years. Humanity’s growing impact on the climate and biosphere contributes to widespread extinctions.

overview.text: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest planet in the Solar System. It is a gas giant whose atmosphere is mostly hydrogen and helium, and it takes 11.86 years to orbit the Sun. Its early inward movement influenced the formation history of the other planets.

Jupiter rotates quickly—about once every ten hours—giving it a visibly flattened shape. Its banded atmosphere contains powerful storms, including the Great Red Spot, and its fluid metallic-hydrogen interior generates a very strong magnetic field.

key_facts.text: The four largest moons are Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto. Ganymede is larger than Mercury.
Jupiter has a faint ring system made mainly of dust, including halo, main, and outer gossamer ring regions.
Jupiter’s ongoing interior contraction produces more heat than the planet receives from the Sun.
Jupiter is the third-brightest natural object in Earth’s night sky, after the Moon and Venus, and has been observed since prehistoric times.

overview.text: Electric current is the net rate at which electric charge crosses a surface. In familiar circuits, charged particles move through a conductor; these particles are called charge carriers. Depending on the material, carriers may be electrons, ions, or holes. Current is associated with magnetic fields, heating, light production, and electromagnetic waves used in communication. Its SI unit is the ampere (A), equal to one coulomb per second, and an ammeter measures it.

key_facts.text: In ordinary electrical circuits, electrons commonly carry current through wires; electrolytes use ions, while plasmas contain ions and electrons.
In semiconductors, both electrons and holes can serve as charge carriers.
Current-created magnetic fields are used in motors, generators, inductors, and transformers.
Joule heating from current in ordinary conductors can produce light in incandescent bulbs.
Time-varying currents emit electromagnetic waves used to broadcast information in telecommunications.

overview.text: Microwaves are a form of electromagnetic radiation between radio waves and infrared: their wavelengths are shorter than those of other radio waves but longer than infrared. The exact boundaries vary among fields, so microwave ranges do not have one universally fixed cutoff.

Microwaves matter because they can both exchange information and generate heat. Their technology includes communication links, radar, satellite communication, spectroscopy, industrial heating, and cooking; heating occurs when microwaves rotate polar molecules and produce heat.

key_facts.text: Microwave signals generally travel by line of sight. Unlike lower-frequency radio, they do not diffract around hills, follow Earth’s surface as ground waves, or reflect from the ionosphere.

This line-of-sight behavior limits terrestrial links to the visual horizon, about 40 miles (64 km); at high frequencies, atmospheric gases can reduce practical communication distances to around a kilometer.
Engineers often identify microwave frequencies with radar-band labels such as S, C, X, Ku, K, and Ka.
Other applications include remote sensing, radio astronomy, particle accelerators, medical diathermy, collision-avoidance systems, and garage-door or keyless-entry devices.

overview.text: The Wars of the Roses were a series of conflicts over the English throne from 1455 to 1487. They pitted supporters of rival Plantagenet branches: York, associated with a white rose, and Lancaster, associated with a red rose by 1485. The wars grew amid political and socioeconomic troubles following the Hundred Years’ War and the instability of Henry VI’s rule.

After Edward IV’s death in 1483, his son Edward V was deposed by his uncle Richard III amid controversy. Henry Tudor defeated and killed Richard at Bosworth Field in 1485, then became Henry VII. His marriage to Elizabeth of York linked the rival claims, while the remaining Yorkist opposition was defeated at Stoke Field in 1487.

key_facts.text: The First Battle of St Albans in 1455 began the fighting; Richard, Duke of York, captured Henry VI and was appointed Lord Protector by Parliament.
The Yorkist victory at Towton in 1461 was followed by Edward IV’s formal coronation in June of that year.
In 1470, Edward IV fled to Flanders and Henry VI was briefly restored, but Edward returned with Burgundian aid and defeated Warwick at Barnet.
The conflict was called the Civil Wars during the period itself and for several centuries afterward; the name “Wars of the Roses” reflects the houses’ rose emblems.

overview.text: Roald Dahl was a British author whose work included children's literature and short stories; he also wrote poetry and screenplays. He became prominent as a writer in the 1940s.

His children's books combine macabre situations and dark comedy with child characters who face villainous adults, while also emphasizing kindness and warmth. His works include James and the Giant Peach, Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda, The Witches, Fantastic Mr Fox, The BFG, and The Twits. For older audiences, he wrote collections such as Tales of the Unexpected.

key_facts.text: During the Second World War, Dahl served in the Royal Air Force as a fighter pilot and later as an intelligence officer.
Dahl's short stories are particularly associated with unexpected endings.
He was born in Wales to Norwegian immigrant parents and lived most of his life in England.

overview.text: Christmas is a Christian liturgical feast commemorating the birth of Jesus, though many non-Christians also observe it as a cultural holiday. The Nativity narrative in the New Testament places Jesus’s birth in Bethlehem to Mary and Joseph. It says that, because there was no room at the inn, Jesus was born in a stable, and angels announced the event to shepherds.

Most Christians celebrate Christmas on December 25, although the exact date of Jesus’s birth is uncertain. The church fixed December 25 as the observance in the early fourth century; some Eastern Christian churches use December 25 on the Julian calendar, which corresponds to January 7 on the Gregorian calendar. Christian theology emphasizes God becoming human to atone for humanity’s sins rather than knowing the exact birthday.

key_facts.text: In the Western tradition, preparation begins with Advent; Christmastide historically lasts twelve days and ends with Twelfth Night.
Recognizable customs include gift-giving, caroling, church services, Nativity plays, special meals, and displays such as Christmas trees, lights, and nativity scenes.
Santa Claus, Father Christmas, Saint Nicholas, and Christkind are related figures associated with bringing gifts to children during the Christmas season.

overview.text: Pride and Prejudice is a novel of manners by English author Jane Austen, published in 1813. It follows Elizabeth Bennet’s development as she confronts the consequences of hasty judgments and learns to distinguish superficial goodness from genuine goodness.

The Bennet family’s financial situation drives the plot: Longbourn is entailed, meaning it can pass only through the male line, and Mr. Bennet has not saved enough to provide for his five daughters. Marriage therefore becomes an urgent practical concern. The novel has also inspired adaptations and related works in drama, film, television, reprints, and sequels.

key_facts.text: Austen wrote the novel when she was 20–21; it was her third novel written and her second to be published.
Elizabeth Bennet is the novel’s protagonist and central character of development.
The Bennet family has five daughters, while Longbourn’s inheritance restriction favors male heirs.
The novel has remained widely read and has generated many adaptations and derivative works.

overview.text: Christianity is an Abrahamic monotheistic religion based on the Bible and the teachings of Jesus. Christian teaching centers on Jesus as the Son of God and Messiah (Christ), who was crucified and, according to the Gospels, rose from the dead. This resurrection-centered message is called the gospel, meaning “good news.” The four canonical Gospels are Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

Christianity began in the 1st century in Judaea as a Judaic sect and spread around the eastern Mediterranean. The inclusion of non-Jewish converts helped it separate from Judaism. Major historical developments include Constantine’s legalization of Christianity in 313, the Council of Nicaea in 325, the East–West Schism of 1054, and the Protestant Reformation. Christianity later expanded globally through missions, evangelism, migration, and trade.

key_facts.text: The Old Testament serves as the respected background for the Gospels in early Christian tradition.
Christian traditions differ on salvation, church authority, ordination, and Christology—the study of beliefs about Christ.
The three main branches identified in the source are Catholicism, Protestantism, and Eastern Orthodoxy; Oriental Orthodoxy is another prominent branch.
Ecumenism means efforts to promote unity among different Christian churches.
The early disciples spread Christianity despite significant persecution, especially around the eastern Mediterranean.

overview.text: Greece, officially the Hellenic Republic, occupies the southern tip of the Balkan Peninsula in Southeastern Europe. Its geography includes a mainland, nine regions, and thousands of islands. The Ionian Sea lies west of the mainland, while the Aegean Sea and Turkey lie to the east; Albania, North Macedonia, and Bulgaria border it to the north.

Athens is Greece’s capital and largest city; Thessaloniki and Patras are the next largest cities named in the source. Greece’s extensive coastline and island geography are central features of its location in the Mediterranean region.

key_facts.text: Greece is described as having the longest coastline on the Mediterranean.
The country’s eastern position connects it to Turkey both by land and across the Aegean Sea.
The Greek mainland forms the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula.

overview.text: Dionysus is a god in ancient Greek religion associated with wine, fruit and vegetation, fertility, festivity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy, and theater. He was also called Bacchus. In his cult, wine, music, and ecstatic dance were understood as ways of escaping fear and ordinary social restraints. His thyrsus—a fennel-stem staff often associated with ivy and honey—could represent both blessing and destructive power.

His cults took varied forms, and his origins were uncertain: traditions connected him with Thrace, Asia Minor, Mycenaean Greece, or different divine and mortal parentages. Festivals honoring him included sacred dramas that helped drive the development of Western theater. Some traditions also connect him with the dead and with dying-and-rising patterns, though comparisons with other figures require care.

key_facts.text: In Orphic traditions, Dionysus could be presented as the son of Zeus and Persephone, an underworld aspect of Zeus, or the twice-born son of Zeus and the mortal Semele.
Wine was a religious focus in his cult and was treated as Dionysus’s earthly incarnation; it could ease suffering, bring joy, and inspire divine madness.
His maenads are linked with offerings to the dead, while Dionysus can serve as a divine connection between the living and the dead.
Romans identified Bacchus with Liber Pater, a deity associated with viniculture, wine, male fertility, and traditions surrounding coming of age and citizenship.
Roman authorities treated independent Bacchanalia festivals as subversive because they crossed customary class and gender boundaries, eventually restricting them to state-approved forms.

overview.text: La traviata is a three-act opera by Giuseppe Verdi with an Italian libretto by Francesco Maria Piave. It draws on Alexandre Dumas fils’s La Dame aux camélias (1852), itself adapted from his 1848 novel. The opera is also notable for a clash over its setting: Verdi and Piave wanted a contemporary world, but La Fenice’s authorities required a setting around 1700. Later realistic productions in the 1880s restored the creators’ original approach.

key_facts.text: The title is glossed in English as “The Wayward Woman”; the opera was originally called Violetta, after its main character.
Its first performance took place on 6 March 1853 at La Fenice in Venice.
La traviata is among the most frequently performed operas.
The opera’s literary source is connected to both Dumas fils’s 1852 play and his 1848 novel.

overview.text: Count Dracula is a fictional character and the title antagonist of Bram Stoker’s 1897 Gothic-horror novel Dracula. He is regarded as a prototype and archetype of the vampire in later fiction and is identified as one of the best-known fictional figures of the Victorian era. Later books, films, cartoons, and video games have added to or changed characteristics associated with him, so portrayals of Dracula are not all identical.

key_facts.text: Dracula can turn other people into vampires by biting them and drinking their blood.
The character was partly inspired by Vlad III Dracula, the 15th-century Wallachian prince also known as Vlad the Impaler; Stoker probably did not know of this connection.
Possible additional inspirations included Sir Henry Irving, Buffalo Bill, and other actors with aristocratic backgrounds whom Stoker had met.

overview.text: The van der Waals equation is an equation of state—a model relating pressure, molar volume, and temperature in fluids. It applies to both liquid and gas states and treats fluids as molecules with finite size and intermolecular interactions. Its success in predicting behavior around the critical point made it an important model of phase change. It approximates intermolecular potential as hard repulsion plus weak attraction at a distance.

key_facts.text: Dutch physicist Johannes Diderik van der Waals first derived the equation in his 1873 doctoral thesis.
It was the first successful thermodynamic model to treat fluids as finite-size molecules with intermolecular interactions.
Its predictions near a fluid’s critical point agreed qualitatively and quantitatively with experiments.
Van der Waals received the 1910 Nobel Prize in Physics for these accomplishments.

overview.text: Charlemagne was a Frankish ruler of the Carolingian dynasty. He became king of the Franks in 768, sole ruler three years later, and king of the Lombards in 774. Campaigns in Bavaria, Saxony, northern Spain, and elsewhere extended his rule across much of Western and Central Europe, creating lasting political and social changes in medieval Europe.

In Rome in 800, Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor. Although historians debate the coronation’s significance, the title represented the height of his authority and made him a forerunner of the later Holy Roman Emperors. His reforms in government, law, education, military organization, and religion accompanied a period of cultural activity called the Carolingian Renaissance.

key_facts.text: Charlemagne was the eldest son of Pepin the Short and ruled jointly with his brother Carloman before becoming sole king.
He supported the papacy and removed the Lombards from power in northern Italy in 774.
His imperial title brought him into conflict with the Eastern Roman Empire at Constantinople.
Charlemagne died in 814 and was buried at the Palatine Chapel in Aachen, his imperial capital.

overview.text: On September 11, 2001, al-Qaeda carried out coordinated suicide attacks in the United States using 19 hijackers and four commercial airplanes. Two planes struck the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers in New York City, one hit the Pentagon in Virginia, and passengers on the fourth plane revolted before it crashed in Pennsylvania.

The attacks caused enormous loss of life and shaped U.S. foreign policy, leading to the invasion of Afghanistan and the broader Global War on Terror. They also prompted changes in airport security, antiterrorism laws, and intelligence practices around the world.

key_facts.text: The first World Trade Center plane hit at 8:46 a.m.; the second hit at 9:03 a.m. Both towers later collapsed.

The fourth hijacked plane, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers fought back. Canada’s assistance to diverted aircraft became known as Operation Yellow Ribbon.
The attacks killed 2,977 people and caused thousands of injuries, long-term health effects, and extensive property damage.
NATO invoked Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty in response; this was the provision’s only usage to date according to the supplied material.
Major memorials include the National September 11 Memorial & Museum in New York, the Pentagon Memorial, and the Flight 93 National Memorial in Pennsylvania.

overview.text: Nebraska is a landlocked state in the U.S. Midwest, with Lincoln as its capital and Omaha as its largest city. It borders South Dakota, Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas, Missouri, and Iowa; Missouri and Iowa lie across the Missouri River.

Nebraska combines the gently rolling Dissected Till Plains in the east with the treeless prairie of the Great Plains across much of the west. Historic trails, including the route of the Lewis and Clark Expedition, cross the state. The Transcontinental Railroad and Homestead Acts contributed to rapid settler growth and agricultural development in the 1870s and 1880s.

key_facts.text: Nebraska joined the United States as a state in 1867, two years after the Civil War ended.
Its legislature is unicameral, meaning it has one legislative chamber; members are elected without official political-party affiliation.
Nebraska is one of only two states that divide electoral votes by district rather than awarding them winner-take-all statewide; Maine is the other.
Indigenous peoples including the Omaha, Ponca, Pawnee, Otoe, Missouria, and Lakota lived in the region for thousands of years before European exploration.

overview.text: John Brown (1800–1859) was an American abolitionist and deeply religious evangelical Christian who rejected pacifism. He believed armed action was necessary to end slavery after peaceful efforts had failed, viewing abolition as both a Christian duty and an application of the Declaration of Independence’s principle that all people are created equal.

Brown gained national attention during Bleeding Kansas, a violent struggle over whether Kansas would permit slavery. In 1859, he raided the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, hoping to arm enslaved people and begin a wider liberation movement. The raid and his trial escalated sectional tensions that the following year led to Southern secession and the Civil War.

key_facts.text: In May 1856, Brown and his sons killed five supporters of slavery at the Pottawatomie massacre, responding to the pro-slavery sacking of Lawrence.
During Bleeding Kansas, Brown commanded anti-slavery forces at the battles of Black Jack and Osawatomie.
Brown seized the Harpers Ferry armory, but only a few enslaved people joined his revolt.
He was found guilty of treason against Virginia, murdering five men, and inciting a slave insurrection; he was hanged on December 2, 1859.
Brown became a heroic martyr and icon to many Northerners, while others portrayed him as a madman or terrorist.

overview.text: A tornado, also called a twister, is a rapidly rotating column of air reaching from Earth’s surface to the base of a cumulonimbus or cumulus cloud. It often appears as a condensation funnel, sometimes with rotating dust and debris near the ground, but a visible funnel is not universal.

Tornadoes vary greatly in size, wind speed, and path. Most have winds below 180 kilometers per hour, are about 80 meters wide, and travel only several kilometers; the most extreme can exceed 480 kilometers per hour, span more than 3 kilometers, and remain on the ground for over 100 kilometers. Pulse-Doppler radar and storm spotters help detect them.

key_facts.text: Recognized types include multiple-vortex tornadoes, landspouts, and waterspouts.
Waterspouts form over bodies of water and are generally classified as non-supercellular tornadoes, though their status as “true” tornadoes is debated.
Tornadoes occur most commonly in North America, especially the central and southeastern United States, a region commonly called Tornado Alley.
Radar systems can identify patterns such as hook echoes and debris balls in velocity and reflectivity data; storm spotters are another detection method.

overview.text: Lord of the Flies is William Golding’s 1954 debut novel about prepubescent British boys stranded on an uninhabited island. Their disastrous attempt to govern themselves descends into savagery, making the novel a study of morality, leadership, and the tension between civility and chaos. It is popularly assigned in schools.

key_facts.text: The novel was Golding’s debut work.
Its setting is an uninhabited island.
The boys’ central challenge is trying to govern themselves.
The novel examines morality, leadership, civility, and chaos.
It is popularly assigned in schools.

overview.text: Alexander III of Macedon, usually called Alexander the Great, ruled Macedon from 336 to 323 BC. The son of Philip II, he became king at age 20 after his father’s assassination and spent most of his reign leading campaigns across Asia and Egypt. By age 30, he had created an empire stretching from Greece to northwestern India.

Alexander invaded the Achaemenid Persian Empire beginning in 334 BC. Victories at Issus and Gaugamela broke Persian power, allowing him to conquer the empire. His conquests spread Greek settlements and culture, and his death conventionally marks the beginning of the Hellenistic period.

key_facts.text: The philosopher Aristotle tutored Alexander until he was 16. After becoming king, Alexander took leadership of the League of Corinth, an organization created by Philip II.
At Issus and Gaugamela, Alexander won decisive victories that broke Achaemenid power; he subsequently overthrew Darius III and conquered the empire.
During his invasion of India, Alexander defeated King Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, but a troop mutiny forced him to turn back at the Beas River.
Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BC. Afterward, civil wars among the Diadochi, or his successors, led to the breakup of his empire.
Alexander founded more than twenty cities, including Alexandria in Egypt; the spread of Greek culture helped shape Hellenistic civilization.

overview.text: Dragons are mythical creatures found in folklore across the world. They are usually serpentine and may combine traits from different animals, such as wings and claws. Cultures often portray them as powerful, awe-inspiring beings, but their roles can range from benevolent to hostile.

Dragon traditions differ sharply by culture. Chinese dragons are associated with water and imperial authority, while Western traditions often depict dragons as fire-breathing embodiments of evil. Dragons also appear in the works of several modern authors.

key_facts.text: Ancient Mesopotamian art includes dragon-like creatures that could be either hostile or benevolent.
Chinese dragons were linked with rain, the sea, and other forms of water; beginning in the Han dynasty, they also became emblems of imperial power.
Greek drakontes were supernatural serpents. Myths often show heroes or gods defeating them, while cult traditions associated them with healing and wealth.
Dragons feature in modern fiction by authors including J. R. R. Tolkien, Ursula K. Le Guin, and George R. R. Martin.

overview.text: Mansa Musa (c. 1280–c. 1337) was the ninth mansa, or ruler, of the Mali Empire. Mali reached its territorial peak during his reign. Its wealth rested largely on controlling and taxing northern salt routes and gold from Bambuk and Bure, linking West African imperial power to long-distance trade.

In 1324, Musa traveled to Mecca on hajj with an enormous entourage and a vast supply of gold. His lavish gift-giving in Cairo is said to have affected gold’s value in Egypt and drew attention across the Muslim world. He also expanded Mali to include Gao and Timbuktu and cultivated ties with other Muslim states.

key_facts.text: Mali’s territory included lands in present-day Guinea, Senegal, Mauritania, The Gambia, and Mali.
Musa recruited scholars from the wider Muslim world, including the Andalusian poet Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, helping establish Timbuktu as a center of Islamic learning.
Construction associated with his reign includes a portion of Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu.
Although contemporary accounts portray Musa as extraordinarily wealthy, the exact size of his fortune cannot be calculated reliably.

overview.text: Aldous Leonard Huxley (1894–1963) was an English writer and philosopher whose bibliography ranged across nearly 50 books, including fiction and nonfiction, essays, narratives, poems, travel writing, and screenplays. He began by publishing short stories and poetry, then wrote both witty social-satirical novels and grimly serious ones.

In Brave New World (1932), Huxley presented a dystopia, while Island (1962), his final novel, presents a utopia. He was also a pacifist who explored philosophical mysticism and universalism, addressing those subjects in works such as The Perennial Philosophy and The Doors of Perception.

key_facts.text: Huxley earned a degree in English literature from Balliol College, Oxford.
The Perennial Philosophy (1945) illustrates commonalities between Western and Eastern mysticism.
The Doors of Perception (1954) interprets Huxley’s own psychedelic experience with mescaline.
He was elected a Companion of Literature by the Royal Society of Literature in 1962.

overview.text: Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 in D minor, Op. 125, is a choral symphony and his final complete symphony. Composed between 1822 and 1824 and first performed in Vienna on 7 May 1824, it is regarded by many critics and musicologists as a major achievement of Western classical music.

The fourth movement, commonly known as the “Ode to Joy,” features four vocal soloists and a chorus. Its text adapts Friedrich Schiller’s poem “An die Freude,” with additional text by Beethoven, and the movement is in D major.

key_facts.text: The Ninth is described as the first example of a major composer scoring vocal parts in a symphony.
An instrumental arrangement of the choral section became the Anthem of Europe, first adopted by the Council of Europe and later by the European Union.
Beethoven’s original handwritten score, held by the Berlin State Library, was added to UNESCO’s Memory of the World International Register in 2001.

overview.text: The Pythagorean theorem is a Euclidean-geometry relationship for a right triangle. The square built on the hypotenuse—the side opposite the right angle—has the same area as the two squares built on the other sides; in symbols, this is commonly written a² + b² = c².

Named for the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, the theorem connects geometry with coordinate geometry: the squared distance between two points equals the sum of the squared differences of their coordinates. It has been demonstrated through many geometric and algebraic proofs.

key_facts.text: The hypotenuse is always the side opposite the right angle.
The theorem has many different proofs, including geometric and algebraic approaches; some date back thousands of years.
The Pythagorean relation can be extended to higher-dimensional spaces and to some non-Euclidean settings.

overview.text: In mathematics, a set is a collection of different things, called elements or members. These objects can include symbols, geometric figures, variables, functions, and even other sets.

Set theory treats “set” as a primitive notion rather than defining it from simpler concepts. Axioms—basic rules—characterize the properties sets have. In modern mathematics, objects are ultimately defined in terms of sets, giving set theory a foundational role.

key_facts.text: An element is another name for a member of a set.
A set may have another set among its elements.
The axiomatic approach is intended to match intuition about collections.
The source places the foundational use of sets in modern mathematics since the first half of the 20th century.

overview.text: Set, also called Seth or Sutekh, is an ancient Egyptian god associated with deserts, storms, disorder, violence, and foreigners. In the Osiris myth, he is portrayed as a usurper and violent rival who attacks his brother Osiris. Set also has a protective role: he accompanies the sun god Ra’s barque to repel Apep, the serpent of chaos. His connection with the Red Land—the desert—contrasts with Horus’s association with the fertile Black Land.

key_facts.text: In the Osiris myth, Set murders and mutilates his brother Osiris, acting as a usurper.
Isis and Nephthys reassemble Osiris’s body; Isis’s resurrection of him lasts long enough for Horus to be conceived.
Horus seeks revenge against Set, and their conflicts appear in many Egyptian myths.
The Greek form of Set’s name is Seth; Sutekh is an Egyptological form.

overview.text: Sublimation is a phase change in which a substance moves directly from the solid state to the gas state without becoming liquid. It is a direct pathway between two states of matter.
Sublimation is endothermic, meaning it absorbs heat. This energy helps some molecules overcome attractive forces and escape into the vapor phase.

key_facts.text: Deposition is the reverse process: a gas changes directly into a solid.
Examples include dry ice changing into gas and solid iodine becoming gas when heated.
All solids can theoretically sublime, but most do so so slowly that the change is difficult to detect under ordinary conditions.
The heat of sublimation can be calculated as the heat of fusion plus the heat of vaporization.

overview.text: Arthur Miller’s The Crucible is a 1953 American play that dramatizes, with some fictionalization, the Salem witch trials in Massachusetts Bay from 1692 to 1693. Miller shaped this historical subject as an allegory for McCarthyism, the U.S. government’s persecution of people accused of communism.

The play became an important work of American drama. Its first Broadway production received mostly hostile reviews, but a later production succeeded, and the play came to be regarded as a central work in the American-drama canon.

key_facts.text: The first Broadway performance took place on January 22, 1953, at the Martin Beck Theatre.
The original Broadway cast included E. G. Marshall, Beatrice Straight, and Madeleine Sherwood.
The play won the 1953 Tony Award for Best Play.
Its Salem story is dramatized and partially fictionalized rather than presented as a documentary account.

overview.text: A Streetcar Named Desire is a Tennessee Williams play about Blanche DuBois, who moves to New Orleans after personal losses and the decline of her once-prosperous circumstances. She stays with her younger sister, Stella Kowalski, and Stella’s husband, Stanley Kowalski. The play remains among Williams’s most performed works and has inspired adaptations.

key_facts.text: The play was first performed on Broadway on December 3, 1947.
Blanche is presented as a former Southern belle.
The Kowalskis’ apartment is in New Orleans’s French Quarter.
A notable adaptation is the 1951 film directed by Elia Kazan.

overview.text: Glass is an amorphous (non-crystalline) solid that is often transparent and chemically inert. It is commonly formed by rapidly cooling its molten form, a process called quenching. Because it can be shaped readily, glass is used for vessels such as bottles, jars, bowls, and drinking glasses, as well as windowpanes and tableware.

Glass is also important for controlling light: its refractive, reflective, and transmissive properties support lenses, prisms, and optoelectronic materials. Glass fibers extend its uses to communications, thermal insulation, and fiberglass-reinforced plastic.

key_facts.text: Obsidian is a naturally occurring volcanic glass that was used for arrowheads and knives in the Stone Age.
Archaeological evidence places glassmaking at least as early as 3600 BC in Mesopotamia, Egypt, or Syria.
Soda–lime glass contains around 70% silica and accounts for around 90% of modern manufactured glass.
Metal salts can color glass, while vitreous enamels can be painted or printed onto it; these techniques support stained-glass art.
Glass wool traps air for thermal insulation, and glass fibers can be used as optical fibers or to reinforce plastic.

overview.text: Robert Francis Kennedy (RFK, 1925–1968) was a Democratic lawyer and politician who served as U.S. attorney general from 1961 to 1964 and as a senator from New York from 1965 until his death. His career was closely tied to his brother John F. Kennedy: he managed John’s 1960 presidential campaign and later served as a close adviser.

RFK became associated with civil rights, the fight against organized crime, poverty programs, and criticism of U.S. involvement in Vietnam. In 1968 he sought the Democratic presidential nomination, appealing to poor, African American, Hispanic, Catholic, and young voters. Shortly after winning the California primary, Sirhan Sirhan shot him; Kennedy died 25 hours later.

key_facts.text: As chief counsel of the Senate Labor Rackets Committee, Kennedy publicly challenged Teamsters president Jimmy Hoffa over the union’s corrupt practices from 1957 to 1959.
Kennedy won a 1964 New York Senate race against Republican incumbent Kenneth Keating, despite criticism that he was a “carpetbagger” from Massachusetts.
His main challenger for the 1968 Democratic presidential nomination was Senator Eugene McCarthy.

Kennedy wrote Thirteen Days, his account of the Cuban Missile Crisis. As attorney general, he also authorized limited FBI wiretapping of Martin Luther King Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference.

overview.text: Constantinople was founded on the existing city of Byzantium under Constantine the Great and became the Roman Empire’s new capital in 330. It remained a capital after the Roman Empire divided and after the Western Empire fell, marking the period commonly called the Byzantine era. The city stood on a peninsula at the southeastern tip of Thrace, beside the Bosporus and the Sea of Marmara, with the Golden Horn to the north.

Its position made it a gateway between Europe and Asia and between the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Constantinople became known for grand architecture and formidable fortifications. After Ottoman conquest in 1453, it continued as an Ottoman capital until 1922; the historic city now lies at the core of Istanbul.

key_facts.text: Hagia Sophia was a cathedral of the Eastern Orthodox Church and the seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate.
The Theodosian Walls used a double-wall design with a moat and palisades; the city’s surrounding waters reduced the land needing defense.
In 1204, the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, which then became the capital of the short-lived Latin Empire until Byzantine forces recaptured it in 1261.
After the Ottoman conquest in 1453, Constantinople remained an Ottoman capital until 1922; the capital of the Republic of Turkey later moved to Ankara.

overview.text: The Byzantine Empire, also called the Eastern Roman Empire, was the continuation of the Roman Empire centered on Constantinople during late antiquity and the Middle Ages. Its inhabitants called themselves Romans and their state the Roman Empire; “Byzantine” was a later label, coined after the empire ended. Christianity gained official status under Constantine I and Theodosius I, while Greek gradually replaced Latin for official use.

It survived the fall of the Western Roman Empire in the fifth century through recurring cycles of decline and recovery. Arab conquests took Syria, Egypt, and Africa, and later Seljuk incursions cost it much of Asia Minor. The Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople in 1204 caused severe fragmentation; although the city was recovered in 1261, Ottoman annexations eventually culminated in its fall in 1453.

key_facts.text: Under Justinian I (527–565), the empire reached its greatest extent, briefly reconquering much of Italy and the western Mediterranean coast.
Under the Macedonian dynasty, the empire expanded again and experienced a two-century renaissance.
Syria and Egypt fell to the Rashidun Caliphate in the 630s and 640s; Africa fell to the Umayyad Caliphate in 698.
Constantinople remained Europe’s largest and wealthiest city until the 13th century, when Paris overtook it.

overview.text: A rainbow is an optical phenomenon in the sky produced when light interacts with airborne water droplets. Refraction bends the light, internal reflection redirects it inside a droplet, and dispersion separates it into a continuous spectrum, seen as a multicolored arc.

A sunlight rainbow appears opposite the Sun from the observer. From the ground it usually looks like an arc, while an observer above enough mist may see a complete circle; its position is tied to the Sun, observer, and curve’s center.

key_facts.text: A primary rainbow has red on its outer edge and violet on its inner edge.
The primary rainbow forms as light enters a droplet, reflects from its back interior, and exits after being refracted again.
Rainbows can result from rain, mist, spray, or airborne dew—not only ordinary rainfall.
A double rainbow has a second arc outside the primary arc, with its colors appearing in reverse order.

overview.text: South Africa, officially the Republic of South Africa, is Africa’s southernmost country. It has coastlines on the South Atlantic and Indian oceans, borders Namibia, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Eswatini, and completely encloses Lesotho. Its nine provinces include major urban centers such as Johannesburg, Cape Town, and Durban.

The country combines a very deep human history with a politically transformative modern past: archaeological evidence places hominid species there about 2.5 million years ago, while modern humans lived in the region more than 100,000 years ago. European colonization, industrialization, and apartheid shaped its history; universal elections in 1994 followed the beginning of apartheid’s repeal.

key_facts.text: South Africa has three capital cities: Pretoria is the administrative capital, Cape Town the legislative capital, and Bloemfontein the judicial capital.
The indigenous Khoisan peoples were followed by waves of Bantu-speaking migrants from west and central Africa roughly 2,000–1,000 years ago.

The National Party imposed apartheid in 1948, institutionalizing racial segregation; the African National Congress and other activists opposed it, and repeal of discriminatory laws began in the mid-1980s.
South Africa is described as a biodiversity hotspot with distinctive biomes, plant life, and animal life; its cultural and linguistic diversity has also led to the nickname “rainbow nation.”

overview.text: Pablo Ruiz Picasso (1881–1973) was a Spanish painter and sculptor who spent most of his adult life in France. He helped co-found Cubism and helped develop collage and constructed sculpture. His long career ranged across many styles, making him a major figure in 20th-century art.

Two landmark works are the proto-Cubist Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907) and Guernica (1937), an anti-war painting portraying the bombing of Guernica during the Spanish Civil War. Picasso’s work is often organized into periods such as the Blue Period, Rose Period, Analytic Cubism, and Synthetic Cubism.

key_facts.text: Picasso began formal artistic training under his father at age seven and painted in a naturalistic style during childhood and adolescence.
After 1906, Henri Matisse’s Fauvist work encouraged Picasso to explore more radical artistic styles; critics often paired the two artists as modern-art leaders.
The Blue Period is dated 1901–1904, while the Rose Period lasted from 1904 to 1906.
His later work included neoclassical and Surrealist characteristics and often combined elements of his earlier styles.

overview.text: Gavin Newsom is an American Democratic politician who has served as California’s 40th governor since 2019. Before becoming governor, he was San Francisco’s mayor from 2004 to 2011 and California’s lieutenant governor from 2011 to 2019.

His governorship has included attention to infrastructure, housing, climate, gun control, and LGBTQ rights. It also brought criticism of his conduct and leadership during COVID-19, followed by an unsuccessful 2021 recall effort. He won reelection in 2022.

key_facts.text: Newsom was born and raised in San Francisco and studied political science at Santa Clara University.
His political career began with appointments to San Francisco’s Parking and Traffic Commission and Board of Supervisors before his election to the board in 1998.
Before elective office, he founded PlumpJack Group, a winery and hospitality business backed by investor Gordon Getty.
As lieutenant governor, he hosted The Gavin Newsom Show and wrote Citizenville, a book about using digital tools for democratic change.

overview.text: Chromatography is a laboratory method in chemical analysis that separates a mixture into its components. A fluid solvent, called the mobile phase, carries the mixture through a system containing a fixed stationary phase. Because substances interact differently with the stationary phase, they are retained for different times and travel at different apparent speeds, causing separation.

Chromatography has analytical and preparative uses. Analytical chromatography examines small amounts to establish whether substances are present or measure their relative proportions. Preparative chromatography separates components for later use and is a form of purification; the two purposes can overlap.

key_facts.text: The mobile phase can be a gas or a liquid.
The stationary phase may be held in a column, capillary tube, plate, or sheet.
Separation depends on different partitioning between the mobile and stationary phases; a compound’s partition coefficient affects its retention.
Preparative chromatography is associated with higher production costs than analytical work.

overview.text: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, also called Alice in Wonderland, follows Alice after she falls through a rabbit hole into a fantasy world inhabited by anthropomorphic creatures. Lewis Carroll's 1865 children's novel is an example of the literary nonsense genre.

The novel plays with logic and has influenced literature and popular culture, especially fantasy. Its emphasis on delight and entertainment helped change expectations for children's literature. Alice shares her name with Alice Liddell, although scholars disagree about how closely the fictional character was based on her.

key_facts.text: John Tenniel created 42 wood-engraved illustrations for the original edition.
The novel has never been out of print and has been translated into 174 languages.
Its adaptations include film and other screen works, radio, visual art, ballet, opera, and musical theatre.
Carroll published the sequel Through the Looking-Glass in 1871 and the shortened The Nursery “Alice” in 1890.

overview.text: China’s history spans millennia and is rooted in the Yellow and Yangtze river basins, described as one of the oldest cradles of civilization. Traditional histories often organize it around dynastic change: the Shang left the oldest surviving oracle-bone inscriptions, while the Zhou introduced the Mandate of Heaven and helped establish the philosophical foundations of Confucianism, Taoism, and Legalism.

Qin Shi Huang created the first centralized imperial state in 221 BC. Later dynasties—including the Han, Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing—shaped political institutions, culture, technology, and territory. The 1911 Revolution ended imperial rule and created the Republic of China; after further conflict, Mao Zedong proclaimed the People’s Republic of China on the mainland in 1949, while the ROC government retreated to Taiwan. Reform and opening under Deng Xiaoping began in 1978.

key_facts.text: The Han dynasty (202 BC–220 AD) institutionalized Confucianism and fostered paper-making.
The Tang dynasty (618–907) is associated with poetry, culture, and cosmopolitan trade.
The Song dynasty (960–1279) advanced woodblock printing and the imperial examination system, alongside other technological developments.
The Yuan dynasty (1271–1368) followed the Mongol conquest of China; the Ming then restored Han rule and was noted for maritime exploration and arts.
The Qing, the final imperial lineage, was Manchu-led and expanded China to its imperial peak before 19th-century instability and military defeats by foreign powers.

overview.text: China, officially the People’s Republic of China, is a country in East Asia. Its varied landscape includes the Central Plain, the Yangtze and Yellow rivers, deserts, subtropical and temperate forests, plateaus, and mountain ranges such as the Himalayas. Beijing is the capital, while Shanghai is the most populous city by urban area.

China is also associated with a long historical and cultural tradition. Dynastic states emerged there by the second millennium BCE, and the Qin unified the country in 221 BCE. Chinese art and culture have influenced much of Asia, while the Silk Road, Chinese classics, Confucianism, and Daoism are important associations.

key_facts.text: The imperial era is associated with the inventions of paper, printing, gunpowder, and the compass.
After the 1911 Revolution, the Republic of China replaced the empire; in 1949, the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the PRC, while the ROC retreated to Taiwan.
The Great Wall and Grand Canal are among China’s World Heritage Sites.
Chinese cuisine is highly regional: rice is a staple in the south, while wheat is a staple in the north.
China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party and is one of the five permanent members of the UN Security Council.

overview.text: TikTok is a Chinese social networking service built around short-form online video. Users submit videos through a mobile app or website, while recommendation algorithms connect creators and influencers with new audiences. Its worldwide cultural impact includes viral trends in food, fashion, and music.
The platform has also faced scrutiny over privacy, mental health, misinformation, offensive content, and the potentially addictive effects of its algorithm.

key_facts.text: User-submitted videos on TikTok can range from three seconds to 60 minutes.
TikTok surpassed two billion mobile downloads worldwide in April 2020.
Some countries, including India and Afghanistan, have imposed full or partial bans on TikTok.
Many other countries restrict TikTok’s use on government-issued devices for security or privacy reasons.

overview.text: The Chronicles of Narnia is a seven-book portal-fantasy series by C. S. Lewis. Its fictional realm contains magic, mythical beasts, and talking animals. In most books, children from the real world are transported there and become involved in adventures that shape Narnia’s history. The lion Aslan appears throughout the series and sometimes calls on the children to defend Narnia from evil.

Lewis drew on mythology, medieval literature, and cosmology, while Christian theology is interwoven into the series through figures such as Aslan. Lewis preferred to describe these connections as a “supposition” rather than a direct allegory. The books are regarded as classics of children’s literature and have influenced later writing and popular culture.

key_facts.text: The books were originally published from 1950 to 1956 and were illustrated by Pauline Baynes.
The series covers Narnia’s entire history, from its creation in The Magician’s Nephew to its destruction in The Last Battle.
Except in The Horse and His Boy, the protagonists are children from the real world.
The series has been adapted for radio, television, stage, film, and video games.

overview.text: Plasma is a state of matter formed when another classical state—often a gas—becomes substantially ionized. It contains many charged particles, such as ions and electrons. Stars are almost entirely plasma, and plasma also fills much of the thin matter between galaxies, making it a major form of matter in the universe.

Plasma is uncommon on Earth but can be produced artificially. Its charged particles make it electrically conductive and cause it to interact strongly with collective electromagnetic fields. These properties connect plasma to technologies such as plasma etching and to efforts to develop fusion energy.

key_facts.text: A plasma may contain neutral particles as well as charged ones; this is called partially ionized plasma. Neon signs and lightning are examples.
Plasma can be generated by heating a neutral gas or exposing it to a strong electromagnetic field.
The transition to plasma has no single sharp boundary: whether a substance qualifies depends on the conditions and scientific context.
Plasma particles and the plasma as a whole respond sensitively to externally applied electromagnetic fields.

overview.text: Marbury v. Madison (1803) was a Supreme Court case arising during the transfer of power from Federalist president John Adams to Democratic-Republican president Thomas Jefferson. William Marbury, whose judicial commission had not been delivered, asked the Court to issue a writ of mandamus—a legal order requiring a government official to act.

Chief Justice John Marshall’s opinion held that James Madison’s refusal to deliver the commission was illegal, but the Court could not grant Marbury’s request. It struck down section 13 of the Judiciary Act of 1789 because it expanded the Court’s jurisdiction beyond the Constitution. This decision articulated judicial review: the authority of courts to invalidate laws that violate the Constitution.

key_facts.text: The dispute followed Adams’s last-minute appointments and Jefferson’s instruction that undelivered commissions not be delivered.
Marbury sued Madison, the secretary of state, after Madison repeatedly withheld his commission.
The Court found that the law granting it jurisdiction over Marbury’s request exceeded the Constitution’s limits.
Because striking down section 13 removed the Court’s jurisdiction, it did not issue the requested writ of mandamus.

overview.text: Say’s Law, also called the law of markets, is a classical economics proposition named after Jean-Baptiste Say. It holds that producing goods creates purchasing power and demand for other goods: production provides something valuable to exchange, making production the source of demand.

The law became tied to debates over whether an economy can experience a general glut—widespread excess supply relative to demand—and whether government intervention is necessary. It supported laissez-faire arguments, was widely accepted in the nineteenth century, and was challenged by Keynesian economics during the Great Depression, especially during periods of high unemployment.

key_facts.text: Say presented the idea in his work A Treatise on Political Economy.
The claim that Say’s Law rules out a general glut is disputed: some interpreters make that argument, while Petur Jonsson’s account says Say acknowledged that general gluts can occur.
The doctrine was used to support the belief that a capitalist economy could naturally move toward full employment and prosperity without government intervention.
Nineteenth-century versions were modified to incorporate the idea of boom-and-bust cycles.

overview.text: The Nernst equation is an electrochemical thermodynamic relationship used to calculate the reduction potential of a redox reaction. It begins with the standard electrode potential and accounts for absolute temperature, the number of electrons transferred, and the chemical activities of the reacting species. Activities are often approximated by concentrations, making the equation useful for connecting electrode potentials with actual chemical conditions.

key_facts.text: It applies to either a half-cell reaction or a full-cell reaction.
The equation concerns both reduction and oxidation species in a redox reaction.
It is named for Walther Nernst, a German physical chemist who formulated it.

overview.text: Fought in 490 BCE, the Battle of Marathon pitted Athens and its ally Plataea against a Persian expedition commanded by Datis and Artaphernes. It ended King Darius I’s first attempt to subjugate Greece after Persian forces landed near Marathon in Attica.

Using marshy and mountainous terrain that restricted Persian cavalry, the Greeks attacked under the Athenian general Miltiades and enveloped the Persian force. The Persian defeat ended the first invasion and made Marathon a major turning point in the Greco-Persian Wars.

key_facts.text: The invasion followed Athenian and Eretrian support for the Ionian Revolt against Persian rule; Persia captured Eretria before reaching Marathon.
Athens requested Spartan help, but Sparta did not send troops because a religious festival was under way.
The Persian army relied mainly on missile troops; Miltiades strengthened the Greek flanks, which wheeled inward and routed the Persians.
Darius began preparing another expedition after the defeat, but an Egyptian revolt delayed it; his son Xerxes later resumed preparations for a second invasion.

overview.text: A circle is a plane shape made up of all points that lie at the same distance from a central point. It is a fundamental geometric figure with a clear connection between its center, radius, and boundary.

Circles appear in nature and form the basis of the wheel, with related inventions such as gears supporting much of modern machinery. Their mathematical study has contributed to geometry, astronomy, and calculus.

key_facts.text: The fixed distance from the center to any point on the circle is the radius.
A diameter is a segment joining two points on the circle that passes through the center.
The region enclosed by a circle is called a disc.
Examples of natural circles include the full moon and slices of round fruit.

overview.text: Lazarus of Bethany is a New Testament figure whose life is restored by Jesus four days after his death, according to the Gospel of John. The event is presented as one of Jesus’ miracles.

Within John’s account of Jesus’ seven signs, the raising of Lazarus is described as the climactic sign, emphasizing Jesus’ power over death. Bethany is identified with modern Al-Eizariya in the West Bank, whose name means “the place of Lazarus.”

key_facts.text: The Eastern Orthodox Church venerates Lazarus as Righteous Lazarus, the Four-Days Dead.
Eastern Orthodox and Catholic traditions preserve differing accounts of Lazarus’s later life.
A separate Lazarus appears in Luke’s parable of the rich man and Lazarus; he is not the Bethany figure.

overview.text: Norway, officially the Kingdom of Norway, is a Nordic country in Northern Europe occupying the western and northern parts of the Scandinavian Peninsula. Its kingdom includes the Svalbard archipelago and the remote Arctic island Jan Mayen; Bouvet Island is a dependency rather than part of the kingdom.

Oslo is Norway’s capital and largest city. Norway borders Sweden to the east and Finland and Russia to the northeast, while its long coastline faces the Skagerrak, North Sea, Norwegian Sea, and Barents Sea.

key_facts.text: Norway’s unified kingdom was established in 872 through the merger of smaller kingdoms.
From 1537 to 1814, Norway was part of Denmark–Norway; from 1814 to 1905, it was in a personal union with Sweden.
Norway was neutral in World War I and remained neutral in World War II until Nazi Germany invaded it in April 1940.
Norway claims the Antarctic territories of Peter I Island and Queen Maud Land.

overview.text: In mathematics, a matrix organizes numbers or other mathematical objects in a rectangle of rows and columns. Its dimensions record its row and column counts: an m × n matrix has m rows and n columns, while a square matrix has equal counts. In linear algebra, matrices serve as linear maps; they also represent geometric transformations and coordinate changes, and reduce many numerical-analysis problems to matrix computations.

Common operations include entrywise addition, scalar multiplication, transposition, and matrix multiplication. Matrix multiplication requires the first matrix’s column count to equal the second’s row count and represents composition of linear transformations. Unlike multiplication of numbers, matrix multiplication generally depends on order. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero.

key_facts.text: If A is m × n and B is n × p, then AB is m × p; each entry comes from the dot product of a row of A with a column of B.

Row operations include adding one row to another, multiplying a row by a nonzero constant, and switching two rows. They help solve linear equations and find matrix inverses through Gauss and Gauss–Jordan elimination.
A matrix with one row is called a row matrix or row vector; one with one column is a column matrix or column vector.
The eigenvalues of a square matrix are the roots of its characteristic polynomial.

overview.text: The Tiananmen Square protests, also called the June Fourth Incident, were student- and worker-led demonstrations in Beijing from 15 April to 4 June 1989. Sparked by the death of former pro-reform CCP general secretary Hu Yaobang, they reflected concerns about inflation, corruption, political participation, and changing economic guarantees. Student demands included democracy, press and speech freedoms, government accountability, and constitutional due process.

After martial law, troops entered Beijing on 4 June and fought demonstrators and others trying to block them. Death estimates range from several hundred to the low thousands, with thousands more wounded. The aftermath included arrests, censorship, Western arms embargoes, and curtailed political liberalization while market reforms continued. The photograph of the unidentified “Tank Man” circulated internationally and became one of the most recognizable images of the twentieth century.

key_facts.text: A student hunger strike in May broadened support for the movement, which spread to about 400 cities.
The State Council declared martial law on 20 May; as many as 300,000 troops were mobilized but initially halted by mass nonviolent resistance.
Most killings occurred in Beijing’s western suburbs along Chang’an Avenue, rather than in the square itself.
Mass arrests of protesters helped catalyze Operation Yellowbird, while the government tightened control of reporting about the events.
Political liberalization was curtailed after the crackdown, while market-oriented economic reforms continued and accelerated after 1992 under strong state direction.

overview.text: Ray Bradbury’s Fahrenheit 451 is a dystopian novel set in a future American society where books are outlawed and firemen burn those that are found. It follows Guy Montag, a fireman who becomes disillusioned with censoring literature and destroying knowledge; he ultimately leaves his job and commits himself to preserving literary and cultural writings.

The novel connects book burning with censorship, repression, and threats to reading and free expression. Bradbury developed it during the Second Red Scare and McCarthy era, drawing on Nazi book burnings and ideological repression in the Soviet Union; he later also described mass media’s ability to reduce interest in literature as a concern behind the book.

key_facts.text: Bradbury combined elements from his short stories “Bright Phoenix” and “The Pedestrian” in the 1951 novella The Fireman, which became the basis for Fahrenheit 451.
Fahrenheit 451 was completed and published as a novel in 1953.
The novel’s subject matter led to censorship in apartheid South Africa and in various schools in the United States.
Its adaptations include François Truffaut’s 1966 film, a 2018 television film, stage productions, radio dramas, and an interactive-fiction video game.

overview.text: Cuba is an island country in the Caribbean, consisting of its namesake main island plus 4,195 islands, islets, and cays. It lies where the Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico, and Atlantic Ocean meet. Havana is the capital and largest city.

Cuba is culturally considered part of Latin America. Its history includes Spanish imperial rule and independence after 1898, while its population reflects Indigenous, Spanish, and African ancestry. Cuba’s later political history made it a major Cold War flashpoint.

key_facts.text: Cuba is the largest country in the Caribbean by area.
It lies east of the Yucatán Peninsula, south of Florida and the Bahamas, west of Hispaniola, and north of Jamaica and the Cayman Islands.
Cuba’s population reflects pre-Columbian peoples—especially the Taíno and Ciboney—Spanish settlers, and sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade.
The 1959 Cuban Revolution overthrew Fulgencio Batista’s government and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.
The 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis became a major Cold War confrontation and is widely considered the closest the world has come to nuclear war.

overview.text: The Legend of Sleepy Hollow is an 1820 short story by American author Washington Irving. It was published in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., a collection of essays and short stories that helped establish Irving’s literary career. The work is associated with early American fiction and has remained continuously in print, giving it a lasting place in U.S. literary culture.
The story also has a continuing adaptation history, including a 1922 silent film and a 1949 Walt Disney animated version.

key_facts.text: Publication year: 1820.
Irving wrote the story while living in Birmingham, England.
It appeared in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.
The collection contains 34 essays and short stories.

overview.text: Hillary Diane Rodham Clinton is an American politician, lawyer, and diplomat in the Democratic Party. Her career included serving as U.S. first lady, senator from New York, and secretary of state.

She became the first woman to win a major U.S. party’s presidential nomination, as the Democratic nominee in 2016, but lost the Electoral College vote to Donald Trump. Her career connected domestic policy—including health care and children’s programs—with foreign policy, including sanctions on Iran and a strategic pivot toward Asia.

key_facts.text: Born and raised in Chicago, Clinton graduated from Wellesley College in 1969 and Yale Law School in 1973.
She became the first female senator from New York after winning election in 2000, while still serving as first lady.
After losing the 2008 Democratic presidential primaries to Barack Obama, she became secretary of state in 2009.
As secretary of state, she advocated the 2011 military intervention in Libya and faced criticism over the 2012 attack in Benghazi.
Her use of a private email server while secretary of state drew intense scrutiny; no charges were filed.

overview.text: Dance is an art form built from sequences of body movements. These movements may be improvised or deliberately selected, and they can have aesthetic or symbolic meaning. Dance is often performed with musical accompaniment, but it can also be described through its choreography, movement vocabulary, historical period, or place of origin. It serves as both a performance art and a form of personal expression.

Two common group-dance types are theatrical and participatory dance. Dance can have social, ceremonial, competitive, martial, sacred, or other functions. People also dance for exercise, and dancing does not always require fixed choreography.

key_facts.text: Dance may be performed alone or in groups.
A dancer may sometimes play a musical instrument while performing.
Dance performances and competitions occur across the world in many styles and standards.
Dance can be used as exercise or as training for other sports and activities.

overview.text: Herman Melville (1819–1891) was an American writer associated with the American Renaissance. His fiction includes Moby-Dick, Typee, Billy Budd, Sailor, and short stories such as “Bartleby, the Scrivener.”

Melville’s early writing drew on his experiences at sea and in Polynesia, while Moby-Dick showed increasing literary ambition. Although that novel initially found little audience, it was later regarded as one of the Great American Novels.

key_facts.text: Melville went to sea as a merchant sailor in 1839 and joined the whaler Acushnet in 1841 before leaving the ship in the Marquesas Islands.
Typee was Melville’s first book, and Omoo was its sequel; both were travel adventures based on his encounters with island peoples.
Between 1853 and 1856, he published magazine fiction including “Benito Cereno” and “Bartleby, the Scrivener.”
Melville later concentrated on poetry, including Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War, a reflection on moral questions raised by the Civil War.
Billy Budd was unfinished when Melville died and was published posthumously in 1924.

overview.text: Professor James Moriarty is a fictional criminal mastermind created by Arthur Conan Doyle as a formidable opponent for Sherlock Holmes. He first appears in “The Adventure of the Final Problem,” published in The Strand Magazine in December 1893. Moriarty also has a role in The Valley of Fear, although he does not appear directly there.

In the original stories, Moriarty leads an international criminal network, using intelligence and resources to devise crimes and sometimes protect criminals from the law for payment. Holmes compares him to a spider at the center of a web and calls him the “Napoleon of crime.” Later adaptations and pastiches often expand him into Holmes’s main antagonist, although Doyle used the character sparingly.

key_facts.text: Doyle created Moriarty partly as a narrative device for ending Holmes’s stories by killing the hero.
Holmes mentions Moriarty in stories including “The Adventure of the Empty House,” “The Adventure of the Norwood Builder,” and “His Last Bow.”
The title “Napoleon of crime” was adapted from a Scotland Yard inspector’s description of the real-life criminal Adam Worth, who helped inspire Moriarty.
Moriarty appears only twice in Doyle’s original stories; later adaptations give him a much larger role.

overview.text: Macbeth, also called The Tragedy of Macbeth, is a Shakespearean tragedy estimated to have been first performed in 1606. It follows a Scottish general who hears from three witches that he will become king. Driven by ambition and encouraged by his wife, Macbeth murders King Duncan, takes the throne, and uses further violence to protect his position.

The play explores political ambition, power, guilt, paranoia, psychological damage, and tyranny. Macbeth and his wife are ultimately destroyed by the violence they have set in motion. Shakespeare based the story on Holinshed’s Chronicles, though the play differs substantially from the historical Macbeth. A stage superstition led actors to call it “The Scottish Play.”

key_facts.text: Macbeth is Shakespeare’s shortest tragedy.
The play was published in the 1623 Folio, possibly from a theatrical prompt book.
Scholars believe Macbeth contains more allusions to King James I than any other Shakespeare play written during James’s reign.
Macbeth has been adapted into film, television, opera, novels, comics, and other media.

overview.text: A mycorrhiza is a symbiotic association between a fungus and a plant, linking fungal hyphae with plant roots at a cellular interface. It relates to the plant’s rhizosphere—the root system and its surroundings—and has roles in plant nutrition, soil biology, and soil chemistry.
Arbuscular fungi colonize root tissues inside plant cells, whereas ectomycorrhizal fungi colonize them outside the cells.

key_facts.text: The singular is mycorrhiza; plural forms include mycorrhizae and mycorrhizas.
The name comes from Ancient Greek words meaning “fungus” and “root.”
The association is normally mutualistic, but it can be parasitic in particular species or circumstances.

overview.text: The Grand Canal (Dà yùnhé) is an interconnected canal system in northern and eastern China. Its current main stem, the Jing–Hang Grand Canal, is described as extending from Beijing to Hangzhou and linking the Yellow and Yangtze river systems through canals, rivers, and lakes.
