Ares is closely associated with Aphrodite through an affair that becomes a story of divine humiliation: Hephaestus traps the lovers in a net and exposes them to the other gods. During the Trojan War, Aphrodite persuades Ares to support Troy, but the Trojans lose while Athena aids the Greeks.

key_facts.text: Ares’s closest Roman counterpart is Mars, although Roman religion gave Mars a more dignified role as ancestral protector of the Roman people and state.
Some Greek and Asia Minor communities held annual festivals intended to bind or detain Ares as their protector; in parts of Asia Minor, he was also regarded as an oracular deity.

The reported belief that ancient Spartans practiced human sacrifice to Ares is treated cautiously, as it may have arisen from mythic prehistory, misunderstandings, and his violent reputation rather than established reality.

overview.text: Mars was the Roman god of war and an agricultural guardian, reflecting the combined military and farming concerns of early Rome. He was a leading deity of the Roman army, and March—Martius in Latin—was named for him.

Romans associated Mars with military power used to secure peace, unlike the more destructive force often associated with the Greek god Ares. In a Roman founding myth, Mars fathered Romulus and Remus by raping Rhea Silvia, linking him to Rome’s origins; Romans later identified him with Ares under Greek cultural influence.

key_facts.text: The Campus Martius, an area of Rome, took its name from Mars; Augustus later built a temple to Mars Ultor in his forum.
The wolf was sacred to Mars, and a she-wolf nursed Romulus and Remus in the founding myth.
Most festivals of Mars occurred in March and October, months traditionally associated with the beginning and end of military campaigning and farming.
Mars was described as the son of Jupiter and Juno.

overview.text: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and the “Red Planet,” a rocky, desert-like world with a very thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide. Fine dust is widespread, while water exists mainly underground or as ice, frost, and traces in the atmosphere—not as bodies of liquid surface water. The possibility of past or present life on Mars remains under active scientific investigation.

Mars has flat northern plains and cratered southern highlands, along with extinct volcanoes and the enormous Valles Marineris canyon. Its axial tilt gives it seasons. Robotic missions have explored Mars continuously since 1997, and the planet is often proposed as a target for future crewed missions.

key_facts.text: A Martian day, called a sol, lasts about 24.6 Earth hours; a Martian year lasts 687 Earth days.
Olympus Mons, an extinct volcano, is 21.9 km tall, while Valles Marineris extends about 4,000 km.
Mars’s surface gravity is about one-third of Earth’s, and its diameter is about half of Earth’s.
Mariner 4 achieved the first successful Mars flyby in 1965; Mariner 9 became the first spacecraft to orbit Mars in 1971.

overview.text: The Jungle is a novel by American author and journalist Upton Sinclair. It appeared in serial form in the socialist newspaper Appeal to Reason in 1905 and in book form from Doubleday in 1906.

Its social vision presents working-class poverty, immigrant struggle, inadequate support, dangerous work, and corruption among powerful people. The book also evokes hopelessness, cynicism, and cruelty among the powerless. Sinclair intended his account of the meat industry and its labor conditions to advance socialism, but the immediate public reaction focused on health dangers and unsanitary practices.

key_facts.text: In 1904, Sinclair spent seven weeks gathering information in Chicago’s meat-packing district of the Union Stock Yards.
Jack London compared the novel with Uncle Tom’s Cabin as a work exposing “wage slavery.”
Public outcry led to sanitation reforms including the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act.

overview.text: Yggdrasil is an immense, sacred ash tree at the center of Norse cosmology. The Nine Worlds and everything else are described as existing around it, making it a central structure of the Norse universe.

Its branches reach into the heavens, while three roots extend to distant wells and springs: Urðarbrunnr, Hvergelmir, and Mímisbrunnr. The gods gather there for traditional assemblies, and several creatures live within the tree.

key_facts.text: Yggdrasil is attested in the Poetic Edda, compiled in the 13th century from earlier traditional sources, and in the Prose Edda, compiled in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson.
The dragon Níðhöggr and the squirrel Ratatoskr are among the creatures associated with Yggdrasil.
Scholars generally connect the names Mímameiðr, Hoddmímis holt, and Læraðr with the tree.
Yggdrasil is identified as an example of sacred trees and groves in Germanic paganism and mythology.

overview.text: Hans Christian Andersen (1805–1875) was a Danish writer who also produced plays, travelogues, novels, and poems, but he is best remembered for his literary fairy tales. His stories became embedded in Western collective consciousness and are accessible to children while presenting lessons associated with virtue.
The tales have been translated into more than 125 languages and have inspired ballets, plays, and animated and live-action films, giving Andersen’s fairy tales a broad cultural reach.

key_facts.text: The fairy-tale body consists of 156 stories published across nine volumes.
Major titles include “The Emperor’s New Clothes,” “The Little Mermaid,” “The Snow Queen,” “The Ugly Duckling,” “The Little Match Girl,” and “Thumbelina.”
Andersen’s tales have inspired ballets, plays, animated films, and live-action films.

overview.text: Animal Farm, originally titled Animal Farm: A Fairy Story, is George Orwell’s satirical allegorical novella and beast fable. It follows anthropomorphic animals who rebel against their human master on Manor Farm, hoping to create a utopian society.

The rebellion is betrayed when the pigs establish a dictatorship, leaving the farm in a dystopian state nearly identical to the one the animals opposed. Orwell connected the story to events leading up to the Russian Revolution and the Stalinist era of the Soviet Union.

key_facts.text: The novella was first published in England on August 17, 1945.
Orwell described the work as a satire against Stalin and sought to unite political purpose with artistic purpose.
The original title included the subtitle A Fairy Story; American publishers dropped that subtitle when the book was published in 1946.
Orwell wrote the book between November 1943 and February 1944, and several publishers initially rejected it.

overview.text: Yom Kippur, Judaism’s holiest day of the year, is observed annually on the tenth of Tishrei, usually in late September or early October. Its central themes are atonement and repentance.
It is associated with Rosh Hashanah as one of the High Holy Days and is the last of Judaism’s Ten Days of Repentance. Traditional observance emphasizes prayer, confession, fasting, and self-denial.

key_facts.text: The name Yom Kippur is commonly translated as “Day of Atonement.”
Traditional observances include extended synagogue prayer services, full fasting, ascetic practices, and confession of sins.
Some Reconstructionist Jewish communities focus less on sin and more on personal goals, accomplishments, and yearly intentions.

overview.text: The United States of America, also called the United States or U.S., is a federal republic primarily located in North America. It includes 50 states and the federal capital district, Washington, D.C. The 48 contiguous states lie between Canada and Mexico, while Alaska is in the northwest and Hawaii is in the Pacific Ocean.

The United States also asserts sovereignty over five major island territories and other uninhabited islands in Oceania and the Caribbean. Its territory expanded through the purchase, settlement, and conquest of lands controlled by European powers and Indigenous peoples.

key_facts.text: The 48 contiguous states border Canada to the north and Mexico to the south.
Alaska is a semi-exclave in the northwest, while Hawaii is an island chain in the Pacific Ocean.
Washington, D.C., is a federal capital district, separate from the 50 states.
The United States asserts sovereignty over five major island territories, as well as various uninhabited islands in Oceania and the Caribbean.

overview.text: Orion is a prominent constellation, or set of stars, named after a hunter in Greek mythology. It is one of the 88 modern constellations and was among the 48 listed by the second-century AD astronomer Ptolemy. Orion is especially prominent during winter evenings in the Northern Hemisphere and is associated with bright stars, the Orion Nebula, and the Orionids meteor shower.

key_facts.text: Orion’s Belt is a short, straight-line asterism made of three stars.
Rigel and Betelgeuse are Orion’s two brightest stars; both are slightly variable supergiants.
The constellation contains the Orion Nebula, one of the brightest nebulae in the sky.
The annual Orionids meteor shower has its radiant in Orion and is associated with Halley’s Comet.

overview.text: The Caspian Sea is the world’s largest inland body of water and is also described as the world’s largest lake, although it is commonly called a sea. It lies east of the Caucasus and west of Central Asia, north of the Iranian Plateau and south of southern Russia. Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran, and Turkmenistan border it.

The Volga, Europe’s longest river, provides its main freshwater inflow at the shallow northern end. Deep central and southern basins produce regional differences in temperature, salinity, and ecology. The Caspian is associated with caviar and oil industries, but pollution and dams on rivers flowing into it have harmed its ecology.

key_facts.text: Its surface is about 27 meters below sea level, while its southern seabed reaches 1,023 meters below sea level.
Its salinity is approximately 1.2%, or about one-third that of average seawater.
The name “Caspian” comes from the ancient Iranic Caspi people.

overview.text: Refractive index, usually written n, compares the speed of light in vacuum with its speed in a material: n = c/v. In a medium, both light’s speed and wavelength are reduced relative to their vacuum values, while vacuum has an index of 1. At a boundary between materials, the index helps determine how strongly light bends, or refracts, and how much light is reflected.

Refractive index can depend on wavelength. This produces dispersion, in which white light separates into colors in prisms and rainbows, and can cause chromatic aberration in lenses. In absorbing materials, a complex-valued index can also describe attenuation: its imaginary part represents the weakening of light, while its real part describes refraction.

key_facts.text: Snell’s law relates the indices and angles at an interface: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.
A material’s reported refractive index should include the measurement wavelength because the value may change across the visible spectrum.
Refractive index also affects the critical angle for total internal reflection and the amount of reflected light at an interface.
High-index glass allows eyeglass lenses to be thinner and lighter; plastics generally have lower indices and lower densities than glass.

overview.text: Hamlet, also titled The Tragedy of Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, is a tragedy William Shakespeare wrote sometime between 1599 and 1601. Set in Denmark, it follows Prince Hamlet’s attempt to avenge his father’s murder by his uncle Claudius, who killed him to seize the throne and marry Hamlet’s mother.

The play has had a major influence on English-language literature and has been repeatedly adapted. It is widely regarded as one of the greatest plays, and its textual history includes three early versions that preserve different lines and passages.

key_facts.text: Hamlet is Shakespeare’s longest play.
The three early versions are the First Quarto (1603), Second Quarto (1604), and First Folio (1623).
The early versions do not contain exactly the same text; each has lines or passages absent from the others.
Proposed sources for the play range from ancient Greek tragedies to Elizabethan dramas.

overview.text: A wedding is a ceremony in which two people are united in marriage. Its form varies greatly across cultures, ethnicities, religions, countries, social classes, and sexual orientations, so “wedding” refers to many different customs rather than one fixed ritual.
Wedding ceremonies often combine spoken promises, public recognition, and symbolic customs. They may also include religious or literary elements, and a reception can follow the ceremony.

key_facts.text: An authority figure or celebrant may publicly proclaim the marriage.
Presented symbols or gifts can include rings, flowers, money, or other meaningful items.
Music, poetry, prayers, and readings from religious texts or literature may be part of the ceremony.
Special wedding garments are often worn.
A wedding reception sometimes follows the ceremony.

overview.text: Hanuman is a Hindu deity revered as a divine vanara, or monkey-like being, and as a devoted companion of Rama. He is central to the Ramayana, while stories about him also appear in the Mahabharata and Puranas. Known by names including Maruti, Bajrangabali, and Anjaneya, Hanuman is traditionally connected with Vayu, the celestial wind-god. Vaishnava traditions commonly describe him as Vayu’s son and incarnation, while Shaiva tradition regards him as an incarnation of Shiva.

Hanuman represents the combination of heroic strength and initiative with loving devotion, self-control, faith, and commitment. He is traditionally portrayed as celibate. Although early texts and archaeological evidence do not show prominent Hanuman-centered devotion, a major following and broader theological importance developed later, especially during the second millennium CE; subsequent worship has included images and temples.

key_facts.text: Medieval Bhakti figures such as Samarth Ramdas portrayed Hanuman as a symbol of nationalism and resistance to oppression.
In Vaishnava thought, Madhvacharya connected Vayu’s aid to Vishnu’s incarnations with Hanuman’s assistance to Rama.
Later literature associated Hanuman with martial arts, meditation, and scholarly pursuits.
Hanuman’s religious symbolism joins Shakti, or power, with Bhakti, or devoted love.

overview.text: Ukraine is a country in Eastern Europe and Europe’s second-largest country after Russia. It lies between Russia and several European states and has shores on the Black Sea and Sea of Azov. Kyiv is its capital and largest city; Ukrainian is the official language.

The region was a major center of East Slavic culture under Kievan Rus’. Ukraine became a constituent republic of the Soviet Union in 1922 and independent in 1991. Its fertile land makes it an important grain exporter.

key_facts.text: Ukraine’s land neighbors are Belarus, Poland, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania, Moldova, and Russia.
The Cossack Hetmanate emerged in central Ukraine in the 17th century and was later partitioned between Russia and Poland.
The Holodomor was a human-made famine in the early 1930s that killed millions of Ukrainians.

After the 2014 Euromaidan protests, Russia occupied and annexed Crimea, while conflict in Donbas involved Russia and Russian-backed separatists; a new phase of the war began with Russia’s invasion in 2022.

overview.text: The House on Mango Street is a 1984 novel by Mexican-American author Sandra Cisneros. Told through a series of vignettes—short, self-contained scenes—it follows Esperanza Cordero, a 12-year-old Chicana girl, during a year in a Hispanic neighborhood of Chicago as she enters adolescence.

The novel is a coming-of-age work shaped by questions of identity, gender, race, sexuality, and social class. It is considered a modern classic of Chicano literature and has been studied in feminist theory; its difficult subjects include domestic violence, puberty, sexual harassment, and racism.

key_facts.text: Cisneros drew partly on her own experience in writing the novel.
The novel received the American Book Award from the Before Columbus Foundation.
Tanya Saracho adapted the novel into a stage play, produced in Chicago in 2009.
Its treatment of sensitive subjects has led to challenges and threats of censorship.

overview.text: Gravity is a fundamental interaction that draws material objects toward one another. In Newton’s law of universal gravitation, it is an attractive force between any two bodies: its strength increases with their masses and decreases with the square of the distance between them. General relativity instead describes gravity as curvature of spacetime caused by the distribution of mass.

Gravity acts across unlimited distances, though it weakens with separation. It helped gather early-universe matter into stars, galaxies, and clusters. Near a planet, gravity acts toward the planet’s center, gives objects weight, and is modified by the planet’s rotation.

key_facts.text: Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity, proposed in 1915, provides the modern description of gravity.
A black hole is an extreme case of spacetime curvature; after crossing its event horizon, not even light can escape.
Quantum gravity seeks to combine gravity with the other fundamental interactions in a single framework, sometimes called a “theory of everything.”
Gravity is essential to understanding mechanisms responsible for surface water waves and lunar tides, substantially contributes to weather patterns, and helps guide plant growth through gravitropism.

overview.text: The Roman Senate (Latin: Senātus Rōmānus) was ancient Rome’s aristocratic governing assembly. Its role changed across Rome’s monarchy, Republic, and Empire: under the kings it mainly advised the king and also helped choose new kings; in the Republic, its influence rose to a high point in the middle Republic, then weakened in the late Republic and after the establishment of the Principate.

Later reforms reduced its authority: Diocletian made it politically irrelevant, and shifting the government away from Rome turned it into a municipal body; Constantine created a second senate at Constantinople. Its long afterlife makes it a distant predecessor of modern legislative and senatorial bodies, though its powers varied greatly over time.

key_facts.text: In the early Republic, magistrates appointed senators for life unless Roman censors expelled them; those magistrates initially held more power than the Senate.
The Senate’s late-Republic decline began after reforms associated with the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus.
After Romulus Augustulus was deposed in 476, the Western Senate continued under Odoacer and then Ostrogothic rule before disappearing; its last recorded public act was in 603.
Some medieval Roman aristocrats used the title senator, but it was honorific and did not represent the continued existence of the classical Senate.

overview.text: The Holy Roman Empire was a decentralized polity centered in Central Europe whose territories and influence changed substantially over time. Its origins are associated with Charlemagne’s coronation as Roman Emperor in 800; the imperial title was revived in 962 when Otto of Saxony was crowned. The empire depended on cooperation between emperors and powerful, often independent vassals rather than tight central rule. Its imperial office was traditionally elective, chosen by a small group of mostly German prince-electors and archbishops. After reforms in the late  fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, its institutions endured until Emperor Francis II dissolved the empire on August 6, 1806, during the Napoleonic Wars.

key_facts.text: The empire initially linked the kingdoms of Germany, Italy, and, from 1032, Burgundy under the emperor’s overlordship.
By the fifteenth century, effective imperial governance was concentrated in Germany, while control over Italy and Burgundy had largely faded.
The House of Hohenstaufen oversaw the empire’s mid-thirteenth-century peak in territorial expansion and power, followed by overextension and partial collapse.
After 1512, the empire was also known as the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation.
Francis II’s dissolution followed Napoleon’s creation of the Confederation of the Rhine from German states aligned with France.

overview.text: War and Peace is an epic novel by Russian author Leo Tolstoy. Set during the Napoleonic Wars, it combines a fictional story with discussions of history and philosophy. Its central historical backdrop is the French invasion of Russia and its aftermath.

The narrative follows five interlocking stories involving Russian aristocratic families, showing Napoleon’s impact on Tsarist society. The work is an internationally praised classic of world literature and is regarded alongside Anna Karenina as one of Tolstoy’s finest literary achievements.

key_facts.text: Its Russian title is Война и мир, romanized as Voyna i mir.
An early version appeared serially beginning in 1865; Tolstoy rewrote the work before its complete publication in 1869.
An earlier version, titled The Year 1805, was serialized in The Russian Messenger from 1865 to 1867.
Tolstoy resisted placing the work in a single genre, describing it as not a novel, poem, or historical chronicle; later sections include extended philosophical discussions.

overview.text: The Great Gatsby is a 1925 tragedy novel by American writer F. Scott Fitzgerald. Set on Long Island near New York City during the Jazz Age, it follows first-person narrator Nick Carraway’s interactions with Jay Gatsby, a mysterious millionaire seeking to reunite with Daisy Buchanan, his former lover.

The novel is closely associated with social class, inherited versus self-made wealth, and a cynical view of the American Dream. Although it was initially a commercial disappointment, its reputation grew dramatically during World War II, helping make it a standard part of American high-school education and popular culture.

key_facts.text: Fitzgerald drew inspiration from a youthful romance and from the lavish parties he attended on Long Island’s North Shore.
The novel was published by Scribner’s in April 1925 and received generally favorable reviews, despite weak early sales.
During World War II, free copies distributed to American soldiers overseas helped trigger the novel’s renewed popularity and critical study.
Francis Cugat’s dust-jacket design, titled “Celestial Eyes,” impressed Fitzgerald, who incorporated its imagery into the novel.

overview.text: Vera Rubin was an American astronomer known for pioneering studies of galaxy rotation rates. By comparing predicted and observed motion in galactic rotation curves, she identified the galaxy rotation problem: galaxies moved in ways that did not match predictions. This discrepancy became a key piece of evidence for dark matter. Later measurements using 21-centimeter hydrogen-line radio telescopes strengthened the case. Rubin is especially associated with galaxy rotation curves and dark matter in modern astronomy.

key_facts.text: Her full name was Vera Florence Cooper Rubin; she lived from 1928 to 2016.
She received the Bruce Medal, the Royal Astronomical Society’s Gold Medal, and the U.S. National Medal of Science.
The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile was named in her honor.
Rubin advocated for women in science and mentored aspiring female astronomers.

overview.text: John Coltrane was an American jazz saxophonist, bandleader, and composer whose career made him a major figure in jazz and 20th-century music. He began in bebop and hard bop, later helping pioneer modal jazz and standing at the forefront of free jazz.

His music developed an increasingly spiritual character, especially on A Love Supreme (1965). Coltrane also connected with major jazz figures through performances and recordings, including work associated with Miles Davis and Thelonious Monk.

key_facts.text: Coltrane was born and raised in North Carolina, moved to Philadelphia after high school, and made his professional debut in 1945.
He led at least fifty recording sessions and appeared on many albums by other musicians.
His second wife, Alice Coltrane, was a pianist and harpist.

overview.text: Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez was a Spanish Baroque painter and the leading artist at the court of King Philip IV of Spain and Portugal. He worked during Spain’s Golden Age.

Velázquez began with a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner marked by bold brushwork. He painted historical and cultural scenes, royal portraits, and portraits of commoners, culminating in Las Meninas (1656).

key_facts.text: His full name was Diego Rodríguez de Silva y Velázquez; he was baptized in 1599 and died in 1660.
His paintings became models for 19th-century realist and Impressionist painters.
Twentieth-century artists including Pablo Picasso, Salvador Dalí, and Francis Bacon reinterpreted some of his iconic images.
Most of his work entered the Spanish royal collection; some portraits were sent abroad as diplomatic gifts, especially to the Austrian Habsburgs.

overview.text: Heart of Darkness is an 1899 novella by Polish-British novelist Joseph Conrad. Sailor Charles Marlow recounts his assignment as captain of a steamer for a Belgian company in the African interior.

Marlow’s expedition leads toward an ivory-trading station far up the river, where he is to find Kurtz. The setting connects the story to the Congo Free State, then a private colony of Belgium’s King Leopold II. The novella explores imperial power, racism, morality, and the unstable boundary between “civilized” people and “savages.”

key_facts.text: Conrad does not name the river directly, though the narrative is associated with the Congo River and Congo Free State.
The work first appeared as a three-part serial in Blackwood’s Magazine in 1899.
The novella provided inspiration for Francis Ford Coppola’s 1979 film Apocalypse Now.
Conrad draws parallels between London and Africa as places of “darkness.”

overview.text: Treasure Island is an adventure and historical novel by Scottish author Robert Louis Stevenson. Published as a book in 1883, it is set in the eighteenth century and centers on buccaneers and buried gold. It is also treated as a coming-of-age story, with its reputation built partly on atmosphere, memorable characters, and action.

The novel matters beyond its original story because it strongly influenced later portrayals of pirates in popular culture. Familiar pirate imagery associated with the book includes tropical islands, treasure maps marked with an X, and one-legged sailors accompanied by parrots.

key_facts.text: The work originally carried the title The Sea Cook: A Story for Boys.
It first appeared in serial form from 1881 to 1882 in Young Folks, using the title Treasure Island or the Mutiny of the Hispaniola and the pseudonym “Captain George North.”
Cassell & Co. published the first book edition on November 14, 1883.
Treasure Island has been frequently dramatized and adapted since its publication.

overview.text: Voltage, or electric potential difference, compares electric potential at two points. In a static electric field, it corresponds to the work needed per unit charge to move a positive test charge between them. Its SI unit is the volt (V).

As a scalar quantity, voltage describes a comparison between two points; it can be associated with energy supplied, dissipated, or stored. Measuring it usually involves a voltmeter and a reference point such as ground.

key_facts.text: A capacitor can have voltage because electric charge builds up.
Electromagnetic induction in a generator can produce voltage.
Cells and batteries can create voltage through electrochemical processes.
Photovoltaic, piezoelectric, and thermoelectric effects are other ways voltage can arise.

overview.text: The domestic dog (Canis familiaris or Canis lupus familiaris) is a domesticated descendant of wolves. Dogs and modern gray wolves share a common ancestor. Hunter-gatherers selectively bred dogs during the Late Pleistocene, making dog domestication older than agriculture; genetic studies suggest the process may have begun more than 25,000 years ago.

Dogs have been bred for desired behaviors, sensory capabilities, and physical attributes, so breeds vary widely in shape, size, and color. They perform roles including hunting, herding, protection, therapy, companionship, and aiding disabled people. Dogs have also adapted to human behavior: they can understand and communicate with humans, making the human–canine bond an important subject of study.

key_facts.text: Dogs can thrive on a starch-rich diet that would be inadequate for other canids, an adaptation associated with their long relationship with humans.
Compared with humans, dogs have more developed senses of smell and hearing but less acute visual acuity.
Dog communication includes eye gaze, facial expression, vocalization, body posture, and chemical signals such as scents and pheromones. Urination can mark territory, especially in a new environment.

overview.text: Campbell’s Soup Cans is Andy Warhol’s 1961–1962 series of 32 paintings. Each presents a different variety of Campbell’s soup in the same 20-by-16-inch format. First exhibited in July 1962 at the Ferus Gallery in Los Angeles, the series became a major example of Pop art, a movement that brought imagery from consumer culture into fine art. Its uniform presentation also challenged older ideas about originality and artistic subjects.

Warhol’s experience as a commercial illustrator shaped his interest in the packaging of everyday products. The series helped provoke debate about the relationship between commercial imagery and high art, while later related paintings, drawings, stencils, and screen-print portfolios expanded the Campbell’s soup-can image beyond the original 32 canvases.

key_facts.text: The original 32 canvases are distinct from later screen-print sets, which are sometimes mistakenly treated as the same series.
Art dealer Irving Blum preserved the original canvases; the Museum of Modern Art acquired them in 1996.
The series is widely regarded as a canonical symbol of Pop art and has had a lasting presence in popular culture.
The works’ central subject is not soup itself but Warhol’s artistic depiction of commercial packaging.

overview.text: The Battle of Thermopylae was fought in 480 BCE between the Achaemenid Persian Empire under Xerxes and an alliance of Greek city-states led by Sparta under Leonidas. Lasting three days, it was a prominent battle in the Greco-Persian Wars and the second Persian invasion of Greece.

A Greek force used the narrow pass to hold back the much larger Persian army. After Ephialtes revealed a path behind the Greek position, Leonidas dismissed most of his troops and stayed with a rear guard that included 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians. Their defense became famous as a last stand.

key_facts.text: Themistocles’ strategy paired the defense of Thermopylae with the naval Battle of Artemisium, aiming to block the Persian advance by land and sea.
The Greek force initially numbered about 7,000, including an estimated 300 Spartans; modern estimates put the Persian army at roughly 120,000–300,000 soldiers.
After the Persian capture of Thermopylae, the Greek fleet defeated the invaders at Salamis, and a Greek victory at Plataea the following year ended the second Persian invasion.
Thermopylae is often used to illustrate how training, equipment, and favorable terrain can strengthen a defending force.

overview.text: Wave interference is a physics phenomenon in which two coherent waves are combined by adding their displacements or intensities while taking their phase difference into account. The resulting wave may have greater or lower amplitude: waves that are in phase produce constructive interference, while waves that are out of phase produce destructive interference. Its central idea is that combining waves changes the amplitude of the resulting wave.

key_facts.text: Interference is observed with light and radio waves.
Acoustic, surface-water, and gravity waves can also show interference.
Matter waves and electrical waves in loudspeakers are additional examples.

overview.text: Sherlock Holmes is a fictional detective created by British author Arthur Conan Doyle. Calling himself a “consulting detective,” he handles cases for many clients, including Scotland Yard, using observation, deduction, forensic science, and logical reasoning.

The stories are usually narrated by Dr. John H. Watson, Holmes’s friend and biographer, who generally accompanies him. Their recurring London setting includes 221B Baker Street. The character and stories have influenced mystery writing and popular culture through adaptations in many media.

key_facts.text: Holmes first appeared in A Study in Scarlet (1887). His first series of short stories began in The Strand Magazine with “A Scandal in Bohemia” in 1891.
The original Holmes canon eventually comprised four novels and 56 short stories; nearly all are set between 1880 and 1914.
Sherlock Holmes fandom was one of the first cohesive fan communities and helped establish modern fandom practices.

overview.text: Baltimore, also called Baltimore City, is Maryland’s most populous city and an independent city outside county jurisdiction. Established as a port in 1706 and a town in 1729, it grew around commerce and later became a major transportation and manufacturing center.

Baltimore is strongly associated with the War of 1812: the British bombardment of Fort McHenry prompted Francis Scott Key to write the poem that became “The Star-Spangled Banner,” designated the U.S. national anthem in 1931. The city also saw some of the earliest violence associated with the Civil War during the 1861 Pratt Street Riot.

key_facts.text: The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, built in 1830, connected producers in the Midwest and Appalachia with Baltimore’s port.
Baltimore’s Inner Harbor was the second-leading U.S. port of entry for immigrants after New York’s Ellis Island, helping the city become a major manufacturing center.
Fell’s Point, Federal Hill, and Mount Vernon are among the nation’s earliest National Register Historic Districts.
Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins University are the city’s top employers; Baltimore is also home to the Orioles of Major League Baseball and the Ravens of the National Football League.

overview.text: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian of the Italian Renaissance. From 1498 to 1512, he served as a senior official of the Florentine Republic, handling diplomatic and military affairs. After the Medici returned to power, he lost his post, was exiled following a mistaken treason suspicion, and turned to political writing.

Machiavelli is chiefly associated with The Prince, a treatise on rule written around 1513. It argues that rulers may need morally troubling policies when political necessity demands them, making the work controversial. His Discourses on Livy, composed around 1517, has been linked to the development of modern republicanism.

key_facts.text: The Prince, or Il Principe, was published in 1532, five years after Machiavelli’s death.
Some commentators have interpreted The Prince as a manual for would-be tyrants seeking power and an absolute regime.
Machiavelli’s name became associated with unscrupulous political conduct because of policies discussed in The Prince.
Machiavelli’s political works influenced later Enlightenment-era authors such as Jean-Jacques Rousseau and James Harrington.

overview.text: Victor-Marie Hugo (1802–1885) was a French Romantic author whose work included novels, poetry, essays, plays, and journalism. His most famous novels are The Hunchback of Notre-Dame and Les Misérables, making those titles key literary associations.

Hugo stood at the forefront of the French Romantic movement through works such as Cromwell and Hernani. He was also a politician and human-rights activist; his opposition to absolutism and literary stature helped establish him as a national hero in France.

key_facts.text: Hugo was renowned in France for poetry collections including Les Contemplations and La Légende des siècles, or The Legend of the Ages.
His writing inspired later musical works, including the opera Rigoletto and the musicals Les Misérables and Notre-Dame de Paris.
His political outlook changed from youthful royalism to strong support for republicanism; he served as both a deputy and a senator.
He campaigned for abolishing capital punishment and slavery, and he produced more than 4,000 drawings.

overview.text: Easter, also called Pascha or Resurrection Sunday, is a Christian festival commemorating the resurrection of Jesus from the dead. The New Testament describes this as occurring on the third day after his burial following his crucifixion. Easter is the culmination of the Passion of Jesus and follows Lent, a 40-day period associated with fasting, prayer, and penance.

Easter follows Holy Week, which includes Palm Sunday, Maundy Thursday, and Good Friday. Its date is movable rather than fixed, and Eastertide begins on Easter Sunday and continues for seven weeks, concluding with Pentecost. In Western Christian practice, its date follows a rule based on the first full moon on or after the vernal equinox.

key_facts.text: The name Pascha comes from the same linguistic tradition as Passover; Easter is connected with Passover through its name, calendar position, symbolism, and the Gospel accounts of Jesus’s final week.
The First Council of Nicaea in 325 established a rule for celebrating Easter on the first Sunday after the relevant spring full moon.
Christian observances include sunrise services or nighttime vigils, Paschal greetings, flowering a cross, and displaying Easter lilies.
Easter eggs can symbolize the empty tomb; egg hunts and the Easter Bunny are customs observed by Christians and some non-Christians.

overview.text: Gustav Holst was an English composer, arranger, and teacher, best known for the orchestral suite The Planets. His music was shaped by Richard Wagner, Richard Strauss, the early-20th-century English folksong revival, and Maurice Ravel, influences that helped him develop an individual style.

Holst’s work in music education included teaching at St Paul’s Girls’ School and directing music at Morley College. The Planets brought him international success after World War I, but he disliked celebrity and preferred composing and teaching. His music later influenced composers such as Benjamin Britten and Michael Tippett.

key_facts.text: He studied at the Royal College of Music under Charles Villiers Stanford.
An arm condition ended his hopes of becoming a pianist; he then supported himself by playing trombone professionally.
He directed music at Morley College from 1907 to 1924 and taught at St Paul’s Girls’ School from 1905 until his death in 1934.
By the 1980s, recordings of much of his output had become available after a period in which most of his music received little attention.
His influence extended to younger English composers including Edmund Rubbra, Michael Tippett, and Benjamin Britten.

overview.text: American Gothic is a 1930 painting by Grant Wood, an American artist associated with Regionalism. Wood was known for paintings depicting the rural American Midwest.
The painting has become an iconic example of early twentieth-century American art, making it a central association with Wood’s career.

key_facts.text: Grant DeVolson Wood lived from 1891 to 1942.
Wood is identified as a representative of Regionalism.
American Gothic is especially associated with Wood’s reputation as an artist.

overview.text: The Korean Peninsula is a peninsular region in East Asia. In the broader geographic sense of “Korea,” it includes the peninsula, Jeju Island, and smaller islands. China lies to the north and Russia to the northeast, across the Amnok (Yalu) and Duman (Tumen) rivers; Japan lies southeast across the Korea Strait.

Since 1945, the region has been politically divided at or near the 38th parallel between North Korea and South Korea. Both states proclaimed independence in 1948. The Korean War, fought from 1950 to 1953, ended in stalemate without a peace treaty, and a demilitarized zone was created between them.

key_facts.text: The initial post-1945 division placed the Soviet military occupation zone in the north and the American zone in the south; reunification was originally intended.
The Demilitarized Zone, or DMZ, approximates the original partition between the two countries.
The modern name Korea developed from Goryeo, the kingdom that reunified the Later Three Kingdoms and incorporated the ruling class of Balhae.
Japan formally annexed the Korean Peninsula in 1910; Japanese rule ended with Japan’s surrender in 1945.

overview.text: Activation energy is the energy barrier reactants must overcome before transforming into products. In the Arrhenius model of reaction rates, it is the minimum energy that must be available for a chemical reaction to occur. Molecules can cross this barrier only when they have enough kinetic energy, making temperature an important condition for many reactions.

key_facts.text: Activation energy is symbolized Ea and is measured in kilojoules per mole or kilocalories per mole.
The term was introduced in 1889 by Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius.
A reaction occurs when enough reactant molecules have kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation-energy barrier.

overview.text: Bears are carnivoran mammals in the family Ursidae, classified among the caniforms, or dog-like carnivorans. The family has eight living species spread across varied habitats in North America, South America, and Eurasia, with a range extending into parts of the Southern Hemisphere. Typical bears have bulky bodies, stocky legs, shaggy hair, long snouts, small rounded ears, short tails, and five-clawed, flat-footed paws.

Bears are associated with strong senses, varied diets, denning, and impressive movement: despite their heavy appearance, they can run, climb, and swim. They also have an important conservation profile, since habitat loss and illegal trade threaten several species.

key_facts.text: Polar bears are mostly carnivorous, giant pandas mostly herbivorous, and the other six living species are omnivorous.
Bears are generally solitary, apart from courting pairs and mothers with their young; they also have an excellent sense of smell.
Most species use dens during winter and may hibernate for as long as 100 days.
Six bear species are classified as vulnerable or endangered; habitat encroachment and illegal trade in bear parts are major pressures.

overview.text: Loki is a god in Norse mythology whom some scholars describe as a trickster. A shape-shifter, he engineers the death of Baldr. With the jötunn Angrboða, Loki fathers Hel, the wolf Fenrir, and the world serpent Jörmungandr.

The gods bind Loki, while serpent venom torments him and Sigyn catches it in a bowl. During Ragnarök, he is foretold to break free and fight the gods among the jötnar. He and Heimdallr are also foretold to kill one another.

key_facts.text: In mare form, Loki gives birth to Sleipnir, an eight-legged horse. He also appears as a salmon and a fly.
Loki’s parents are Fárbauti, a jötunn, and Laufey, a goddess. His sons with Sigyn are Narfi or Nari and Váli.
Loki is attested in the Poetic Edda, Prose Edda, Heimskringla, skaldic poetry, the Norwegian Rune Poem, and Scandinavian folklore.
Loki may be depicted with his mouth stitched shut on the Snaptun Stone and bound on the Kirkby Stephen Stone and Gosforth Cross.

overview.text: Agatha Christie (1890–1976) was an English author associated with the “Golden Age of Detective Fiction” and especially mystery writing. Her recurring detectives include Hercule Poirot, Miss Marple, and Tommy and Tuppence; Poirot first appeared in The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1920), while Miss Marple debuted in The Murder at the Vicarage (1930).

Christie also wrote drama: The Mousetrap is a murder-mystery play performed in London’s West End since 1952. She was nicknamed the “Queen of Crime” or “Queen of Mystery” and was made a Dame in 1971 for her contributions to literature.

key_facts.text: She published six novels under the pseudonym Mary Westmacott.
And Then There Were None is one of the top-selling books of all time, with about 100 million copies sold.
Her work in hospital dispensaries during both world wars gave her knowledge of poisons that she later used in her fiction.
In 1955, Christie became the first recipient of the Mystery Writers of America’s Grand Master Award.

overview.text: Mesopotamia is a historical region of West Asia centered on the Tigris–Euphrates river system in the northern Fertile Crescent. It corresponds roughly to modern Iraq; southwestern Iran lies just beyond it, marking a transition toward the Persian plateau.

The region is associated with some of the earliest developments of the Neolithic Revolution, beginning around 10,000 BC, and with some of the world’s earliest civilizations. From recorded history onward, Sumerians and Akkadians were followed by powers including Assyria and Babylonia.

key_facts.text: Mesopotamia’s early Neolithic developments helped establish its association with the beginnings of agriculture and civilization.
Sargon of Akkad’s rise around 2350 BC began a long period characterized by successive empires and kingdoms.
By the early second millennium BC, Assyria was associated with northern Mesopotamia and Babylonia with the south.
The Achaemenid Empire under Cyrus the Great conquered Mesopotamia in 539 BC; Alexander the Great conquered it in 332 BC.
Later, parts of Mesopotamia were contested by the Roman and Sassanid Persian empires until the seventh-century Muslim conquests.

overview.text: The Mali Empire was a West African empire that lasted from about 1235 to 1610. It grew from a small Mandinka kingdom in the Manding region near the upper Niger River and became a major power after Sundiata Keita conquered the Sosso Empire. At its height, Mali was the largest empire in West Africa and influenced regional language, laws, and customs.

Mali’s rulers were called mansas. Mansa Musa became especially famous for his pilgrimage to Mecca from 1324 to 1326, during which his spending of gold caused significant inflation in Egypt. Mali remained sizeable into the 1500s, but neighboring states and the Songhai Empire weakened it; after a defeat near Djenne in 1599, the empire rapidly broke apart.

key_facts.text: Sundiata’s conquest of Sosso around 1235 marked Mali’s emergence as a major power; the Kouroukan Fouga is identified as its constitution.
The title mansa came into use for Mali’s kings or emperors after Sundiata’s death.
Mansa Musa took power around 1312 and was succeeded by Maghan I around 1337.
The traveler Ibn Battuta visited Mali during the 19-year reign of Mansa Suleyman.
After Mali’s final decline, the Keita dynasty retreated to Kangaba, where its members became provincial chiefs.

overview.text: Washington, D.C., officially the District of Columbia, is the federal capital of the United States and the country’s only federal district. It lies on the Potomac River across from Virginia and is surrounded by Maryland. As the seat of the federal government, it contains institutions such as the White House, U.S. Capitol, and Supreme Court Building.

The city hosts many national monuments and museums, located most prominently on or around the National Mall. Familiar examples include the Lincoln Memorial, Washington Monument, and Jefferson Memorial.

key_facts.text: The Residence Act of 1790 approved the capital district along the Potomac; the federal government moved from Philadelphia to Washington in 1800.
Pierre Charles L’Enfant designed the city in 1791. Its four quadrants meet at the Capitol Building.
The District of Columbia originally included land from Maryland and Virginia; Congress returned Alexandria and surrounding land to Virginia in 1846.
Washington has a locally elected mayor and council, but Congress retains power to overturn the district’s local laws.

overview.text: Washington is a U.S. state in the Pacific Northwest. It borders the Pacific Ocean, Oregon, Idaho, and the Canadian province of British Columbia. Olympia is the capital, while Seattle is the most populous city.

Washington’s geography ranges from temperate rainforests and mountain ranges in the west to a semi-arid basin in the east, center, and south, where intensive agriculture is practiced. Puget Sound is a glacier-carved Pacific inlet with islands, fjords, and bays. Mount Rainier is an active stratovolcano and the state’s highest elevation.

key_facts.text: The state’s name honors George Washington; “Washington state” distinguishes it from the national capital.
Washington entered the Union as the 42nd state in 1889, after being formed from the western part of Washington Territory.
Most residents live in the Seattle metropolitan area, a transportation, business, and industrial center on Puget Sound.
Lumber, agriculture, commercial fishing, and manufacturing are major parts of Washington’s economic profile.

overview.text: George Washington was a Virginia-born Founding Father who commanded the Continental Army during the American Revolutionary War. Despite shortages, low morale, and setbacks, he led Patriot forces toward victory and American independence. He is commonly remembered as the “Father of His Country.”

After presiding over the Constitutional Convention, Washington became the first U.S. president, serving from 1789 to 1797. He built a strong national government, pursued neutrality during the French Revolution, and established lasting presidential precedents. A Mount Vernon planter who owned enslaved people, he opposed slavery late in life and provided for their eventual manumission in his will.

key_facts.text: Washington commanded the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War.
After crossing the Delaware River, he won the battles of Trenton in late 1776 and Princeton in early 1777.
A combined French and American force under Washington won the decisive victory at Yorktown in 1781; the Treaty of Paris later recognized U.S. independence.
His 1796 Farewell Address emphasized national unity and warned against regionalism, partisanship, and foreign influence.

overview.text: Iceland is a Nordic island country in the North Atlantic, between the Arctic Ocean and the North Atlantic Ocean. It lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge between Europe and North America, and its capital and largest city is Reykjavík.

Iceland lies on a rift between tectonic plates, and its geologic activity includes geysers and frequent volcanic eruptions. Its interior is a volcanic plateau with sand and lava fields, mountains, glaciers, and glacial rivers flowing through lowlands to the sea.

key_facts.text: Iceland is described as Europe’s westernmost and most sparsely populated country.
The Gulf Stream gives Iceland a temperate climate despite its high latitude, just south of the Arctic Circle.
The country’s official language is Icelandic.

overview.text: Chlorine (Cl), atomic number 17, is a halogen located between fluorine and bromine in the periodic table. At room temperature it is a yellow-green gas, highly reactive and a strong oxidizing agent.

Its reactivity makes elemental chlorine useful in bleach, disinfectants, swimming-pool sanitation, and chemical manufacturing such as PVC production. At high concentrations it is poisonous and was first used as a poison-gas weapon in World War I. Chloride ions, however, are necessary to all known life.

key_facts.text: Chlorine has the highest electron affinity of any element and the third-highest electronegativity on the revised Pauling scale, behind oxygen and fluorine.
Commercial elemental chlorine is produced from brine by electrolysis, mainly through the chloralkali process.
Because chlorine is so reactive, it occurs in Earth’s crust as chloride compounds such as table salt rather than as free chlorine; seawater contains huge chloride reserves.
The name chlorine comes from the Ancient Greek word khlōrós, meaning “pale green,” a reference to its color.

overview.text: Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930) was a British writer and physician born in Edinburgh. He is best known for four novels and fifty-six short stories about Sherlock Holmes, a fictional consulting detective assisted by Dr. Watson.

Doyle’s first Holmes work was the novel A Study in Scarlet (1887), followed by stories and novels including “A Scandal in Bohemia” and The Hound of the Baskervilles. These works became milestones of crime fiction. He also created Professor Challenger, who first appeared in the speculative-fiction novel The Lost World.

key_facts.text: Doyle studied medicine, worked as a doctor and surgeon on sea voyages, and later opened an unsuccessful medical practice in Portsmouth.
The Strand Magazine published twenty-four monthly Holmes stories beginning with “A Scandal in Bohemia”; Doyle became one of the period’s most famous and well-paid authors.
Doyle had Holmes killed in “The Final Problem” (1893), but public outcry preceded the detective’s return in The Hound of the Baskervilles.
Beyond Holmes, Doyle wrote humorous stories about Brigadier Gerard, a fictional Napoleonic soldier.
Doyle personally investigated two closed cases, and both accused men were eventually exonerated.

overview.text: Joseph Stalin (born Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili) was a Soviet revolutionary and politician who led the Soviet Union from the mid-1920s until his death in 1953. He became its de facto dictator in the 1930s and shaped Soviet ideology through Marxism–Leninism and Stalinism.

His government replaced Lenin’s New Economic Policy with a centralized command economy, using collectivization and Five-Year Plans to pursue industrialization, while the Great Purge brought imprisonment and executions. In World War II, Stalin’s USSR signed a 1939 non-aggression pact with Nazi Germany; after Germany invaded in 1941, the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945. Postwar rivalry between Soviet-backed and U.S.-backed blocs became known as the Cold War.

key_facts.text: The Great Purge (1934–39) targeted people labeled “enemies of the working class”; more than a million were imprisoned and at least 700,000 executed.
During postwar reconstruction, the Soviet Union developed a nuclear weapon in 1949.
Stalin served as Communist Party General Secretary from 1922 to 1952 and as the Soviet Union’s Premier from 1941 to 1953.
After Stalin’s death, Nikita Khrushchev denounced him and began the process of de-Stalinization.

overview.text: Stephen Crane (1871–1900) was an American poet, novelist, and short-story writer associated with Realism, early American Naturalism, and Impressionism. His writing is marked by vivid intensity, distinctive dialects, irony, and themes of fear, spiritual crisis, and social isolation.

His 1893 novel Maggie: A Girl of the Streets is a Bowery tale generally considered the first work of American literary Naturalism. The Red Badge of Courage (1895), a Civil War novel, brought him international acclaim and became an American classic. He also wrote journalism and short fiction such as “The Open Boat,” “The Blue Hotel,” “The Bride Comes to Yellow Sky,” and The Monster.

key_facts.text: After the SS Commodore sank on his way to Cuba, Crane spent 30 hours adrift in a dinghy and later described the ordeal in “The Open Boat.”
Crane accepted work as a war correspondent and later covered conflicts in Greece.
His writing made a deep impression on Ernest Hemingway and is thought to have influenced the Modernists and the Imagists.
Crane died of tuberculosis in a Black Forest sanatorium in Germany at age 28, in 1900.

overview.text: The periodic table organizes chemical elements in rows called periods and columns called groups. It represents the periodic law: when elements are ordered by atomic number, their chemical properties recur in patterns. Elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical characteristics, making the table a central tool for understanding chemistry.

Dmitri Mendeleev produced the first generally accepted periodic table in 1869. Because some elements were not yet known, he left gaps and successfully predicted properties of some missing elements. Later discoveries about atomic numbers and quantum mechanics helped explain the table’s underlying structure.

key_facts.text: Metallic character generally increases down a group and from right to left across a period; nonmetallic character increases toward the upper right.
The table is divided into four roughly rectangular regions called blocks.
In 1945, Glenn T. Seaborg’s work led to recognizing the actinides as f-block rather than d-block elements.
By 2010, the first 118 elements were known, completing the table’s first seven rows; the heaviest elements still required further chemical characterization.
Elements beyond atomic number 94 are described as synthetic, meaning they must be produced artificially rather than obtained naturally.

overview.text: Jonathan Swift’s 1726 prose novel follows Lemuel Gulliver, an English traveler who visits strange, distant lands. Its imaginary societies—tiny Lilliput, giant-inhabited Brobdingnag, intellectually impractical Laputa, and the land of the rational Houyhnhnms—give Gulliver different perspectives on human behavior and social life.

The book is a satire: its fantastic voyages examine political quarrels, flawed customs, and weaknesses in human nature rather than serving only as a children’s adventure. Although often treated as children’s literature, it was written as political satire and remains a subject of literary study.

key_facts.text: The novel’s original title identifies it as a four-part account by Lemuel Gulliver, “First a Surgeon, and then a Captain of Several Ships.”
In Lilliput, Gulliver encounters tiny people involved in petty political disputes; in Brobdingnag, giants criticize European customs.
Laputa is associated with intellectuals whose ideas are impractical and disconnected from reality.
The Houyhnhnms are rational horses who live peacefully alongside savage, human-like creatures called Yahoos.
Swift also satirizes the popular literary genre of travelers’ tales, using imaginary voyages to critique society.

overview.text: Spain, officially the Kingdom of Spain, is a country in Southern and Western Europe occupying most of the Iberian Peninsula. Its territory also includes the Canary Islands in the eastern Atlantic, the Balearic Islands in the western Mediterranean, and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa.

Peninsular Spain borders France, Andorra, and Portugal and meets the Atlantic Ocean, the Bay of Biscay, and the Mediterranean Sea. Spanish is the official language nationally, while other regional languages have co-official status in their respective autonomous communities.

key_facts.text: Madrid is Spain’s capital and largest city; Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Bilbao, and Málaga are among its other major urban areas.
Spain’s North African territories give it borders involving Morocco; its peninsular territory is also near Gibraltar.
Spain is a secular parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.
The country is commonly associated geographically with both the Atlantic-facing west and the Mediterranean-facing east and south.

overview.text: Spain, officially the Kingdom of Spain, occupies most of the Iberian Peninsula and also includes islands and territories in North Africa. Its history includes Roman Hispania, the Visigothic Kingdom, Muslim-ruled Al-Andalus, and the Christian kingdoms that gradually reclaimed the peninsula. The union of Castile and Aragon in 1479 is often treated as Spain’s de facto national unification.

During the Age of Discovery, Spain explored and conquered in the New World, completed the first circumnavigation of the globe, and built a large empire connected by global trade in precious metals. Major later turning points include the Peninsular War, the loss of most American colonies, the Spanish Civil War, Francoist dictatorship, and the eventual restoration of democracy.

key_facts.text: The 1479 dynastic union of the Crowns of Castile and Aragon under the Catholic Monarchs is often viewed as Spain’s de facto unification.
The Reconquista culminated in the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada, completing the expulsion of Islamic rule from the peninsula.
The 18th-century Nueva Planta decrees centralized Spain under the Bourbons and strengthened royal authority.
The Peninsular War against Napoleonic forces lasted from 1808 to 1814; Spain later lost most of its American colonies.
The Spanish Civil War lasted from 1936 to 1939 and was followed by Francoist dictatorship from 1939 to 1975.

overview.text: New Zealand, also called Aotearoa, is an island country in the southwestern Pacific, east of Australia across the Tasman Sea. Its two main landmasses—the North Island and South Island—lie alongside more than 700 smaller islands. Tectonic uplift and volcanic eruptions created varied terrain, including the Southern Alps. Wellington is the capital, while Auckland is the most populous city.

Polynesians settled the islands between about 1280 and 1350 and developed a distinctive Māori culture. European exploration followed with Abel Tasman’s 1642 sighting and James Cook’s 1769 landing and mapping. The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 by British representatives and Māori chiefs; later colonial conflicts involved extensive Māori land loss.

key_facts.text: The Māori names for the main islands are Te Ika-a-Māui (North Island) and Te Waipounamu (South Island).
New Zealand’s islands were the last large habitable landmass settled by humans.
English, Māori, and New Zealand Sign Language are the country’s official languages.

overview.text: Mass density—also called volumetric mass density or specific mass—is a substance’s mass divided by its volume. It is commonly represented by the Greek letter ρ (rho). Density is an intensive property: increasing the amount of a substance increases its mass, not its density.

Density helps compare materials and is relevant to buoyancy, purity, and packaging. Relative density, or specific gravity, compares a material’s density with that of a standard material, usually water; a value below one relative to water indicates that the substance floats in water.

key_facts.text: Density is not the same as weight per unit volume; weight per unit volume is more specifically called specific weight.
Density changes with temperature and pressure, with generally much larger changes in gases than in solids or liquids.
Heating the bottom of a fluid can cause convection: the warmed, less-dense fluid rises relative to denser unheated material.
The reciprocal of density is sometimes called specific volume, a term used in thermodynamics.
Osmium is identified as the densest known element at standard conditions for temperature and pressure.

overview.text: Paul, also called Saul of Tarsus, was a first-century Christian apostle who spread Jesus’ teachings and founded Christian communities in Asia Minor and Europe. He was not one of the Twelve Apostles, but he became an important missionary figure of the Apostolic Age. Paul’s letters and the Acts of the Apostles are the main sources for his life and work.

According to Acts, Paul had persecuted Jesus’ followers before experiencing a vision, temporary blindness, healing, and baptism while traveling to Damascus. He then proclaimed Jesus as the Jewish messiah and Son of God and made three missionary journeys to non-Jewish communities. His writings became major foundations for Christian theology, although scholars disagree about which letters he actually wrote.

key_facts.text: Paul claimed to have encountered Jesus after the resurrection, though he had not known Jesus during his lifetime.
Whether non-Jewish converts should be circumcised was one issue Paul debated in the early church.
Fourteen of the New Testament’s 27 books have traditionally been attributed to Paul, but only seven are undisputed by scholars as authentic.
Lutheran and other Christian traditions have often interpreted Paul as teaching salvation through faith rather than adherence to Jewish law.

overview.text: A flower is the reproductive structure of a flowering plant. Its typical design has four rings: sepals support the flower, petals often attract pollinators, stamens present pollen, and the female gynoecium receives pollen and helps direct it toward the egg.

Pollination moves pollen between male and female parts, sometimes with help from animals, wind, or water. After fertilization, the developing seed contains an embryo, while the flower’s female part forms a fruit that protects the seed and can aid its dispersal.

key_facts.text: A group of flowers is called an inflorescence.
Pollination can occur between different plants or within the same plant, including within one flower.
Flowers first evolved roughly 150–190 million years ago, during the Jurassic Period.
Flower structure, including size, shape, color, and scent, varies greatly among flowering plants.

overview.text: Nathaniel Hawthorne (1804–1864) was an American novelist and short-story writer whose work often examines history, morality, and religion. Much of his writing centers on New England, and many works have an anti-Puritan inspiration. His fiction is associated with the Romantic movement, particularly dark Romanticism, and often explores the inherent evil and sin of humanity through moral messages and psychological complexity. Together, these features connect Hawthorne’s New England settings with questions of belief, sin, and moral conduct.

key_facts.text: Hawthorne was born in Salem, Massachusetts, and graduated from Bowdoin College in 1825.
In 1837, he collected short stories previously published in periodicals as Twice-Told Tales.
His first work was the novel Fanshawe, published in 1828; he later tried to suppress it because he considered it inferior to his later writing.
The Scarlet Letter was published in 1850, followed by a succession of other novels.

overview.text: German (Deutsch) is a West Germanic language in the Indo-European family, spoken mainly in Western and Central Europe. It is the majority and an official or co-official language in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and Liechtenstein; it is also official in Luxembourg, Belgium, and South Tyrol, and recognized as a national language in Namibia.

German is closely related to English, Dutch, Afrikaans, Frisian, and Scots, while also sharing vocabulary with Scandinavian languages. Modern German developed from Old High German, ultimately from Proto-Germanic. It has influenced philosophy, theology, science, and technology, and has three standard varieties: German, Austrian, and Swiss Standard German.

key_facts.text: German grammar uses four cases—nominative, accusative, genitive, and dative—and three grammatical genders: masculine, feminine, and neuter.
German has a broad range of dialects, some of which receive regional or national government protection.
Most German vocabulary comes from the Germanic branch of Indo-European; later borrowings include words from Latin, Greek, French, and especially modern English.
The Council for German Orthography is the main international body that regulates German spelling.

overview.text: A leaf is a principal appendage of the stem in a vascular plant, usually growing laterally above ground and specialized for photosynthesis. Its mostly green color comes from chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy from the Sun. Most leaves are flattened into a blade, or lamina, with distinct upper and lower surfaces. Pores called stomata exchange gases, while palisade mesophyll is the primary photosynthetic tissue in most leaves. Collectively, leaves are called foliage.

key_facts.text: Leaf shape, size, texture, and color vary among plant species.
Broad, flat leaves with complex venation are called megaphylls; plants bearing them are called megaphyllous or broad-leaved.
Lycopod leaves are microphylls: simple leaves with a single vein and a different evolutionary origin from megaphylls.
Leaves occur in varied forms and settings: aquatic leaves may be submerged, succulent leaves may be thick and juicy, and bulb scales may grow below ground.
Some leaf-like structures are actually flattened stems or leaf stems, including phylloclades, cladodes, and phyllodes.

overview.text: Dungeons & Dragons (D&D or DnD) is a fantasy tabletop role-playing game created by Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson and first published by TSR in 1974. Unlike a conventional wargame, it has players each control a character in a fictional setting, while a Dungeon Master (DM) referees, narrates, and portrays the setting’s non-player characters. Players usually cooperate as a party, solving problems, exploring, and fighting across multiple sessions.

Its open-ended structure makes the group’s decisions central: the DM applies or interprets rules, and dice resolve uncertain actions such as attacks, damage, and difficult tasks. Characters are defined by abilities, species, and class, then generally grow through experience and levels. A single quest is an adventure; linked adventures form a campaign, which may use a published setting or a world created by the DM. D&D matters because its publication is commonly associated with the beginning of modern role-playing games and it influenced role-playing video games.

key_facts.text: D&D developed from miniature wargames; a variation of the 1971 game Chainmail served as its initial rules system.
In 1977, the game split into Basic Dungeons & Dragons and the more rules-heavy Advanced Dungeons & Dragons. The 2000 third edition formed the basis of the d20 System.

A twenty-sided die can help determine whether an attack hits, while other polyhedral dice can determine damage. For risky tasks, outcomes can depend on ability scores, skills, and the task’s Difficulty Class, with relevant ability bonuses added.
The main rules are presented in the Player’s Handbook, Dungeon Master’s Guide, and Monster Manual; play also requires character sheets and polyhedral dice.
A campaign can take place in settings such as Greyhawk, Dragonlance, Forgotten Realms, Ravenloft, or Eberron, or in a world invented by the DM.

overview.text: Jorge Luis Borges was an Argentine short-story writer, essayist, poet, and translator who became a major figure in Spanish-language and international literature. His collections Ficciones and El Aleph, published in the 1940s, explore dreams, labyrinths, chance, infinity, archives, mirrors, fictional authors, and mythology.

Borges’s writing connects imaginative storytelling with philosophical questions and fantasy. His work contributed to philosophical literature and the fantasy genre, while also influencing magical realism in twentieth-century Latin American literature.

key_facts.text: Born in Buenos Aires, Borges moved to Switzerland with his family in 1914, studied at the Collège de Genève, and returned to Argentina in 1921.
After returning to Argentina, he published poems and essays in surrealist literary journals and worked as a librarian and public lecturer.
In 1955, Borges became director of the National Public Library and a professor of English literature at the University of Buenos Aires.
He shared the first International Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett in 1961, helping bring him wider international attention.

overview.text: Margaret Mead (1901–1978) was an American cultural anthropologist, author, and speaker who became a frequent presence in mid-twentieth-century mass media. Her first ethnographic book, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), examined adolescence and sexuality and brought her national visibility.

In Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies (1935), Mead explored gender roles and personality through fieldwork in Papua New Guinea. She is regarded as a founding figure in public anthropology, though her ethnography of the South Pacific and Melanesia became the subject of vigorous academic debate.

key_facts.text: Her research included work with the Omaha people and in Manus, Papua New Guinea, and Bali; she later returned to Papua New Guinea, Bali, and Samoa for longitudinal studies.
Mead was curator of ethnology at the American Museum of Natural History from 1946 to 1969.
Her book Keep Your Powder Dry used ethnographic examination of American life to support mobilization for World War II.
She served as president of the American Association for the Advancement of Science in 1975.

overview.text: Malcolm X (born Malcolm Little, later known as el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz) was an African American Muslim minister and civil-rights activist who became a prominent public figure during the U.S. civil-rights movement. After joining the Nation of Islam in prison, he became its leading public spokesman, advocating Black empowerment and separation from white Americans while criticizing Martin Luther King Jr.’s emphasis on nonviolence and integration.

In the 1960s, Malcolm X broke with the Nation of Islam, embraced Sunni Islam after making the Hajj to Mecca, and founded organizations including the Organization of Afro-American Unity. His public views consequently changed over time, and he moved toward a broader connection with the mainstream civil-rights movement. He was assassinated in New York City on February 21, 1965.

key_facts.text: The name “X” symbolized his unknown African ancestral surname and rejected “Little,” which he associated with a slaveholder’s name.
He served as a Nation of Islam spokesman from 1952 until his transition to Sunni Islam in 1964, after first encountering the movement in prison.
After the Hajj, he adopted the name el-Hajj Malik el-Shabazz, roughly meaning “The Pilgrim Malcolm the Patriarch.”
His autobiography, produced in collaboration with Alex Haley, was published posthumously in 1965.
Malcolm X’s ideas strongly influenced the Black Power movement, and streets and schools in the United States were later named in his honor.

overview.text: Harriet Elisabeth Beecher Stowe (1811–1896) was an American author and abolitionist. Her 1852 novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin depicts the harsh conditions experienced by enslaved African Americans, giving her work a clear antislavery focus.

The book connected literature with public debate over slavery: it attracted a mass audience in the United States and Great Britain, energized antislavery forces in the American North, and provoked anger in the South.

key_facts.text: Uncle Tom’s Cabin reached millions as both a novel and a play.
Stowe wrote more than 30 books, including novels, three travel memoirs, and collections of articles and letters.
Her public role included taking positions and participating in debates on social issues beyond her fiction.

overview.text: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself. Thus 2, 3, and 5 are prime, while 4 and 6 are composite; 1 is not prime. Every natural number greater than 1 is either prime or has a unique factorization into primes, apart from the order of the factors. This makes primes fundamental building blocks of number theory.
There are infinitely many primes, but no known simple formula separates them from composite numbers. The prime number theorem models their distribution among large numbers statistically.

key_facts.text: 2 is the only even prime; every other prime is odd. In decimal notation, primes greater than 5 can end only in 1, 3, 7, or 9.

Goldbach’s conjecture says every even integer greater than 2 is the sum of two primes. The twin prime conjecture says infinitely many prime pairs differ by 2; both are unresolved mathematical questions.
Public-key cryptography relies on the practical difficulty of factoring large numbers into their prime factors.

overview.text: Wyoming is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. Its western half is dominated by Rocky Mountain ranges and rangelands, while its eastern half is high-elevation prairie known as the High Plains. Cheyenne is the state capital and most populous city.

Wyoming’s federal lands include Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks, as well as national forests, monuments, and recreation areas. The state is generally drier and windier than other states, with both semiarid and continental climate patterns.

key_facts.text: Wyoming entered the Union as the 44th state on July 10, 1890.
As a territory, Wyoming granted women the right to vote in 1869; in 1890, it became the first state to allow women citizens to vote. Its nickname is “The Equality State.”
Tourism and mineral extraction—including coal, natural gas, oil, and trona—are central parts of Wyoming’s economy.
The Transcontinental Railroad reached southern Wyoming in 1867, helping establish towns including Cheyenne.

overview.text: René Descartes (1596–1650) was a French philosopher, mathematician, and scientist whose work was foundational to mathematics and modern philosophy. He linked geometry with algebra to create analytic geometry and developed a systematic method of inquiry influential in early modern philosophy. His work addressed epistemology, philosophy of mind, and metaphysics, and his best-known philosophical statement was “I think, therefore I am.” His Meditations on First Philosophy continues to be studied, and his work influenced the development of modern science.

key_facts.text: The Cartesian coordinate system is named after Descartes.
Descartes was a key figure in the Scientific Revolution.
He deliberately set his views apart from earlier philosophers rather than simply accepting their authority.
His analytic geometry helped facilitate the later development of infinitesimal calculus and analysis.

overview.text: World War I, also called the First World War or Great War, was a global conflict fought from 28 July 1914 to 11 November 1918 between the Allied and Central Powers. Its causes included Germany’s rise, imperial rivalries, alliance blocs, and an arms race. The assassination of Austro-Hungarian heir Franz Ferdinand by Gavrilo Princip helped trigger the crisis that led Austria-Hungary to declare war on Serbia. Germany’s invasion of Belgium brought the United Kingdom into the war; the Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers, while Japan and Italy joined the Allies.

The Western Front became a near-continuous line of fortified trenches, while the Eastern Front was more dynamic. The war also saw the first large-scale use of machine guns, artillery, aircraft, chemical weapons, and tanks. Its political consequences included the collapse of four empires, new national boundaries, and the creation of the League of Nations to help maintain world peace.

key_facts.text: Major battles at Verdun, the Somme, and Passchendaele failed to break the stalemate on the Western Front.
The United States joined the Allies in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare against Atlantic shipping.
After the Bolsheviks seized power in Russia in October 1917, Soviet Russia signed an armistice with the Central Powers in December and a separate peace in March 1918.
The Treaty of Versailles required Germany to surrender significant territory, disarm, and pay large reparations.
The conflict caused an estimated 15 to 22 million deaths, including deaths connected to war crimes and genocides.

overview.text: West Side Story is a musical conceived by Jerome Robbins, with music by Leonard Bernstein, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim, and a book by Arthur Laurents.
