Inspired by Romeo and Juliet, it relocates the tragic romance to the mid-1950s Upper West Side of Manhattan, a multiracial blue-collar neighborhood.

Tony, a former Jet, falls in love with Maria, the sister of Sharks leader Bernardo, while the Jets and Sharks compete for control of their neighborhood. Its dark subject matter, sophisticated music, and extended dance scenes helped mark a turning point in musical theatre.

key_facts.text: The Jets are white, while the Sharks are recent migrants from Puerto Rico; police attempt to keep order between the rival gangs.
The original 1957 Broadway production was directed and choreographed by Robbins and marked Sondheim’s Broadway debut.
The 1961 film adaptation, co-directed by Robert Wise and Robbins, won ten Academy Awards, including Best Picture.

overview.text: Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician and journalist who became the country’s fascist dictator, known as Il Duce. He founded the fascist movement in 1919, became prime minister after the March on Rome in 1922, and transformed the Kingdom of Italy into a one-party totalitarian dictatorship.

Mussolini’s rule involved aggressive expansion and increasing cooperation with Nazi Germany. Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia helped lead to the Rome–Berlin Axis, and Mussolini entered World War II on Germany’s side in 1940. After defeats, he was removed in 1943, later headed a German-backed puppet regime in northern Italy, and was executed by partisans in 1945.

key_facts.text: Before becoming a fascist, Mussolini was a radical socialist journalist. He was expelled from the Italian Socialist Party after supporting military intervention in World War I.
The 1929 Lateran Treaty established Vatican City.
The League of Nations condemned Italy’s invasion of Ethiopia, helping push Mussolini closer to Adolf Hitler; the Rome–Berlin Axis formed in 1936.
After Mussolini’s removal in 1943, German forces rescued him and made him the figurehead of the Italian Social Republic, a collaborationist regime in German-occupied northern Italy.

overview.text: “The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock” is T. S. Eliot’s first professionally published poem. It follows the shifting thoughts of its title character through stream of consciousness and takes the form of a dramatic interior monologue. Prufrock is an isolated urban man unable to act decisively, making his private hesitation a central feature of the poem’s Modernist perspective.

Eliot began writing the poem in 1910; it appeared in Poetry magazine in 1915 and was later collected in Prufrock and Other Observations. Its unusual style helped mark a movement away from late-19th-century Romantic and Georgian poetry toward Modernism.

key_facts.text: The poem’s structure reflects Eliot’s reading of Dante and includes references to the Bible, Shakespeare, Andrew Marvell, and French Symbolist writers.
Prufrock dwells on physical and intellectual inertia, missed opportunities, and a perceived lack of spiritual progress.
Major emotional concerns include regret, embarrassment, longing, sexual frustration, ageing, mortality, and a sense of decay.
At publication, the poem was considered outlandish; it later became recognized as a major work of modern literature.

source.title: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock

overview.text: The Big Bang is a physical theory describing the universe’s expansion from an early state of very high density and temperature. As the universe expanded, it cooled, allowing subatomic particles and then atoms to form; primordial hydrogen, helium, and lithium later helped form stars and galaxies through gravity, aided by dark matter. Associated evidence includes light-element abundances, galaxy redshifts, the cosmic microwave background (CMB), and large-scale structure.

Modern Big Bang cosmology also incorporates cosmic inflation, an early phase of accelerated expansion used to explain the universe’s observed uniformity and address the horizon and flatness problems. Supernova redshift measurements show that expansion is accelerating, an observation attributed to dark energy.

key_facts.text: The CMB was discovered in 1964; its uniformity across the sky and energy spectrum fit models of a hot, dense early universe.
In the modern picture, inflation is followed by reheating, which converts the energy driving inflation into a hot, dense plasma.
Alexander Friedmann derived mathematical equations for an expanding universe in 1922, while Edwin Hubble published an early empirical observation of expansion in 1929.
Remaining unresolved issues include the matter–antimatter imbalance, the nature of dark matter, and the origin of dark energy.

overview.text: Freyja is a Norse goddess and a member of the Vanir, alongside her twin brother Freyr and father Njörðr. She is associated with love, beauty, fertility, war, gold, and seiðr, a form of magic concerned with seeing and influencing the future. Modern forms of her name include Freya, Freyia, and Freja.

Freyja rules Fólkvangr, a heavenly field where she receives half of those who die in battle; Odin receives the other half in Valhalla. Her hall is Sessrúmnir. Recognizable symbols include Brísingamen, a chariot drawn by cats, the boar Hildisvíni, and a falcon-feather cloak. Her stories appear in Eddic and skaldic poetry, sagas, and later Scandinavian folklore.

key_facts.text: Freyja’s husband, Óðr, is frequently absent; she searches for him under assumed names and is said to shed red-gold tears.
Freyja has numerous names, including Gefn, Hörn, Mardöll, Sýr, Vanadís, and Valfreyja.
Scholars have connected Freyja with the valkyries, female figures associated with choosing the slain on battlefields.
Freyja’s name influenced Scandinavian plant names, although some were later changed to honor the Virgin Mary during Christianization.

overview.text: The Quran (also spelled Qur’an or Koran) is Islam’s central religious text. Muslims believe it is God’s revelation, delivered orally to Muhammad through the angel Gabriel over about 23 years. It is arranged in 114 chapters called surahs, each made up of verses called ayahs.

The Quran presents itself as a guide for humanity and alludes to narratives also found in biblical and apocryphal traditions, often emphasizing their moral lessons. Its Arabic recitation is central to Muslim prayer; tajwid refers to the specialized prosody used for reciting it, while tafsir is commentary that explains its verses.

key_facts.text: Beyond its religious role, the Quran is regarded as a major work of Arabic literature and has significantly influenced the Arabic language.
According to Islamic tradition, Muhammad’s companions both memorized revelations and recorded them; after his death, Abu Bakr ordered a compilation, and Uthman established a standard version.
Qira’at are canonical oral readings of the Quran. They include minor differences in wording and nuance while preserving its core message.
Hadith are traditions about Muhammad’s words and actions that provide additional guidance alongside the Quran for most Islamic schools of thought.

overview.text: Percussion instruments make sound when struck or scraped by a beater, by hand, or against another instrument; rattles and rubbing are also included among percussion actions. “Percussion” is a practical family label rather than one fully systematic scientific class: instruments in it can belong to idiophone, membranophone, aerophone, or chordophone groups.

In orchestral music, the percussion section commonly includes timpani, snare and bass drums, tambourine, cymbals, and triangle. It may also include whistles, sirens, or a blown conch shell. Thus, the orchestral section gathers instruments that do not all belong to the same scientific class.

key_facts.text: Timpani, snare drum, bass drum, and tambourine are membranophones, while cymbals and triangle are idiophones.
Applying percussive techniques directly to the human body is called body percussion.
Glockenspiel and xylophone are keyboard percussion instruments even though they do not have piano keyboards; celesta is normally outside the percussion section.
The percussion family is believed to include the oldest musical instruments.

overview.text: Joseph Conrad (born Józef Teodor Konrad Korzeniowski) was a Polish-British novelist and story writer who mastered English prose despite not speaking English fluently until his twenties. His fiction often uses nautical settings to depict people facing crises in a world he presents as indifferent, difficult to understand, and lacking moral order. Writing near the peak of the British Empire, Conrad drew on Poland’s experience under occupying empires and on his own merchant-navy service to examine imperialism, colonialism, and the human psyche.

key_facts.text: Critics variously classify Conrad as a literary impressionist or an early modernist, while also noting elements of nineteenth-century realism in his work.
Lord Jim exemplifies Conrad’s anti-heroic characters; his narrative style and such characters influenced numerous authors.
His fiction drew on his experiences in the French and British merchant navies.
Conrad lived from 1857 to 1924.

overview.text: π (pi) is the circle constant: for any circle, circumference divided by diameter has the same value, approximately 3.141592653589793.... It appears in formulas throughout mathematics and physics. In notation, lowercase π denotes this constant, while capital Π denotes a product of a sequence, analogous to capital Σ for summation.

key_facts.text: π is irrational: it cannot be expressed exactly as a ratio of integers, and its decimal expansion neither ends nor settles into a repeating pattern.
π is transcendental, meaning it is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with rational coefficients. This implies that squaring the circle with compass and straightedge is impossible.
Around 250 BC, Archimedes developed an algorithm that could approximate π to arbitrary accuracy.

overview.text: Margaret Hilda Thatcher (1925–2013) was a British stateswoman who led the Conservative Party from 1975 to 1990 and served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1979 to 1990. She was the first woman to hold that office.

Her political and economic program, known as Thatcherism, emphasized individual liberty, privatizing state-owned companies, and reducing trade-union power. A Soviet journalist called her the “Iron Lady,” a nickname associated with her uncompromising leadership style.

key_facts.text: Before becoming prime minister, Thatcher studied chemistry at Oxford, worked briefly as a research chemist, and was elected to Parliament for Finchley in 1959.
Victory in the 1982 Falklands War helped restore her popularity and was followed by a Conservative landslide in the 1983 election.
She survived a 1984 assassination attempt by the Provisional IRA in the Brighton hotel bombing and won a political victory during the 1984–85 miners’ strike.
Thatcher resigned as prime minister and Conservative leader in 1990 after a leadership challenge; John Major succeeded her as prime minister.

overview.text: The Venus de Milo, also called Aphrodite of Melos, is an ancient Greek marble sculpture from the Hellenistic period, generally dated to the second century BC. It depicts Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love; Venus is her Roman counterpart. The statue was discovered on the island of Milos in 1820.

Made of Parian marble and standing over two meters tall, the sculpture is missing both arms, whose original positions remain uncertain. Its fame expanded through photographs and copies, and it influenced nineteenth-century art and the early twentieth-century Surrealist movement.

key_facts.text: The sculpture has been attributed to Alexandros of Antioch on the basis of a now-lost inscription, but both the inscription’s name and its connection to the statue are disputed.
A marble hand holding an apple was found near the statue; recent scientific analysis supports the view that the hand belonged to the sculpture, possibly connecting it with the apple of discord.
The Venus de Milo has been displayed at the Louvre Museum since 1821 and became a central work in its antiquities collection after the Napoleonic Wars.
Earlier scholars dated the statue to the early fourth century BC, but later interpretation placed it in the Hellenistic period; some scholars subsequently judged it more critically.

overview.text: Madagascar, officially the Republic of Madagascar, is an island country in the Indian Ocean off southeastern Africa. It includes the main island of Madagascar and smaller peripheral islands; its capital and largest city is Antananarivo.

Madagascar’s long separation from other landmasses allowed its plants and animals to evolve in relative isolation. More than 90% of its wildlife is endemic, meaning it occurs naturally nowhere else, and the country is classified as a biodiversity hotspot.

key_facts.text: Madagascar is the world’s fourth-largest island and the second-largest island country.
The island separated from Africa about 180 million years ago and from the Indian subcontinent about 90 million years ago.
France annexed Madagascar in 1897; Madagascar became independent in 1960.
Malagasy and French are the country’s official languages.

overview.text: William Faulkner (1897–1962) was an American writer whose novels and short stories are closely associated with Yoknapatawpha County, a fictional Mississippi setting modeled on Lafayette County, where he spent much of his life. This invented county is one of the central associations of his writing.

His works include Sartoris, The Sound and the Fury, As I Lay Dying, Light in August, and Absalom, Absalom! Faulkner received the 1949 Nobel Prize in Literature for his contribution to the modern American novel, making him a major recognition point in American literature.

key_facts.text: Faulkner was born in New Albany and raised in Oxford, Mississippi.
He wrote his first novel, Soldiers' Pay (1925), after moving to New Orleans.
Sartoris (1927) was his first work set in Yoknapatawpha County.
Two of his works, A Fable and The Reivers, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

overview.text: Winston Churchill was a British statesman, military officer, and writer whose career included long service in Parliament and leadership in both Conservative and Liberal governments. He became prime minister in May 1940, led a national government through Britain’s Second World War effort, and returned to office in 1951 after serving as opposition leader.

His career also connects World War II with the early Cold War: in the 1930s he urged rearmament against Nazi Germany, and later warned of an “iron curtain” marking Soviet influence in Europe. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953.

key_facts.text: Before entering high office, Churchill served in the British Army, became a war correspondent and author, and was elected a Conservative MP in 1900.
As First Lord of the Admiralty during World War I, he oversaw the disastrous Dardanelles attack, connected with the Gallipoli campaign; he resigned from government in 1915.
After the Conservatives lost the 1945 election, Churchill became Leader of the Opposition. He lost the 1950 election but returned as prime minister in 1951.
Churchill remained an MP until 1964 and was given a state funeral after his death in 1965.

overview.text: Charles Robert Darwin (1809–1882) was an English naturalist, geologist, and biologist whose work shaped evolutionary biology. He proposed that all species descended from a common ancestor and explained evolutionary branching through natural selection, in which the struggle for existence has an effect comparable to artificial selection in selective breeding. This framework explains the unity and diversity of life.

During the five-year HMS Beagle voyage (1831–1836), Darwin made observations that supported Charles Lyell’s idea of gradual geological change and later investigated the distribution of wildlife and fossils. He devised natural selection in 1838. After Wallace sent an essay describing the same idea, they jointly submitted their theories in 1858; Darwin published his theory in On the Origin of Species in 1859.

key_facts.text: On the Origin of Species (1859) presented Darwin’s theory with compelling evidence. The Descent of Man (1871) examined human evolution and sexual selection.
Darwin’s work on coral reefs and barnacles earned him the Royal Medal in 1853; The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs (1842) was his first scientific work.
Natural selection initially faced competing explanations. Broad scientific consensus that it was evolution’s basic mechanism emerged with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s–1950s.

overview.text: San Francisco, officially the City and County of San Francisco, is known for steep rolling hills, varied architecture, and neighborhoods including Chinatown and the Mission. Familiar landmarks include the Golden Gate Bridge, cable cars, and Alcatraz. The city also has museums, music organizations, and performing-arts institutions.

Its history includes Indigenous Yelamu Ohlone habitation, settlements from New Spain in 1776, rapid growth during the 1849 California Gold Rush, and rebuilding after the 1906 earthquake and fire. In the wider Bay Area, San Francisco is associated with technology, universities, and transportation links to surrounding communities.

key_facts.text: The Presidio of San Francisco and Mission San Francisco de Asís were established on June 29, 1776, by settlers from New Spain; both names honor Francis of Assisi.
The 1849 California Gold Rush drove rapid growth, and San Francisco became a consolidated city-county in 1856.
After the 1906 earthquake and fire destroyed three-quarters of the city, San Francisco was rebuilt and hosted the Panama–Pacific International Exposition in 1915.
The city’s postwar cultural history includes the beatnik and hippie countercultures, the Summer of Love, and the gay-rights movement.
San Francisco’s light rail and bus network, together with BART and Caltrain, connects nearly every part of the city with the wider region.

overview.text: Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was the 26th president of the United States, serving from 1901 to 1909 after William McKinley’s assassination. A leader of the Progressive movement, he promoted the “Square Deal,” which supported breaking up corporate trusts, regulating railroads, and improving food and drug standards.

Roosevelt had already gained national attention by leading the Rough Riders in Cuba during the 1898 war against Spain. As president, he championed conservation, expanded the Navy, began the Panama Canal project, and used American diplomacy and naval power more actively abroad.

key_facts.text: Roosevelt wrote The Naval War of 1812, helping establish his reputation as a historian and writer before his presidency.
His antitrust campaigns earned him the nickname “the Trust Buster.”
He sent the Great White Fleet on a round-the-world voyage to display U.S. naval power.
Roosevelt received the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize for helping end the Russo-Japanese War.
After losing the 1912 Republican nomination, he ran for president under the Bull Moose Party; the Republican split helped Woodrow Wilson win.

overview.text: Inspector Javert is a fictional character and main antagonist in Victor Hugo’s 1862 novel Les Misérables. A former prison guard who becomes a police inspector, Javert represents a rigid, authoritarian view of justice. He pursues the protagonist Jean Valjean after Valjean violates parole and steals from Petit Gervais, making Javert one of the novel’s central forces of conflict.

key_facts.text: The novel gives Javert no first name.
His defining traits include legalism, authoritarianism, and a lack of empathy toward criminals.
Javert’s career progresses from prison guard to police inspector.
The source gives his presumed birth year as 1780 and his death date as June 7, 1832.

overview.text: Robots are programmable machines that automatically perform complex sequences of actions, using internal or external control. They may be autonomous or semi-autonomous, and most are designed for function rather than a humanlike appearance. Robotics is the field concerned with designing, building, operating, and applying robots, including their control systems, sensors, and information processing.

Robots matter because they can handle repetitive or dangerous work in manufacturing and extreme environments. The field includes industrial and medical machines, drones, swarm robots, and microscopic devices—not only humanoid machines. Their growing use also raises concerns about technological unemployment and the ethics of military applications.

key_facts.text: Ancient societies had accounts of automata: configurable machines designed to imitate humans or animals. Industrial-era advances brought practical automated, remote-controlled, and wireless-controlled machines.
William Grey Walter created electronic autonomous robots in Bristol in 1948, while computer numerical control machine tools also emerged in the late 1940s.
George Devol built Unimate, described as the first commercial digital programmable robot, in 1954. General Motors bought it in 1961 for lifting hot metal from die-casting machines.
Bio-inspired robotics draws ideas from nature, and soft robotics developed as a newer branch of the field.

overview.text: Wilfred Edward Salter Owen was an English poet and soldier, and one of the leading poets of the First World War. His war poetry portrays the horrors of trench combat and gas warfare, contrasting with the confidently patriotic verse written by some earlier war poets, including Rupert Brooke.

Among Owen’s best-known poems are “Dulce et Decorum Est,” “Anthem for Doomed Youth,” “Futility,” “Insensibility,” and “Strange Meeting.” His poetry was strongly influenced by his mentor Siegfried Sassoon.

key_facts.text: Owen lived from 18 March 1893 to 4 November 1918.
He was killed in action at age 25, one week before the Armistice.
Most of his best-known works were published after his death.

overview.text: Henrik Johan Ibsen (1828–1906) was a Norwegian playwright and a leading figure in nineteenth-century drama. He pioneered theatrical realism, using drama to examine social life and moral questions behind respectable appearances. His major plays include Brand, Peer Gynt, A Doll’s House, Ghosts, An Enemy of the People, The Wild Duck, Hedda Gabler, and The Master Builder.

Ibsen established himself as a theater director in Norway during the 1850s and gained international recognition with Brand and Peer Gynt in the 1860s. Many of his later plays use realistic prose, Norwegian settings, and bourgeois environments while challenging contemporary expectations about family morality and propriety.

key_facts.text: Peer Gynt is an early verse play with strong surreal elements; afterward, Ibsen shifted to realistic prose.
Ibsen lived mainly in Italy and Germany for 27 years before moving to Christiania, now Oslo, in 1891.
Critics frequently rate The Wild Duck and Rosmersholm highly, while Ibsen himself regarded Emperor and Galilean as his masterpiece.
Ibsen influenced writers including George Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde, and James Joyce.

overview.text: The Himalayas are a mountain range in Asia separating the plains of the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau. They include Mount Everest, the highest peak on Earth, and more than 100 peaks above 7,200 meters. The range formed as the Indian tectonic plate collided with the Eurasian plate, and it extends in a long west-northwest-to-east-southeast arc.

The range spans Nepal, India, China, Bhutan, and Pakistan. Rivers including the Indus, Ganges, and Tsangpo–Brahmaputra rise nearby, while the Himalayas have strongly shaped South Asian and Tibetan cultures; many peaks are sacred in Hinduism and Buddhism.

key_facts.text: The Himalayas are bordered by the Karakoram and Hindu Kush to the northwest, the Tibetan Plateau to the north, and the Indo-Gangetic Plain to the south.
Several summits are off-limits to climbers, including Kangchenjunga from the Indian side, Gangkhar Puensum, Machapuchare, and Nanda Devi.
Mount Kailash is nearby but belongs to the geologically distinct Tibetan Transhimalaya, not the Himalayas proper.
The Himalayan arc is about 2,400 kilometers long; its width ranges from about 350 kilometers in the west to 151 kilometers in the east.

overview.text: Vikings were seafaring people from Scandinavia—present-day Denmark, Norway, and Sweden—who from the late 8th through the late 11th centuries raided, traded, and settled across parts of Europe. Their longships carried them as far as the Mediterranean, North Africa, the Middle East, Greenland, and Vinland, a place identified with present-day Newfoundland.

They founded settlements and governments in areas including the British Isles, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy, and the Baltic region, while also using Eastern European trade routes. Vikings influenced the political development of northern and eastern Europe, including England and Kievan Rus’. They spoke Old Norse, used runes, and gradually converted from Old Norse religion to Christianity.

key_facts.text: On routes along the Dnieper and Volga, Vikings were also called Varangians. Some Rus Vikings served as Byzantine imperial bodyguards before attacking Constantinople.
Viking society included farmers, fishermen, craftsmen, and traders, not only raiders.
During the Viking Age, the Scandinavian homelands gradually consolidated from smaller kingdoms into Denmark, Norway, and Sweden.
Horned helmets are a modern stereotype: the source notes no evidence that Vikings wore them, and the costume image emerged in the 19th century.

overview.text: Judaism is an Abrahamic, monotheistic religious and cultural tradition of the Jewish people. Religious Jews understand it as a way of observing the Mosaic covenant, believed to have been established between God and the Jewish people. Its central scriptural collection is the Tanakh, also called the Hebrew Bible, whose divisions are the Torah (Teaching), Nevi'im (Prophets), and Ketuvim (Writings).

Judaism also includes extensive traditions of interpretation and law. These include the Oral Torah, the Mishnah, the Talmud, Halakha (Jewish law), and other rabbinic writings. Jewish movements differ especially in how they understand Jewish law, rabbinic authority, and religious tradition; major modern movements include Orthodox, Conservative, and Reform Judaism. Jewish texts and ideas also influenced Christianity and Islam.

key_facts.text: The Torah can mean the Five Books of Moses, but it is also used more broadly for Jewish teachings and rabbinic literature.
Halakha means “the Way” and refers to Jewish law.
Rabbinic Judaism teaches that God revealed Written and Oral Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai.
Jews are an ethnoreligious group: Jewish identity includes people born Jewish and people who convert to Judaism.

overview.text: Horus—also called Heru, Har, Her, or Hor—is a major ancient Egyptian deity associated with kingship, healing, protection, the sun, and the sky. He was commonly represented as a falcon or as a human with a falcon’s head. Different forms of Horus emphasized different aspects of this layered deity.

In the most familiar family tradition, Horus is the son of Isis and Osiris. As Osiris’s heir, he is the rival of Set, who murdered Osiris; Egyptian kings were traditionally regarded as manifestations of Horus during life and of Osiris after death.

key_facts.text: The earliest recorded form of Horus was the tutelary deity of Nekhen in Upper Egypt and was specifically associated with the ruling pharaoh.
Horus was worshipped from at least late prehistoric Egypt through the Ptolemaic and Roman periods.
Some traditions identify Hathor as Horus’s mother, and sometimes as his wife, instead of identifying Isis as his mother.
Egyptologists describe the recorded forms of Horus as distinct gods or as complementary manifestations of a broader deity.

overview.text: Piracy is maritime robbery or criminal violence aimed at ships or coastal areas, usually to steal cargo, valuables, or take hostages. Across world history, narrow channels and other predictable shipping routes repeatedly created opportunities for raiders.

Piracy also illustrates the importance of state authority: privateering was similar maritime raiding conducted with government authorization, while piracy was treated as a crime. The practice has ancient roots, remains a modern security concern, and was later romanticized through books and films about the Age of Sail.

key_facts.text: The earliest documented examples date to the 14th century BC, when the Sea Peoples attacked ships in the Aegean and Mediterranean.
Historic piracy hotspots included Gibraltar, the Strait of Malacca, Madagascar, the Gulf of Aden, and the English Channel.
Piracy is recognized both under customary international law and under the domestic laws of many states.
Modern pirates have often used small motorboats and automatic firearms to board ships, including near Somalia and in the Strait of Malacca and Singapore.
The 1724 book A General History of the Pyrates helped shape popular images of piracy and influenced later works such as Treasure Island and Peter Pan.

overview.text: Suicide is the intentional act of causing one’s own death. It is studied scientifically as part of self-destructive behavior and raises cultural and philosophical questions involving religion, honor, and the meaning of life. Risk factors can include mental, neurodevelopmental, and physical disorders, substance abuse, and acute stress connected to financial or academic difficulties, relationship problems, harassment, or bullying.

Prevention efforts include limiting access to methods of suicide, treating mental disorders and substance abuse, psychotherapy, and careful media reporting. Cultural views vary: most religions disapprove of suicide, while seppuku was historically respected during Japan’s samurai era as a response to failure or a form of protest. Assisted suicide is associated with severe pain or imminent death and is legal in many countries.

key_facts.text: Suicidology is the scientific study of suicide and self-destructive behavior.
People who have previously attempted suicide face a higher risk of future attempts.
An estimated 727,000 people died by suicide worldwide in 2021, about 1.1% of deaths that year.
Seppuku, also called harakiri, was a form of suicide respected in Japan’s samurai era in connection with failure or protest.
Suicide and attempted suicide are no longer illegal in most Western countries, although suicide remains a criminal offense in some countries.

overview.text: Abstract Expressionism was a U.S. art movement that emerged after World War II and gained mainstream acceptance in the 1950s. Its center was the New York School, whose artists included Jackson Pollock, Mark Rothko, Willem de Kooning, Arshile Gorky, and Lee Krasner. The movement combined the emotional intensity of German Expressionism with visual ideas from European avant-garde movements and drew on Surrealist methods of spontaneous, subconscious creation.

The movement extended beyond painting to collage and sculpture. It became the first specifically American movement to gain international influence, helping place New York City at the center of the Western art world. Its cultural influence declined by the early 1960s; reactions against its emphasis on individualism helped lead to Pop art and Minimalism.

key_facts.text: The term had earlier uses: it was reportedly used in Germany in 1919 and by Alfred Barr in 1929 for works by Wassily Kandinsky. Robert Coates applied it to American art in 1946.
Other figures associated with the New York School included Franz Kline, Norman Lewis, Adolph Gottlieb, Clyfford Still, Robert Motherwell, Theodoros Stamos, and Jack Tworkov.
Associated sculpture included work by David Smith and Louise Nevelson, showing that the movement was not limited to painting.
Critics Clement Greenberg and Harold Rosenberg promoted artists in the movement. Rosenberg’s idea of the canvas as an “arena in which to act” helped define action painting.

overview.text: Francisco Franco Bahamonde was a Spanish general and politician who led the Nationalist forces in overthrowing the Second Spanish Republic during the Spanish Civil War (1936–1939). He then led Spain from 1939 until his death in 1975; this period is known as Francoist Spain.

Franco became generalissimo and head of state in 1936, unified the Nationalist movement, and built an authoritarian regime centered on nationalism and political repression. Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany supported him, while Spain remained officially neutral during World War II but favored the Axis powers. In his final years, Franco restored the monarchy, and King Juan Carlos helped lead Spain’s transition to democracy after Franco’s death.

key_facts.text: Franco rose rapidly in the army while serving in Spanish Morocco, becoming a brigadier general at age 33 in 1926.
Postwar repression included forced labor, concentration camps, and executions; estimates of deaths varied widely.
During the Cold War, economic reforms helped produce rapid growth known as the “Spanish miracle,” while Franco gained Western support as an anti-communist leader.
Historians disagree over how to classify Franco’s regime, describing it variously as a military dictatorship, para-fascist regime, or fully fascist state.

overview.text: Salvador Dalí (1904–1989) was a Spanish Surrealist artist known for precise draftsmanship and striking, bizarre imagery. His art explored dreams, the subconscious, sexuality, religion, science, and close personal relationships.

Born in Figueres, Catalonia, Dalí studied fine arts in Madrid, moved toward Surrealism in the late 1920s, and joined the Surrealist group in 1929. The Persistence of Memory was completed in 1931. He also worked in sculpture, film, graphic arts, animation, fashion, and photography.

key_facts.text: Dalí’s early influences included Impressionism and Renaissance artists; he later became interested in Cubism and other avant-garde movements.
He lived in France during the Spanish Civil War and moved to the United States in 1940, where he achieved commercial success.

After returning to Spain in 1948, Dalí announced a return to Catholic faith and developed a style he called “nuclear mysticism,” combining interests in classicism, mysticism, and scientific developments.
Dalí’s public support for the Francoist regime, commercial activities, and the quality and authenticity of some late works were controversial.

overview.text: Virginia Woolf’s 1927 novel follows the Ramsay family during visits to the Isle of Skye in Scotland from 1910 to 1920. Its central situation is Mr. Ramsay’s postponement of a visit to a nearby lighthouse, set against life at the family’s summer house.

The novel gives priority to thoughts and observations over dialogue and direct action. Its multiple focalisation—a technique that shifts attention among perspectives—supports explorations of loss, subjectivity, art, perception, childhood emotions, and adult relationships.

key_facts.text: The Ramsay family includes Mrs. Ramsay, Mr. Ramsay, and their eight children.
Woolf’s novel follows and extends modernist approaches associated with Marcel Proust and James Joyce.
The postponed lighthouse visit becomes a way to examine family tensions, allegiances, and the significance of an apparently small decision.
The family’s summer house stands beside the rocky coast of Scotland.

overview.text: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy by William Shakespeare about the romance of two young Italians whose families are feuding. The play presents love amid inherited family conflict, and its title characters are regarded as archetypal young lovers.

Shakespeare adapted a story with Italian roots and earlier English retellings, while expanding supporting roles and subplots. Believed written between 1591 and 1595, the play first appeared in a 1597 quarto and later inspired stage, film, musical, and opera adaptations.

key_facts.text: The plot belongs to a tradition of tragic romances reaching back to antiquity; predecessors include Matteo Bandello’s Italian tale and Arthur Brooke’s 1562 verse version.
Its dramatic design shifts between comedy and tragedy to heighten tension. Characters use different poetic forms, and Romeo becomes more skilled at the sonnet as the play develops.
The first quarto, published in 1597, was considered poor in quality; later editions revised the text toward Shakespeare’s original.
The play was among Shakespeare’s most popular during his lifetime and, along with Hamlet, is one of his most frequently performed.

overview.text: Salman Rushdie (born 1947) is an Indian-born British and American novelist. His work often combines magical realism with historical fiction and deals with connections, disruptions, and migrations between Eastern and Western civilizations. His novels commonly feature Indian settings, protagonists, or family relationships.

Midnight’s Children (1981) is Rushdie’s second novel. The Satanic Verses (1988), his fourth, brought death threats and a debate over censorship after some readers viewed its depiction of Muhammad as irreverent; Iran’s leader Ruhollah Khomeini issued a fatwa calling for Rushdie’s death.

key_facts.text: Midnight’s Children won the Booker Prize in 1981.
Rushdie graduated from the University of Cambridge with a history degree in 1968.
He was knighted in 2007 for services to literature.
His 2012 memoir, Joseph Anton, recounts his life after the events surrounding The Satanic Verses.

overview.text: A fractal is a geometric shape with detailed structure at arbitrarily small scales. Many fractals show self-similarity, meaning similar patterns recur as the shape is enlarged or reduced. Exact repetition at every scale is a stricter form of self-similarity; successive magnifications of the Mandelbrot set illustrate this idea.

Fractals differ from ordinary geometric figures in how they scale. Their fractal dimension describes this behavior and may be non-integer, generally exceeding the shape’s conventional, or topological, dimension. Fractal patterns have been rendered or studied in visual, physical, and aural media and found in nature, technology, art, and architecture; they also appear in geometric depictions of many chaotic processes.

key_facts.text: Some fractal curves are nowhere differentiable, meaning they have no ordinary derivative at any point. Although such a curve is topologically one-dimensional, its fractal dimension indicates that it fills space more efficiently than an ordinary line.

Mathematicians do not have one universally accepted formal definition of “fractal.” Mandelbrot proposed describing shapes that can be divided into parts that are at least approximately reduced copies of the whole.
Fractals can describe processes changing over time, not only visible geometric patterns.
Fractal ideas developed from early work on recursion, through nineteenth-century studies of continuous nondifferentiable functions, to twentieth-century computer-based modeling.

overview.text: Night is Elie Wiesel’s 1956 memoir, based on his experiences with his father in Nazi concentration camps at Auschwitz and Buchenwald in 1944–1945. It begins in the Nazi-established ghetto in Sighet, Romania, and follows their movement through multiple camps during the Holocaust.

Major concerns include the loss of faith, disgust with humanity, and the reversal of parent-child roles as Wiesel becomes caregiver to his weakened father. The narrative ends shortly after the U.S. Army liberates Buchenwald in April 1945.

key_facts.text: The original Yiddish title translates as “And the World Remained Silent.”
Wiesel’s father died in January 1945 after deteriorating from dysentery and a beating; Wiesel remained silent nearby because he feared being beaten too.
The work was published in Argentina in Yiddish in 1956, followed by the French La Nuit in 1958 and the English Night in 1960.
Night is the first volume of a trilogy completed by Dawn and Day.
Although Wiesel called the work his deposition, scholars have debated how fully it should be treated as an unvarnished factual account.

overview.text: A march is a musical composition built around a strong, regular rhythm. Historically, it was written for soldiers moving in lockstep; as a genre, it belongs to martial music and is especially associated with military bands and parades.

Marches can vary greatly in character: some are brisk or militaristic, while others are solemn or mournful. March writing also appears within larger classical works, showing that the form can serve both practical movement and dramatic musical expression.

key_facts.text: Wagner’s Götterdämmerung includes an emotional funeral march, demonstrating that march music is not limited to military settings.
John Philip Sousa is associated with brisk Romantic marches.
Examples of march writing occur in Beethoven’s Eroica Symphony and Chopin’s Sonata in B-flat minor.
Other cited examples include Schubert’s Marches Militaires, Sibelius’s “Jäger March,” and Handel’s “Dead March” in Saul.

overview.text: Prometheus is a Titan in Greek mythology who created and aided humanity in its earliest days. He defied the Olympian gods by stealing fire and giving it to humans, and is also associated with intelligence and the human arts and sciences.

Zeus punished this defiance by binding Prometheus to a rock, where an eagle ate his liver as it regrew each night. Major versions of the myth, especially Hesiod’s, say that the hero Heracles eventually freed him.

key_facts.text: Several versions of the myth credit Prometheus with creating humans from clay.
He is sometimes presented as the father of Deucalion, the hero of a flood story.
Some accounts place his torment at Mount Elbrus or Mount Kazbek in the Caucasus.
In later Western tradition, Prometheus came to represent scientific striving and the danger of overreaching; Frankenstein (1818) carries the alternate title The Modern Prometheus.

overview.text: Boko Haram—officially Jama'at Ahl al-Sunna li al-Da'wa wa al-Jihad—is a jihadist militant organization founded by Mohammed Yusuf in 2002. Based in northeastern Nigeria, it has also operated in Chad, Niger, northern Cameroon, and Mali.

The movement sought to purify Sunni Islam in northern Nigeria and eventually overthrow the Nigerian government. After its insurgency began in 2009, it became associated with attacks on security forces and civilians, suicide bombings, massacres, and mass abductions. The conflict caused extensive deaths, displacement, and food crises.

key_facts.text: Abubakar Shekau led Boko Haram from 2009 until his death in 2021 during fighting in Sambisa Forest; the organization also split into other groups after 2009 and 2015.
In April 2014, Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in Borno State, Nigeria.
The group gained control of territory around Borno in 2014 but did not capture Maiduguri, its original base.
Shekau pledged allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant in March 2015; later, hundreds of militants left after internal disputes and formed Islamic State's West Africa Province.

overview.text: Holden Caulfield is a fictional character created by J. D. Salinger and the antihero protagonist and narrator of The Catcher in the Rye (1951). His role in that novel ties him to teenage rebellion and angst; since the book’s publication, he has become an icon of those themes and is regarded as a significant character in twentieth-century American literature.

key_facts.text: The name first appeared in an unpublished 1941 short story and in print in 1945.
Salinger’s stories featuring Holden do not form one consistent timeline, and details about the character and his family can conflict across them.
The Catcher in the Rye presents Holden as 16, while some short stories depict a Holden who was a World War II soldier missing in action in 1944.
Salinger’s first published Holden story was “I’m Crazy,” which appeared in Collier’s on December 22, 1945.

overview.text: Antonín Dvořák (1841–1904) was a Czech composer who frequently used rhythms and other features of folk music from Bohemia and Moravia. He combined these national influences with the symphonic tradition in his music.

Dvořák gained international attention through works such as the Slavonic Dances and Stabat Mater. While directing New York’s National Conservatory, he wrote the Symphony From the New World and Cello Concerto, then returned to Bohemia. His opera Rusalka, premiered in 1901, became his most successful opera.

key_facts.text: Johannes Brahms recommended Dvořák to the publisher Simrock, who commissioned the Slavonic Dances; their success helped establish Dvořák internationally.
The Symphony From the New World and the Cello Concerto were written during Dvořák’s American period.
In 1893, while staying in Spillville, Iowa, Dvořák wrote String Quartet No. 12 in F major, Op. 96, known as the American.
Most of Dvořák’s operas use Czech librettos and express Czech national spirit; Rusalka premiered in 1901.

overview.text: Richard Milhous Nixon was the 37th president of the United States, serving from 1969 until his resignation in 1974. A Republican, he represented California in Congress and served eight years as vice president under Dwight D. Eisenhower before winning the presidency in 1968.

Nixon’s presidency combined major foreign-policy changes—including reduced U.S. involvement in Vietnam, a 1972 visit to China, and negotiations with the Soviet Union—with domestic measures such as establishing the Environmental Protection Agency. His second term was consumed by Watergate, a political scandal involving a break-in and a cover-up. Facing likely impeachment, Nixon resigned on August 9, 1974, becoming the only U.S. president to resign.

key_facts.text: Nixon ended U.S. combat involvement in Vietnam and ended the military draft in 1973.
His 1972 visit to China led to diplomatic relations between the two countries; he also finalized the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with the Soviet Union.
His administration established the Environmental Protection Agency and the Occupational Safety and Health Administration and supported environmental laws including the Clean Air Act.
The Watergate scandal began with a break-in at the Democratic National Committee office and expanded through administration efforts to cover it up.
After Nixon resigned, President Gerald Ford issued him a controversial pardon.

overview.text: Hydrogen (H) is the lightest and most abundant chemical element. Under standard conditions it is the colorless, odorless, highly combustible diatomic gas H₂. Stars, including the Sun, mainly contain hydrogen as plasma; on Earth, hydrogen occurs as H₂ and in compounds such as water and organic substances.

Hydrogen is important in chemistry because it readily forms covalent bonds and can appear as the positively charged ion H⁺, whose behavior in water is central to acid–base chemistry and pH. Its emitted and absorbed light also played a significant role in the development of quantum mechanics.

key_facts.text: The most common isotope, ¹H, has one proton, one electron, and no neutrons.
In the early universe, neutral hydrogen formed after the expanding universe cooled enough for electrons to remain bound to protons; later, much hydrogen in intergalactic space was re-ionized.
Henry Cavendish identified hydrogen gas as a distinct substance in the 18th century. Its name means “water-former,” referring to the production of water when it burns.
Most hydrogen is produced by transforming fossil fuels, especially through steam reforming of natural gas. Major industrial uses include fossil-fuel processing and ammonia production for fertilizer.

overview.text: Napoleon Bonaparte, later Napoleon I, was a Corsica-born French general who rose during the French Revolution and became ruler of France, first as First Consul and then as emperor. His campaigns brought French dominance across much of Europe and included invasions of the Iberian Peninsula and Russia. Coalitions eventually defeated him: after abdicating in 1814 and escaping Elba, he returned during the Hundred Days but lost at Waterloo in 1815 and was exiled to Saint Helena. Napoleon’s legacy includes major legal and administrative reforms, especially the Napoleonic Code, alongside centralized rule, repression, and warfare that devastated Europe.

key_facts.text: The Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799 brought Napoleon to power as First Consul; he crowned himself Emperor of the French in December 1804.
At Austerlitz in 1805, Napoleon defeated the Third Coalition, a victory that led to the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire.
His 1812 invasion of Russia ended in a catastrophic winter retreat; defeat at Leipzig in 1813 helped force his first abdication the following year.
The Battle of Waterloo in June 1815 ended Napoleon’s Hundred Days after his escape from Elba and led to his exile on Saint Helena.
His legacy included the Napoleonic Code, public education, and centralized administration, but his regime also suppressed freedoms and reinstated slavery in French colonies.

overview.text: Washington Irving (1783–1859) was an American writer whose work included short stories, essays, biographies, histories, and diplomacy. His short stories “Rip Van Winkle” and “The Legend of Sleepy Hollow” appeared in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent.

Irving was one of the first American writers to earn acclaim in Europe. He encouraged authors such as Henry Wadsworth Longfellow and Edgar Allan Poe and advocated stronger laws to protect American writers from copyright infringement.

key_facts.text: Irving was born and raised in Manhattan in a merchant family.
His 1802 literary debut consisted of observational letters in the Morning Chronicle, published under the pseudonym Jonathan Oldstyle.
The Sketch Book was serialized from 1819 to 1820 while Irving was temporarily in England for his family’s business.
He served as the American ambassador to Spain during the 1840s.

overview.text: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th president of the United States, serving from 1861 until his assassination in 1865. He led the United States through the Civil War, helped defeat the Confederacy, and worked to preserve the Union while advancing the abolition of slavery.

A self-educated frontier lawyer from Kentucky, Lincoln became an Illinois legislator, U.S. representative, and leader of the Republican Party. His election in 1860 was followed by secession in slave states and the Confederate attack on Fort Sumter, which began the Civil War.

key_facts.text: On January 1, 1863, Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring enslaved people in states still in rebellion free.
He delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, a speech that became one of the most famous in American history.
Lincoln promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865.
John Wilkes Booth fatally shot Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C., on April 14, 1865, making Lincoln the first U.S. president to be assassinated.

overview.text: Plate tectonics is the scientific theory that Earth’s rigid lithosphere—the crust and uppermost mantle—is divided into large and smaller plates that move slowly. The theory developed from continental drift and gained broad acceptance after evidence for seafloor spreading was confirmed in the 1960s.

Where plates meet, their motion creates convergent, divergent, or transform boundaries. These interactions help explain earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building, and oceanic trenches, making plate motion a central framework for understanding how Earth’s crust changes.

key_facts.text: Plates include oceanic and continental lithosphere; continental lithosphere is thicker and each type has its own kind of crust.
At convergent boundaries, subduction carries one plate beneath another; at divergent boundaries, seafloor spreading creates new oceanic crust.
Plates move across the softer asthenosphere. Mantle convection contributes to their movement, while sinking, dense oceanic crust at subduction zones is described as the strongest driver.
Plate motion is generally slow, typically ranging from zero to 10 centimeters per year.

overview.text: Iraq, officially the Republic of Iraq, is a country in West Asia and part of the Middle East. It borders Iran, Turkey, Syria, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and the Persian Gulf. Baghdad, the capital and largest city, lies in a country shaped by the fertile plains between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers—the region historically known as Mesopotamia.

Mesopotamia supported early civilizations including Sumer, Akkad, Babylonia, and Assyria, and is associated with major developments such as writing, mathematics, and law codes. In later history, Baghdad became a major intellectual center under the Abbasid Caliphate. Modern Iraq has also been marked by political change and conflict, including the Iran-Iraq War and the 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

key_facts.text: Iraq is a federal parliamentary republic, and Arabic and Kurdish are its official languages.
Most Iraqis are Muslims; important minority communities include Christians, Mandaeans, Yazidis, and others.
Iraq has one of the world’s largest oil reserves and a significant oil and gas industry.
Saddam Hussein led Iraq during its 1980–1988 war with Iran and its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

overview.text: Nuclear weapons are explosive devices powered by nuclear reactions. Fission weapons release energy by splitting atomic nuclei, while thermonuclear weapons combine fission with nuclear fusion. Both produce enormous energy from relatively small amounts of matter, with effects including blast, intense heat, ionizing radiation, fires, and radioactive fallout.

The first nuclear weapons were developed by the United States, United Kingdom, and Canada during World War II in the Manhattan Project. They were used in war at Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945. During the Cold War, nuclear deterrence—including mutually assured destruction—aimed to prevent nuclear warfare through the threat of unacceptable damage.

key_facts.text: Strategic nuclear weapons target civilian, industrial, and military infrastructure, while tactical weapons are intended for battlefield use. The nuclear triad consists of intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched ballistic missiles, and nuclear strategic bombers.
Production requires a large scientific-industrial system, including facilities that produce plutonium or enrich uranium for fissile material.
Hundreds of nuclear explosions would likely produce nuclear winter and nuclear famine, extending the consequences beyond immediate blast, heat, and radiation.
Nuclear weapons are weapons of mass destruction. Their control involves nonproliferation, arms control, disarmament, and organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency.

overview.text: The Gift of the Magi is a short story by American writer O. Henry, first published in 1905. It centers on a young married couple trying to buy secret Christmas gifts for each other with only a small amount of money. The story presents gift-giving as a sentimental subject with a moral lesson and is known for a twist ending generally considered an example of cosmic irony. It has remained popular for adaptations and Christmas presentations.

key_facts.text: It first appeared in The New York Sunday World on December 10, 1905, under the title “Gifts of the Magi.”
It was published in book form in O. Henry’s collection The Four Million in April 1906.
The story was allegedly written at Pete’s Tavern on Irving Place in New York City.

overview.text: The Grand Canyon is a steep-sided canyon in Arizona carved by the Colorado River. It extends 277 miles, reaches up to 18 miles wide, and is more than a mile deep. Its exposed rock layers record nearly two billion years of Earth’s geological history as rivers cut downward through the rising Colorado Plateau.

The canyon and adjacent rim lie within a patchwork of national park, forest, monument, reservation, and Indigenous lands. Native Americans have inhabited the area for thousands of years, and Pueblo peoples regarded the Grand Canyon as a holy site.

key_facts.text: Recent studies support that the Colorado River established its course through the area about 5–6 million years ago, though aspects of the canyon’s formation remain debated by geologists.
Theodore Roosevelt was a major advocate for preserving the Grand Canyon area and visited it repeatedly.
García López de Cárdenas of Spain was the first European known to have viewed the Grand Canyon, arriving in 1540.

overview.text: The Easter Rising, also called the Easter Rebellion, was a six-day armed insurrection in Ireland that began on 24 April 1916 during Easter Week. Irish republicans aimed to establish an independent Irish Republic while the United Kingdom was fighting the First World War. Rebels seized important buildings in Dublin and proclaimed the Irish Republic.

The British Army suppressed the Rising with reinforcements, artillery, and a gunboat; Patrick Pearse accepted an unconditional surrender on 29 April. Courts martial and executions followed, and opposition to the British response helped shift Irish public opinion toward independence. After Sinn Féin’s 1918 electoral victory, it convened the First Dáil and declared independence.

key_facts.text: The main republican forces included the Irish Volunteers, James Connolly’s Irish Citizen Army, and about 200 women of Cumann na mBan.
Sixteen rebels were executed for their roles in the Rising, beginning in May 1916.
About 3,500 people were taken prisoner after the surrender; 1,800 were sent to internment camps or prisons in Britain.
The fighting caused many civilian deaths and left parts of central Dublin in ruins after shelling and fires.

overview.text: The domestic cat (Felis catus), also called the house cat, is a small domesticated mammal in the family Felidae and the order Carnivora. It is an obligate carnivore, with retractable claws, sharp teeth, quick reflexes, and strong night vision suited to hunting small prey such as mice and rats.

Cats are commonly kept for companionship and have also been valued for controlling vermin. They are social animals but typically hunt alone, and they are most active around dawn and dusk. Archaeological and genetic evidence places their domestication in the Near East around 7500 BCE.

key_facts.text: Domestic cats use meows, purrs, trills, hisses, growls, body language, scent marking, and pheromones to communicate.
The domestic cat is the only domesticated species in the family Felidae.
Cats can hear sounds too faint or too high-pitched for humans to hear, including sounds made by small mammals.
Some cats live as feral animals, avoiding human contact; population-control measures include spaying and neutering.

overview.text: A steamboat is a boat propelled mainly by steam power, usually through propellers or paddlewheels. The term generally describes smaller steam-powered vessels used on lakes, rivers, and short-sea routes. Steamboats matter as an important stage in the development of larger steamships, which could operate on the open ocean.

key_facts.text: Steamboat propulsion can drive either propellers or paddlewheels.
The term commonly applies to vessels working on lakes, rivers, and in short-sea shipping.
“Steamship” usually refers to the larger, seaworthy vessels that developed from steamboats and often traveled ocean routes.
Some steam-powered vessels use the prefixes SS, S.S., or S/S for “Screw Steamer,” and PS for “Paddle Steamer.”

overview.text: Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha (“Awakened One”), was a wandering religious teacher who founded Buddhism. Buddhist tradition says he was born in Lumbini to royal parents of the Shakya clan, renounced his home life, and attained nirvana after asceticism and meditation at Bodh Gaya. He then taught across the lower Indo-Gangetic Plain and built a monastic community called the sangha.

His central teaching presented a Middle Way between sensual indulgence and severe asceticism. The Four Noble Truths and Noble Eightfold Path summarize his approach to overcoming ignorance, craving, rebirth, and suffering through ethical conduct, mental discipline, and meditation.

key_facts.text: “Buddha” means “Awakened One” or “Enlightened One”; “Tathāgata” is another title associated with him.
The Noble Eightfold Path includes ethical training, kindness toward others, mindfulness, sense restraint, and meditation.
The Vinaya Piṭaka contains codes for monastic discipline, while the Sūtra Piṭaka collects discourses attributed to him; both were passed down through oral tradition in Middle Indo-Aryan dialects.
Buddhism later developed into traditions including Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and Vajrayāna, and spread beyond the Indian subcontinent.

overview.text: The War of the Triple Alliance, also called the Paraguayan War, was a South American conflict fought from 1864 to 1870 between Paraguay and an alliance of Argentina, the Empire of Brazil, and Uruguay. It began with a conflict between Paraguay and Brazil connected to the Uruguayan War; Argentina and Uruguay joined the war against Paraguay in 1865. It was the deadliest inter-state war in Latin American history, and Paraguay was forced to cede disputed territory to Argentina and Brazil.

key_facts.text: After Paraguay was defeated in conventional warfare, it continued fighting through a 14-month guerrilla resistance.
Much of Paraguay’s civilian population died from battle, hunger, and disease.
Paraguayan president Francisco Solano López was killed by Brazilian forces at the Battle of Cerro Corá on March 1, 1870.
Argentine and Brazilian troops occupied Paraguay until 1876.

overview.text: Gold is the chemical element Au, from the Latin aurum, with atomic number 79. It is a dense, soft, bright yellow metal that is malleable and ductile. Chemically, it is a group 11 transition metal and a noble metal, and it is among the least reactive elements.

Gold’s workability and resistance to corrosion have supported its long use in jewelry, art, and coinage. Its electrical conductivity and resistance to chemical reactions also make it useful in corrosion-resistant electrical connectors.

key_facts.text: Gold does not dissolve in nitric acid alone, but aqua regia—a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids—can dissolve it. This contrast helped give rise to the term “acid test.”
Gold commonly occurs in its native, or elemental, form as nuggets and grains. A natural gold-and-silver solid solution is called electrum.
Gold has played a role in monetary systems, including the gold standard; the international gold standard was abandoned after the 1971 Nixon shock measures.
Gold dissolves in alkaline cyanide solutions, a property used in mining and electroplating.

overview.text: The normal, or Gaussian, distribution is a continuous probability distribution for a real-valued random variable. Its mean μ is also its median and mode; its variance is σ², with σ as the positive standard deviation. It is widely used in statistics and in the natural and social sciences to model real-valued quantities when their distributions are unknown.

Its importance is closely tied to the central limit theorem: the average of many independent observations with finite mean and variance approaches a normal distribution as the number of observations grows. This helps explain why quantities produced by many independent processes, including measurement errors, can be nearly normal.

key_facts.text: “Bell curve” is an informal name for the normal distribution, but other distributions—including the Cauchy, Student’s t, and logistic distributions—can also be bell-shaped.
Any linear combination of a fixed collection of independent normally distributed variables is itself normally distributed.
Normal-distribution methods support analytic treatments of uncertainty propagation and least-squares parameter fitting.
A normal distribution is a poor model when the data do not satisfy the assumption of normality, so using it indiscriminately can be misleading.

overview.text: The imaginary unit is the number written as i that satisfies i² = −1, an equation with no solution among the real numbers. It extends ordinary arithmetic into the complex-number system, where numbers have the form a + bi and a and b are real numbers. This makes it possible to work with quantities involving the square root of a negative number.

The imaginary unit should be distinguished from its additive inverse, −i: both square to −1. In settings where i could be confused with electric current, especially electrical engineering, the same mathematical unit is commonly written as j.

key_facts.text: Any real-number multiple of i is called an imaginary number.
Complex numbers combine real and imaginary parts in the form a + bi.
The two complex square roots of −1 are i and −i.
Electrical engineering commonly uses j for the imaginary unit because i often denotes electric current.

overview.text: South Dakota is a landlocked U.S. state in the North Central region and part of the Great Plains. Pierre is its capital. The Missouri River bisects the state into “East River” and “West River,” while its borders connect it with North Dakota, Minnesota, Iowa, Nebraska, Wyoming, and Montana.

The state’s strongest geographic contrast is between its more populated, crop-growing east and its western side, where ranching predominates and Native American reservations are concentrated. In the southwest, the pine-covered Black Hills—sacred to the Sioux—contain Mount Rushmore, linking South Dakota’s physical geography with a major tourist landmark.

key_facts.text: South Dakota and North Dakota entered the Union simultaneously on November 2, 1889; together they are the 39th and 40th states admitted.
The state’s name comes from the Dakota Sioux, who became dominant in the area by the early 19th century.
A late-19th-century gold rush in the Black Hills and railroad construction accelerated Euro-American settlement; conflict culminated in the Wounded Knee Massacre in 1890.
South Dakota has a temperate continental climate with four distinct seasons; precipitation is generally greater in the east than in the semiarid west.

overview.text: Black holes are extremely compact astronomical bodies whose gravity prevents anything, even light, from escaping. In general relativity, the boundary beyond which escape is impossible is the event horizon. The theory also predicts a central singularity, where spacetime curvature becomes infinite.

Many black holes form when massive stars collapse during supernovae. They can grow by absorbing surrounding matter, while supermassive black holes—millions of solar masses—are believed to exist at the centers of most galaxies. Although black holes do not let light escape from within their horizons, astronomers detect them through glowing infalling matter, stellar motions, and gravitational waves.

key_facts.text: Hawking radiation is predicted to come from event horizons and slowly reduce a black hole’s mass when it is not accreting matter; its emission rate is inversely related to mass.
A black hole’s accretion disk is hot, infalling plasma whose friction can produce visible light and, in extreme cases, a quasar.
Merging black holes can be detected through the gravitational waves they emit.
Cygnus X-1 was the first widely accepted black hole, identified through studies of an X-ray source in a binary system.
The Milky Way’s central radio source, Sagittarius A*, contains a supermassive black hole estimated at about 4.3 million solar masses.

overview.text: Noble gases are the elements of Group 18: helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon, and—under the broadest definition—oganesson. The first six are colorless, odorless, monatomic gases under standard conditions and have very low chemical reactivity. Their outer shell of valence electrons is full, so they have little tendency to take part in chemical reactions.

Their weak attractions to one another give them extremely low boiling points. This combination of low reactivity and unusual physical properties makes them useful when reactions must be prevented: argon can shield welding and fill light bulbs, while helium provides buoyancy and helium and neon can serve as refrigerants.

key_facts.text: The term “noble gas” is used interchangeably with “Group 18” by IUPAC.
Noble-gas atoms interact mainly through weak London dispersion forces; their boiling points are below 165 K.
Industrial noble gases, except radon, are obtained mainly by separating them from air; helium is also recovered as a byproduct of natural-gas mining.
Oganesson is synthetic and extremely short-lived, so its chemistry remains uncertain; it may be a solid and more reactive than the other Group 18 elements.

overview.text: The Appalachian Mountains are a long, southwest–northeast mountain range in eastern North America, stretching about 2,050 miles from central Alabama to Newfoundland. Their alternating ridges and valleys have acted as an east–west travel barrier, influencing transportation and the colonial-era expansion of the United States. Logging and coal mining historically supported much of the regional economy and helped shape a distinct cultural region, while tourism has become increasingly important.

The range contains varied environments, with climates and ecosystems shifting from southern forests to boreal Canada and, at a few high peaks, tundra. Its landscapes are strongly associated with the Appalachian Trail, a long-distance hiking route connecting Maine and Georgia, and with an International Appalachian Trail extension into Canada.

key_facts.text: Mount Mitchell, in North Carolina's Black Mountains, is the range's highest peak at 6,684 feet; the Black Mountains are part of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

The Appalachians are among the world's oldest surviving mountain ranges. Their modern form developed through three mountain-building events beginning about 480 million years ago, followed by extensive erosion.
Southern and high-elevation areas feature trees such as oak, sugar maple, red spruce, and balsam fir; black bears and white-tailed deer are among the widespread mammals.
The Appalachian Trail runs about 2,175 miles from Mount Katahdin in Maine to Springer Mountain in Georgia. Its International extension reaches into New Brunswick and Quebec.

overview.text: J. Robert Oppenheimer, born Julius Robert Oppenheimer, was an American theoretical physicist. During World War II, he directed the Los Alamos Laboratory of the Manhattan Project, which developed the first nuclear weapons. He was present at Trinity, the first atomic-bomb test, on July 16, 1945.

His research included quantum mechanics, nuclear physics, and astrophysics, including theories of neutron stars and black holes. After the war, he advocated international control of nuclear weapons and opposed developing the hydrogen bomb partly on ethical grounds.

key_facts.text: He studied chemistry at Harvard and earned a physics doctorate from the University of Göttingen in 1927 under Max Born.
Scientific ideas associated with him include the Born–Oppenheimer approximation, the Oppenheimer–Phillips process, and work on neutron stars and black holes.
In 1947, he became director of the Institute for Advanced Study and chaired the Atomic Energy Commission’s General Advisory Committee.
In 1954, an Atomic Energy Commission security hearing was held amid his policy stances and past associations; his security clearance was revoked, and the decision was vacated in 2022.
He received the Enrico Fermi Award in 1963 for contributions to theoretical physics.

overview.text: Joseph Heller’s Catch-22 is a satirical war novel and his debut, first published in 1961. It uses a non-chronological, third-person omniscient structure, with events presented out of sequence and through different characters’ viewpoints. Its satire targets military bureaucracy and greed.

Set during World War II from 1942 to 1944, the novel mainly follows antihero Captain John Yossarian, a U.S. Army Air Forces B-25 bombardier. Most events take place on Pianosa, where Yossarian and his fellow servicemen struggle to preserve their sanity while fulfilling military requirements and trying to return home. The novel consequently examines the absurdity of war and military life.

key_facts.text: The fictional 256th U.S. Army Air Squadron is based on Pianosa, an island in the Mediterranean Sea west of Italy.
Yossarian is described as being of Assyrian heritage.
Heller began writing the novel in 1953.
The novel received a film adaptation in 1970 directed by Mike Nichols and a miniseries adaptation in 2019 produced by George Clooney.

overview.text: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) was an English writer and journalist whose novels and short stories remain widely read. His success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and many later novels appeared in weekly or monthly installments. Dickens helped establish serialized fiction as a major Victorian publishing form, often using cliffhangers to maintain suspense.

Dickens is associated with humor, satire, vivid characters, and close observation of society. He campaigned for children’s rights, education, and other reforms. A Christmas Carol remains widely adapted; Oliver Twist and Great Expectations evoke early Victorian London, while A Tale of Two Cities is historical fiction set in London and Paris.

key_facts.text: As a child, Dickens left school at 12 and worked in a boot-blacking factory while his father was imprisoned for debt; he later returned to school and entered journalism.
The Pickwick Papers became a publishing phenomenon after the introduction of Sam Weller, inspiring merchandise and spin-offs.
Bleak House (1853) satirizes England’s judicial system and helped support a reform movement that culminated in legal reform during the 1870s.
“Dickensian” describes conditions or characters resembling Dickens’s works, especially poor working conditions or comically repulsive figures.

overview.text: Bill Clinton (William Jefferson Clinton) was the 42nd president of the United States from 1993 to 2001. A Democrat from Arkansas, he had previously served as the state’s attorney general and governor. He presented himself as a “New Democrat,” associated with a centrist political approach.

Clinton’s presidency combined economic expansion with major domestic legislation, including the North American Free Trade Agreement, and an active foreign policy involving Bosnia, Kosovo, NATO expansion, and Middle East and Northern Ireland peace efforts. His second term was overshadowed by the Monica Lewinsky scandal, which led to his impeachment by the House and acquittal by the Senate.

key_facts.text: Clinton defeated incumbent George H. W. Bush in 1992 and won reelection in 1996 against Bob Dole.
He appointed Supreme Court Justices Ruth Bader Ginsburg and Stephen Breyer.
The House impeachment articles charged Clinton with perjury and obstruction of justice; the Senate acquitted him in 1999.
During the last three years of his presidency, the Congressional Budget Office reported a federal budget surplus.

overview.text: The Great Wave off Kanagawa is a Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock print by Hokusai, made in late 1831 during the Edo period. It shows three boats struggling through storm-tossed water beneath a huge curling wave, with Mount Fuji in the background. As the opening print in Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, it combines a dramatic seascape with the recurring image of the mountain. Its design blends traditions of Japanese printmaking with graphical perspective developed in Europe, and it later influenced European Impressionist artists.

key_facts.text: Its Japanese title, Kanagawa-oki Nami Ura, means “Under the Wave off Kanagawa.”
The print’s use of Prussian blue helped transform Japanese printmaking.
Its influence extended beyond painting: Claude Debussy, Vincent van Gogh, and Claude Monet are among the Western artists and musicians associated with its influence.

overview.text: Russia, or the Russian Federation, lies in Eastern Europe and North Asia. It is the world’s largest country, spans eleven time zones, and shares land borders with fourteen countries, giving it an unusually broad geographic reach.

Moscow is Russia’s capital and largest city, while Saint Petersburg is its second-largest city and a major cultural centre. Russia is also generally considered a great power with significant regional influence.

key_facts.text: The modern Russian Federation emerged in 1991 from the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
Russia’s economy relies heavily on its mineral and energy resources, especially oil and natural gas.
As the Soviet Union’s successor state, Russia retains a permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council.
Russia was the largest and principal constituent of the Soviet Union, established in 1922.

overview.text: Alan Turing was an English mathematician, logician, and computer scientist whose work formalized algorithms and computation. His Turing machine is a theoretical model of a general-purpose computer, making him a major figure in theoretical computer science.

Turing also applied his mathematical and technical skills to wartime codebreaking. At Bletchley Park, he led work on German naval ciphers, while his later projects helped shape early stored-program computers and mathematical biology.

key_facts.text: During World War II, Turing worked at Bletchley Park’s Government Code and Cypher School.
He led Hut 8, worked on German naval cryptanalysis, and improved techniques based on the pre-war Polish bomba, an electromechanical machine used to find Enigma settings.
After the war, he designed the Automatic Computing Engine, an early stored-program computer design.
At the University of Manchester, Turing contributed to early computers and studied mathematical biology, including the chemical basis of morphogenesis.

overview.text: Catalysis is the speeding up of a chemical reaction by adding a catalyst. A catalyst can take part in intermediate steps and then be regenerated, so it is not consumed overall. It works through an alternative mechanism that may be faster than the uncatalyzed route; that route remains possible, so the total reaction rate increases.
Catalysis is widely used in chemical manufacturing: one estimate says catalysts are involved at some stage in producing 90% of commercially produced chemical products.

key_facts.text: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants; a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase.
Enzymes and other biocatalysts are often treated as a separate category of catalysts.
When a reaction is rapid and the catalyst is recycled quickly, a small amount of catalyst can often suffice.
Mixing, surface area, and temperature also affect reaction rates.
A nanocatalyst is a nanoscale catalyst used in applied nanoscience.

overview.text: The Seneca Falls Convention was the first women’s rights convention. Held July 19–20, 1848, at Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, New York, it addressed women’s social, civil, and religious rights. Local female Quakers organized it with Elizabeth Cady Stanton during a visit by Lucretia Mott.

The six-session meeting produced the Declaration of Sentiments and accompanying resolutions, which attendees debated before signing. Women’s voting rights prompted a heated debate, but the suffrage resolution remained. The convention’s declaration helped spread news of the women’s rights movement, and other conventions soon followed.
