key_facts.text: Frederick Douglass, the convention’s sole African American attendee, strongly supported retaining the resolution for women’s suffrage.
Exactly 100 of approximately 300 attendees signed the Declaration of Sentiments, most of them women.
The Rochester Women’s Rights Convention followed in New York two weeks later; national women’s rights conventions began in 1850.
By the 1851 National Women’s Rights Convention, women’s right to vote had become a central issue of the movement.

overview.text: The East India Company was an English, later British, joint-stock company founded in 1600 for Indian Ocean trade. It dealt in commodities such as cotton, silk, spices, tea, and salt, then gained control of large parts of the Indian subcontinent and took on military and administrative functions.

Company rule included torture to extract taxes and policies that resulted in the Great Bengal famine of 1770. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 transferred direct control to the British Crown, creating the British Raj; the company was dissolved in 1874.

key_facts.text: Its original formal name was the Governor and Company of Merchants of London Trading into the East-Indies.
The company maintained its own armed forces, organized into three presidency armies.
By 1858, most of modern India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh, along with Lower Burma, was either company-ruled or governed by princely states tied to the company by treaty.

overview.text: Mountains are elevated parts of a planet’s surface, usually with steep sides and exposed bedrock. There is no universal height cutoff, but mountains are generally distinguished from hills by their greater elevation. Most occur in ranges, although some are isolated summits.

Mountains can form through tectonic forces, erosion, or volcanism over very long periods. Weathering, landslides, rivers, and glaciers gradually wear them down. Their high elevations create colder climates and distinctive ecosystems; steep terrain often limits farming while supporting resource extraction and recreation.

key_facts.text: Mount Everest, in the Himalayas, is identified as Earth’s highest mountain above mean sea level.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the highest known mountain on any planet in the Solar System.
Mauna Kea in Hawaii is identified as Earth’s highest mountain when measured from its submerged base to its summit.

overview.text: Inferno (“Hell”) is the first part of Dante Alighieri’s 14th-century Italian narrative poem the Divine Comedy, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso. It presents a fictionalized Dante traveling through Hell under the guidance of the ancient Roman poet Virgil. As an allegory—a story carrying symbolic meaning—the Divine Comedy portrays the soul’s movement toward God, while Inferno focuses on recognizing and rejecting sin.

key_facts.text: Hell is depicted as nine concentric circles of torment located within Earth.
The sinners in this realm are associated with rejecting spiritual values through appetite, violence, fraud, or malice.
Inferno is the opening section of the three-part Divine Comedy.
Virgil is an ancient Roman poet who guides Dante through Hell.

overview.text: Thornton Wilder’s Our Town is a three-act American play set in the fictional town of Grover’s Corners between 1901 and 1913. It centers on the everyday lives of the town’s citizens, making ordinary community life the subject of its drama.

The play is metatheatrical, meaning it draws attention to itself as a performance. The Stage Manager addresses the audience, answers questions, brings in guest lecturers, and sometimes plays roles. A mostly bare stage and mimed actions favor storytelling over realistic scenery. Our Town premiered in 1938, won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama, and continues to receive revivals.

key_facts.text: Wilder wrote the play; its first performance was at the McCarter Theatre in Princeton, New Jersey, on January 22, 1938.
The Stage Manager is the play’s main character and its direct connection to the audience.
The production generally uses no set or props: actors mime most actions on a largely bare stage.
After its initial production, the play succeeded on Broadway and received the Pulitzer Prize for Drama.

overview.text: King Arthur is a legendary king of Britain, a folk hero, and a central figure in the medieval literary tradition called the Matter of Britain. Welsh sources portray him as a leader of the post-Roman Britons fighting the Anglo-Saxons in the late fifth and early sixth centuries. However, those accounts were written centuries later, and most historians do not consider Arthur historical.

Arthur’s story developed through Welsh mythology and later medieval literature. Geoffrey of Monmouth’s 12th-century work helped popularize figures and episodes associated with Arthur, including Uther Pendragon, Merlin, Guinevere, Excalibur, Mordred, and Avalon. French writer Chrétien de Troyes added Lancelot and the Holy Grail, helping establish Arthurian romance. The legend has no single canonical version.

key_facts.text: Geoffrey of Monmouth portrayed Arthur as a conqueror of the Saxons who established a vast empire; this is a literary portrayal, not established history.
Welsh tradition presents Arthur both as a warrior defending Britain from human and supernatural enemies and as a magical folklore figure sometimes linked with the otherworld Annwn.
In Geoffrey’s version, Arthur’s final battle with Mordred occurs at Camlann, after which Arthur rests in Avalon.
Arthurian literature flourished in the Middle Ages, later declined, revived in the 19th century, and continues through adaptations in modern media.

overview.text: One is the first and smallest positive integer in the natural numbers. It represents a single thing and serves as a basic unit for counting and measurement. Its written form, 1, is a numeral as well as a mathematical symbol.

In mathematics, 1 is the multiplicative identity: multiplying any number by 1 leaves that number unchanged. In digital technology, 1 commonly represents the “on” state in binary code, linking this simple number to computing.

key_facts.text: By convention, 1 is not considered a prime number.
The modern Arabic numeral for 1 developed from earlier Sumerian and Babylonian symbols.
Beyond mathematics, 1 can indicate the first, leading, or top item in a group.

overview.text: Aspirin is the genericized trademark for acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that reduces pain, fever, and inflammation. It also suppresses platelet function, giving it antithrombotic uses and a role in reducing the risk of heart attack, ischemic stroke, and blood clots in people at high risk.

Aspirin’s history connects traditional willow-bark medicine with synthetic chemistry: salicin from willow is converted in the body to salicylic acid. Charles Frédéric Gerhardt first produced acetylsalicylic acid in 1853; Bayer chemists later improved its production, with a pure, stable form made in 1897 and marketed globally as Aspirin by 1899.

key_facts.text: Common side effects include upset stomach; more serious risks include stomach ulcers and bleeding.
Bleeding risk is higher for older people, those who drink alcohol, people taking other NSAIDs, and people using other blood thinners.
Aspirin is generally avoided in children with viral infections because of the risk of Reye syndrome, and it is not recommended late in pregnancy.
It is available without a prescription in most jurisdictions and appears on the World Health Organization’s List of Essential Medicines.

overview.text: Yukio Mishima was the pen name of Kimitake Hiraoka (1925–1970), a Japanese novelist, playwright, and short-story writer. His works include the novels Confessions of a Mask and The Temple of the Golden Pavilion, as well as the autobiographical essay Sun and Steel.

Mishima’s writing is associated with elaborate language, traditional Japanese and modern Western influences, and recurring connections among beauty, eroticism, and death. He was also known for far-right political beliefs and a failed 1970 coup attempt that ended in seppuku.

key_facts.text: Mishima was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature five times during the 1960s; in 1968, the award went to Yasunari Kawabata.
In 1968, he formed the Tatenokai, or “Shield Society,” a private militia devoted to protecting the emperor’s symbolic national dignity.
On November 25, 1970, Mishima and four militia members took a military commandant hostage and unsuccessfully urged the Self-Defense Forces to overthrow a constitutional provision on national defense.
Beyond writing, Mishima worked as an actor, martial artist, and model.

overview.text: Ryūnosuke Akutagawa was a Japanese writer active during the Taishō period. He is closely associated with the Japanese short story and is described as its “father.” His lasting literary association also includes the Akutagawa Prize, described as Japan’s premier literary award and named after him.

key_facts.text: He lived from 1 March 1892 to 24 July 1927.
His art name was Chōkōdō Shujin.
He died by suicide at age 35 after taking an overdose of barbital.

overview.text: Ruth Fulton Benedict was an American anthropologist and folklorist who studied relationships among personality, art, language, and culture. Her 1934 book Patterns of Culture argued that no cultural trait exists in isolation, connecting cultural analysis with broader patterns of human life. [p1, p3]

Benedict studied under Franz Boas at Columbia University, earned her Ph.D., and joined its faculty in 1923. She later led the American Anthropological Association and was a prominent member of the American Folklore Society. [p2, p3]

key_facts.text: Before graduate study at Columbia, Benedict studied anthropology at the New School of Social Research. [p2]
Margaret Mead was among Benedict’s students and colleagues. [p2]
Benedict was born in New York City and graduated from Vassar College in 1909. [p2]
Her work helped redirect anthropology and folklore toward theories treating performance as integral to interpreting culture. [p3]

overview.text: The Broken Column (La Columna Rota) is a 1944 oil-on-masonite self-portrait by Mexican artist Frida Kahlo. She painted it soon after spinal surgery for continuing problems resulting from a serious traffic accident she suffered at age 18. Kahlo appears alone, making physical pain and isolation central to the work.

A crumbling Ionic column replaces Kahlo’s spine, while the cracked landscape echoes her damaged body. Tears, nails piercing her body, and a metal brace reinforce the painting’s imagery of suffering and restriction. The depicted brace is identified as a polio support and may also suggest the physical and social limits imposed on Kahlo’s life.

key_facts.text: The original painting is housed at the Museo Dolores Olmedo in Xochimilco, Mexico City.
Kahlo’s forward-facing expression contrasts with the tears running down her cheeks.
Nails continue down only her right leg, which was shorter and weaker after childhood polio.
The brace shown was one of several that Kahlo actually used; it is now at Casa Azul, her home and museum.

overview.text: Margaret Eleanor Atwood is a Canadian novelist, poet, and literary critic whose writing includes dystopian fiction, poetry, and nonfiction. Her 1985 novel The Handmaid’s Tale is identified as her best-known work. Across her writing, she addresses gender, Canadian identity, religion and myth, the power of language, climate change, genetic engineering, and power politics. Many of her poems are inspired by myths and fairy tales.

key_facts.text: Atwood has also published short fiction, children’s books, and graphic novels, in addition to novels, poetry, and nonfiction.
Her honors include two Booker Prizes, the Arthur C. Clarke Award, the Order of Canada, and the Franz Kafka Prize.
She is a founder of the Griffin Poetry Prize and the Writers’ Trust of Canada.
Atwood invented the LongPen device and related technologies for remote robotic writing.

overview.text: Hungary is a landlocked country in Central Europe spanning much of the Carpathian Basin. It lies within the Danube River’s drainage basin and is dominated by broad lowland plains.

Hungarian statehood began in the late ninth century and developed into a Christian kingdom under Stephen I. After Ottoman conquest and later Habsburg rule, Hungary became part of the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy in 1867. Its modern borders were established by the 1920 Treaty of Trianon; the country later experienced the unsuccessful 1956 revolution and a peaceful transition to democracy in 1989.

key_facts.text: Budapest is Hungary’s capital, largest city, and cultural and economic center.
Hungary shares borders with Slovakia, Ukraine, Romania, Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, and Austria.
Hungarian is the official language and is one of the few European languages outside the Indo-European language family.
Hungary joined the European Union in 2004 and the Schengen Area in 2007.

overview.text: The Planets, Op. 32 is a seven-movement orchestral suite by English composer Gustav Holst, written from 1914 to 1917. Each movement is named for a planet in the Solar System and reflects that planet’s astrological significance. In the final movement, the orchestra is joined by a wordless female chorus.

The suite was first performed in London in 1918 and received its first complete public performance there in 1920. Although some critics initially reacted negatively to its innovative musical style, it soon became popular, influential, and widely performed.

key_facts.text: The premiere took place at Queen’s Hall on September 29, 1918, conducted by Holst’s friend Adrian Boult for an invited audience.
The first complete public performance was given at Queen’s Hall on November 15, 1920, by the London Symphony Orchestra under Albert Coates.
Holst conducted two recordings of the suite, and it was later recorded by conductors, choirs, and orchestras in Britain and internationally.

overview.text: John Steinbeck was an American writer and novelist whose work often focuses on downtrodden or “everyman” protagonists. Much of it is set in central California, especially the Salinas Valley and California Coast Ranges. Fate and injustice are recurring themes, while his writing is also associated with sympathetic humor and social perception. His literary output includes novels, novellas, nonfiction, and short-story collections.

key_facts.text: Steinbeck won the 1962 Nobel Prize in Literature for writing praised for realism, imagination, sympathetic humor, and social perception.
The Grapes of Wrath, published in 1939, won the Pulitzer Prize and is part of the American literary canon.
Of Mice and Men (1937) and The Red Pony (1933) are identified as Steinbeck novellas.
Other major Steinbeck titles include Tortilla Flat, Cannery Row, and the multigenerational novel East of Eden.

overview.text: Saddam Hussein was an Iraqi politician and revolutionary who became president in 1979 and remained in power until his overthrow in 2003. A leading member of the Ba'ath Party, he was associated with Ba'athism, an ideology combining Arab nationalism and Arab socialism. He had already become Iraq’s de facto leader before formally taking office.

His rule was marked by war and repression. Iraq fought Iran in a long, costly war; after Iraq occupied Kuwait, a U.S.-led multinational coalition defeated it in the 1990–1991 Gulf War, followed by United Nations sanctions. Saddam also suppressed Kurdish and Shi'a uprisings. After the 2003 invasion, he was captured, convicted of crimes against humanity, and executed in 2006.

key_facts.text: Saddam joined the Ba'ath Party in 1957 and later served as vice president under Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr.
As vice president, he nationalized the Iraq Petroleum Company and promoted economic diversification.
The Iraqi Ba'ath Party was banned after the 2003 invasion, and Saddam was captured on 13 December 2003.
The Iraqi High Tribunal convicted him over the 1982 killing of 148 Iraqi Shi'a; he was sentenced to death by hanging and executed on 30 December 2006.
Saddam was accused of running a repressive authoritarian government; several analysts described it as totalitarian, though that label is contested.

overview.text: Maxwell's demon is a thought experiment proposed by physicist James Clerk Maxwell in 1867. An imagined agent controls a door between two gas-filled chambers, allowing fast molecules to pass one way and slow molecules the other. The sorting would make one chamber warmer and the other cooler, apparently lowering the system's entropy without work and challenging the second law of thermodynamics.

The puzzle has influenced discussions connecting thermodynamics with information theory. Although versions of the idea have been tested experimentally, none has been shown to violate the second law; these versions differ from the original thought experiment.

key_facts.text: Maxwell initially described the entity as a “finite being” or a being able to play a skillful game with molecules; Lord Kelvin later gave it the name “demon.”
The imagined temperature difference arises because a gas's kinetic temperature depends on the velocities of its molecules.
Most scientists hold that no device can violate the second law in the demon's proposed manner.

overview.text: Snakes are limbless reptiles in the squamate suborder Serpentes. Their elongated bodies are covered in overlapping scales, and they use several kinds of movement, including sidewinding. They are ectothermic vertebrates closely related to lizards and the tuatara.

A major snake adaptation is a highly flexible skull, which allows the mouth to widen around prey much larger than the head. Nonvenomous snakes typically subdue prey by constriction, while venomous species deliver toxins through fangs. Most snakes live on land, but aquatic groups include sea snakes and water snakes.

key_facts.text: Although snakes lack limbs, pythons and boas retain a vestigial pelvic girdle.
Snakes occur on every continent except Antarctica and on most islands, with sea snakes especially widespread in the Indo-Pacific.
Some tree-dwelling snakes can glide briefly by spreading their ribs to flatten and widen the body for lift.
Snake venom can contain neurotoxins, hemotoxins, cardiotoxins, and myotoxins; it is used mainly to paralyze or kill prey rather than for self-defense.

overview.text: Pakistan is a South Asian country whose geography extends from Arabian Sea coastal areas in the south to the Karakoram, Hindu Kush, and Himalayan mountains in the north. Between these regions are plains, deserts, forests, and plateaus, creating a highly varied landscape.

Iran lies to Pakistan’s west, Afghanistan to its northwest, and India to its east, with the Arabian Sea to the south. The country’s regional geography also includes the Kashmir territorial conflict with India, which has led to multiple military confrontations.

key_facts.text: Pakistan overlaps the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates. Sindh and Punjab are on the Indian Plate, while Balochistan, most of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and Gilgit-Baltistan are within the Eurasian Plate.
The Khyber Pass and Bolan Pass have historically served as routes for migration, trade, cultural exchange, and military movement between Central Eurasia and South Asia.
The Kashmir conflict is a territorial dispute between Pakistan and India that has produced multiple military confrontations.

overview.text: DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is a nucleic acid made of two nucleotide chains twisted into a double helix. It carries genetic instructions used in the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known organisms and many viruses. DNA is one of the four major kinds of biological macromolecules.

DNA’s information is encoded by the order of four bases. When its strands separate, that information can be copied; DNA can also serve as a template for RNA, whose sequence helps specify the amino-acid sequence of proteins.

key_facts.text: Each nucleotide contains a base, the sugar deoxyribose, and a phosphate group. The base pairs are adenine–thymine and cytosine–guanine.
The two DNA strands run in opposite directions and contain matching biological information through complementary base pairing.
DNA is transcribed into RNA; during translation, RNA helps determine the order of amino acids in proteins.
In eukaryotic cells, DNA is organized into chromosomes, mostly in the nucleus, with additional DNA in mitochondria and, in plants and some other organisms, chloroplasts.
Bacteria and archaea store their DNA in the cytoplasm, generally in circular chromosomes.

overview.text: Alexander Hamilton was an American Founding Father, military officer, and statesman who was born on the Caribbean island of Nevis. During the Revolutionary War, he served as an artillery officer and George Washington’s aide-de-camp, taking part in the Yorktown campaign. After the war, Hamilton helped promote a stronger national government through the Annapolis Convention, the Constitutional Convention, and The Federalist Papers, writing 51 of its 85 installments.

As the first U.S. secretary of the treasury, Hamilton favored energetic federal leadership, national defense, and a more industrial economy. He argued that the Constitution’s implied powers allowed the federal government to create the First Bank of the United States and address the states’ war debts. These views helped shape the Federalist position in the early republic.

key_facts.text: Hamilton served as treasury secretary from 1789 to 1795 and founded the Federalist Party in 1789.
His financial program funded the First Bank of the United States through measures including an import tariff and a whiskey tax.
Hamilton’s Federalists opposed the Democratic-Republican Party led by Thomas Jefferson.
After a political conflict with Aaron Burr, Hamilton was mortally wounded in a duel at Weehawken, New Jersey, on July 11, 1804, and died the next day.

overview.text: Alaska is a U.S. state in northwestern North America, separated from the contiguous United States and bordered on its eastern side by Canada’s Yukon and British Columbia. Across the Bering Strait, it faces Russia; the Arctic Ocean lies to the north and the Pacific Ocean to the south. This combination of Arctic, Pacific, and North American settings gives Alaska a distinctive place in U.S. geography. Its status as a semi-exclave means it belongs to a country while being separated from that country’s main territory.

key_facts.text: Alaska is the largest U.S. state by area—larger than Texas, California, and Montana combined.
It is the northernmost and westernmost U.S. state and, by longitude, also the easternmost.
Juneau is Alaska’s capital, while Anchorage is its most populous city.
The Russian Empire sold Alaska to the United States in 1867 for $7.2 million.
Alaska became the 49th U.S. state on January 3, 1959.

overview.text: Quetzalcoatl (Nahuatl for “Feathered Serpent”) is a deity in Aztec culture and literature. He is associated with wind, the planet Venus, the Sun, merchants, arts and crafts, knowledge, learning, wisdom, and intelligence. He is also identified as one of several important Aztec gods, alongside Tlaloc, Tezcatlipoca, and Huitzilopochtli.
A distinctive symbol of Quetzalcoatl is the ehēcacōzcatl, a spirally cut conch-shell breastplate connected with wind imagery. Codex drawings show both Quetzalcoatl and Xolotl wearing this object.

key_facts.text: Quetzalcoatl was the patron god of the Aztec priesthood.
Quetzalcoatl, Tlaloc, and Xolotl are all connected with Venus; Tlaloc is described as an ally and rain god, while Xolotl is described as a psychopomp, or guide of the dead.
The ehēcacōzcatl was a conch shell cut through its cross-section; similar objects may have been worn as necklaces by religious rulers.
Post-conquest records sometimes conflated Quetzalcoatl with Ce Acatl Topiltzin, a legendary ruler of Tollan, but historians debate whether those narratives describe historical events.

overview.text: Venus is a Roman goddess associated with love, beauty, desire, sex, fertility, prosperity, and victory. Roman mythology makes her an ancestor of the Roman people through Aeneas, the Trojan survivor who fled to Italy. Romans adapted the myths and iconography of her Greek counterpart Aphrodite. In later Western classical tradition, Venus became a widely referenced embodiment of love and sexuality, often depicted nude.

key_facts.text: Julius Caesar claimed Venus as his ancestor.
Roman religion revered Venus under numerous cult titles and honored her through many religious festivals.
Her functions extended beyond romantic love to include prosperity, fertility, and victory.

overview.text: Jainism, also called Jain Dharma, is an Indian religion that teaches spiritual purity and enlightenment through disciplined nonviolence (ahimsa) toward living creatures. Its tradition is guided by 24 tirthankaras, or “ford-makers,” who are said to have conquered rebirth and attained omniscience. The final tirthankara, Mahavira, is a central historical figure. Jainism’s spiritual goal is moksha, or liberation from karma.

Jain ethics emphasize three connected ideas: ahimsa (nonviolence), anekantavada (the view that reality has many aspects), and aparigraha (non-possession or non-attachment). These principles shape both religious practice and community life. Jainism has two major sub-traditions, the Digambaras (“sky-clad”) and Svetambaras (“white-clad”), which differ in some ascetic practices, views of gender, and canonical texts while sharing core philosophy.

key_facts.text: Mahavira, the 24th and final tirthankara, lived around the sixth or fifth century BCE and was a contemporary of the Buddha.
Anekantavada teaches that no single viewpoint fully captures complex truth or reality, encouraging intellectual humility.
Aparigraha requires monks to renounce property and encourages laypeople to limit possessions and desires.
Most Jains live in India, with diaspora communities in North America, Europe, and East Asia.

overview.text: Anthropology is the scientific study of humanity across the present and past. It examines human behavior, biology, cultures, societies, and linguistics, linking questions associated with both biology and sociology. Its broad scope includes contemporary people as well as archaic humans, making it a way to study human life across time and different social settings.

Its major areas include social anthropology, which studies behavior patterns; cultural anthropology, which examines cultural meaning, including norms and values; linguistic anthropology, which explores language’s influence on social life; and biological anthropology, which studies human biology and evolution alongside close primate relatives. Archaeology investigates past human activity through physical remains, although its disciplinary status varies by region.

key_facts.text: The combined term “sociocultural anthropology” is commonly used for social and cultural anthropology.
Biological anthropology is also called physical anthropology.
Archaeology is sometimes described as the “anthropology of the past.”
In North America and Asia, archaeology is generally treated as a branch of anthropology; in Europe, it may be independent or associated with history and paleontology.

overview.text: The Necklace (French: La Parure), also called The Diamond Necklace, is a short story by Guy de Maupassant. First published in the French newspaper Le Gaulois on February 17, 1884, it is a compact example of the twist ending associated with Maupassant’s style. Recognize it through the combination of Maupassant, its French title, and its concluding reversal.

key_facts.text: Its French title is La Parure.
It first appeared on February 17, 1884.
Its twist ending is described as a hallmark of Maupassant’s style.

overview.text: Roe v. Wade (1973) was a U.S. Supreme Court decision about abortion and constitutional privacy. In a 7–2 ruling, the Court held that the Fourteenth Amendment’s Due Process Clause protected a pregnant woman’s choice to have an abortion before fetal viability, while also recognizing government interests in women’s health and prenatal life. The decision struck down many state abortion laws and became a major focus of U.S. debate over abortion, constitutional interpretation, and the role of moral and religious views in politics. The Court reaffirmed Roe’s central holding in Planned Parenthood v. Casey (1992), but overturned Roe in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization (2022).

key_facts.text: The case was brought by Norma McCorvey, who used the legal pseudonym “Jane Roe,” against Texas district attorney Henry Wade.
McCorvey’s lawyers, Sarah Weddington and Linda Coffee, challenged Texas laws that allowed abortion only when necessary to save the mother’s life.
Roe described a trimester timetable for abortion regulations and required courts to apply “strict scrutiny” to challenged laws.
The decision was highly controversial: some critics accepted its result but objected to its legal reasoning, while others argued it did not go far enough.
Planned Parenthood v. Casey kept Roe’s central holding but replaced its trimester framework with an “undue burden” test.

overview.text: Edward Hopper was an American realist painter and printmaker whose art examines modern American life in urban and rural settings. His distinctive approach uses solitude, light, and shadow to create quiet scenes that invite reflection.

Hopper often set his paintings in New York’s architectural landscapes or the serene environments of New England. His work turns commonplace subjects into subdued drama, especially in scenes that suggest isolation, contemplation, and stories beyond what is directly shown.

key_facts.text: Hopper was born in Nyack, New York, and studied at the New York School of Art under William Merritt Chase and Robert Henri.
He worked in several media, including oil painting, watercolor, and etching.
Nighthawks (1942) is a major example of Hopper’s interest in quiet, introspective scenes from everyday life.
In 1924, Hopper married fellow artist Josephine Nivison, who modeled for many of his works and helped manage his career.

overview.text: Louisa May Alcott (1832–1888) was an American novelist, short-story writer, and poet best known for Little Women (1868). Her career also included fiction for adults and Hospital Sketches, based on her service as a nurse during the American Civil War. Raised in New England by parents associated with transcendentalism, Alcott was encouraged to write early. Financial hardship led her to take other jobs while seeking income from writing. Little Women was loosely based on her childhood with three sisters, linking her life to her most famous novel.

key_facts.text: The sequels named in her biography are Good Wives (1869), Little Men (1871), and Jo’s Boys (1886).
Hospital Sketches brought Alcott critical success in the 1860s.
She sometimes published adult sensation novels and lurid short stories under the pen name A. M. Barnard.
Alcott was an abolitionist and feminist who supported reform movements including temperance and women’s suffrage.

overview.text: In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Artemis is associated with hunting, wilderness, wild animals, childbirth, care of children, and chastity. She is the daughter of Leto and Zeus and the twin sister of Apollo; one account says she was born first and helped at Apollo’s birth. Her Roman equivalent is Diana.

Myths portray Artemis as a wilderness huntress accompanied by nymphs. After the hunter Actaeon saw her bathing, she changed him into a deer, and his dogs killed him. In the Trojan War tradition, Artemis demanded compensation after Agamemnon killed her sacred deer. Later tradition identified her with Selene, the personification of the Moon.

key_facts.text: Artemis was worshipped as a protector of children—especially girls—and animal cubs, as well as a goddess of childbirth and midwifery.
She was one of the three major virgin goddesses, alongside Athena and Hestia.
Her symbols included the bow, arrow, and quiver; the deer was sacred to her.
Her great temple at Ephesus was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World before it was burned.

overview.text: Gas is a state of matter with no fixed shape or volume and is a compressible form of fluid. Its particles are separated by much more space than particles in liquids or solids; this separation can make some gases invisible. Gases may exist as pure substances or mixtures, and the gaseous state is described as occurring between the liquid and plasma states.

key_facts.text: Neon is an example of a gas made of individual atoms.
Oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide are examples of gases made of molecules.
Air is a mixture of gases.
At extremely low temperatures, high-density atomic gases may be classified as Bose gases or Fermi gases based on their statistical behavior.

overview.text: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the Solar System’s second-largest planet after Jupiter. It is a gas giant with an average radius about nine times Earth’s, but its average density is much lower. Saturn takes about 29.45 years to orbit the Sun.

Saturn has a bright, extensive ring system made mostly of ice particles, along with rocky debris and dust. It has many moons, including Titan, its largest moon and the second-largest moon in the Solar System. Titan is also the only moon known here to have a substantial atmosphere.

key_facts.text: Ammonia crystals in Saturn’s upper atmosphere give the planet its pale yellow color.
Saturn’s interior is thought to include a rocky core, metallic hydrogen, liquid hydrogen and helium, and an outer gaseous layer.
Winds in Saturn’s atmosphere can reach about 1,800 kilometers per hour.
Titan is larger than Mercury but less massive than Mercury.

overview.text: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a laboratory method for rapidly making many copies of a chosen DNA sequence. Repeated temperature cycles separate DNA strands, allow short primers to attach to matching sequences, and let a thermostable DNA polymerase build new strands. The newly made DNA becomes a template in later cycles, producing exponential amplification.

PCR matters because it can amplify very small amounts of DNA for genetic testing, biomedical research, ancient-DNA analysis, forensic identification, and detection of infectious agents. Kary Mullis developed the technique at Cetus Corporation in 1983.

key_facts.text: Taq polymerase is a heat-stable enzyme originally isolated from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus.
The main DNA-targeting reagents in PCR are primers, which are short DNA fragments complementary to the target region, and DNA polymerase.
Kary Mullis and Michael Smith jointly received the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
PCR applications include diagnosing genetic disorders, DNA profiling and parentage testing, and nucleic-acid tests for infectious diseases.

overview.text: Carbon is a nonmetallic element with the symbol C and atomic number 6; it belongs to group 14 of the periodic table. Each carbon atom can form up to four covalent bonds, allowing an unusual variety of compounds and polymers. This versatility, together with carbon’s abundance, makes it the common element of all known life; carbon is also the second most abundant element by mass in the human body, after oxygen.

Carbon atoms can join in different arrangements called allotropes, whose properties can differ dramatically. Graphite is black, soft, and electrically conductive, whereas diamond is transparent, extremely hard, and a poor electrical conductor. Other named allotropes include amorphous carbon, fullerenes, carbon nanotubes, and graphene.

key_facts.text: Three isotopes occur naturally: carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, while carbon-14 is radioactive and has a half-life of about 5,700 years.
Carbon’s most common oxidation state in inorganic compounds is +4; +2 occurs in carbon monoxide and some transition-metal carbonyl complexes.
Major inorganic carbon sources include limestone, dolomite, and carbon dioxide; coal, peat, oil, and methane clathrates are important organic deposits.
At standard temperature and pressure, graphite is the most thermodynamically stable carbon allotrope.

overview.text: Shinzō Abe (1954–2022) was a Japanese politician who led the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and served as prime minister in 2006–07 and again from 2012–20. His return to office made him the first former Japanese prime minister to do so since 1948; his nearly nine years in office made him Japan’s longest-serving prime minister.

Abe is closely associated with “Abenomics,” his effort to counter Japan’s economic stagnation, and with a more assertive security policy. His conservative nationalism and views on Japan’s wartime history were controversial. In 2022, he was assassinated in Nara while giving a campaign speech.

key_facts.text: Abe came from a prominent political family: his father was LDP politician Shintaro Abe, and his grandfather was Prime Minister Nobusuke Kishi.
In 2007, Abe initiated the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue involving Japan, the United States, Australia, and India.
A 2015 security law permitted Japan’s Self-Defense Forces to deploy overseas under certain strict conditions, provoking protests.
Tetsuya Yamagami killed Abe in 2022; he confessed that Abe’s alleged ties to the Unification Church motivated the attack.

overview.text: The Salem witch trials were hearings and prosecutions of people accused of witchcraft in colonial Massachusetts from February 1692 to May 1693. The accusations began in Salem Village, now Danvers, but spread to other communities, including Andover and Topsfield. The courts and hangings were held in Salem Town, the regional center for Salem Village.

The episode is remembered as a case of mass hysteria and as a warning about false accusations, religious extremism, isolation, and failures of due process. The trials ended after doubts arose about the validity of the “spectral evidence” used in convictions; later, Massachusetts officials declared the proceedings unlawful and reversed the convictions.

key_facts.text: More than 200 people were accused; 30 were found guilty, and 19 were hanged—14 women and 5 men.
Giles Corey died under torture after refusing to enter a plea, while at least five others died in jail without trial.
Several accusers, mostly teenage girls, later admitted that they had fabricated their charges.
The Massachusetts General Court declared the trials unlawful in 1702, and the colonial legislature annulled the convictions in 1711.

overview.text: Thomas Woodrow Wilson (1856–1924), the 28th U.S. president, served from 1913 to 1921. A former Princeton president and New Jersey governor, he pursued Progressive-era reform through his “New Freedom” agenda. His administration helped begin the modern income tax and created the Federal Reserve System.

Wilson initially kept the United States neutral after World War I began in 1914, but in April 1917 he asked Congress to declare war on Germany after unrestricted submarine warfare sank American merchant ships. He later issued the Fourteen Points and promoted the League of Nations at the Paris Peace Conference, expressing the foreign-policy approach known as Wilsonian idealism.

key_facts.text: In 1912, Wilson defeated William Howard Taft and Theodore Roosevelt, becoming the first Southerner elected president since Zachary Taylor in 1848.
During his first year in office, Wilson authorized widespread racial segregation in the federal bureaucracy and opposed women’s suffrage.
Wilson narrowly won reelection in 1916 over Republican Charles Evans Hughes.
A stroke in October 1919 left Wilson incapacitated; his wife and physician controlled his affairs, and no significant decisions were made.

overview.text: Australia, officially the Commonwealth of Australia, is a country comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, Tasmania, and many smaller islands. It is an environmentally varied continental landmass: the inhabited continent is described as the world’s flattest and driest, while the country includes interior deserts and tropical coastal rainforests. Australia is also classified as megadiverse, with its size contributing to its range of landscapes and climates.

key_facts.text: Australia is a federation of six states and ten territories.
Canberra is the capital; Sydney and Melbourne are the country’s most populous cities.
Its population is highly urbanised and concentrated along the eastern seaboard.
The ancestors of Aboriginal Australians began arriving from Southeast Asia 50,000–65,000 years ago; by British settlement, Aboriginal Australians spoke more than 250 distinct languages.
The colonies federated in 1901, forming the Commonwealth of Australia.

overview.text: Adeline Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) was an English writer and a major 20th-century modernist. She helped pioneer stream-of-consciousness narration as a literary device. After moving to London’s Bloomsbury district, she became a founding member of the influential Bloomsbury Group.

Her major interwar novels include Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), and Orlando (1928). She also wrote the feminist essay A Room of One’s Own (1929), and her work became central to feminist criticism in the 1970s.

key_facts.text: Woolf grew up in an intellectual family; her sister Vanessa Bell became a painter.
Woolf and Leonard Woolf established the Hogarth Press in 1917, which published much of her work.
Her later essay Three Guineas (1938) explored the roots of fascism in society.
Woolf began publishing professionally in 1904 and rose to prominence during the interwar period.

overview.text: Scotland, also called Alba in Scottish Gaelic, occupies the northern part of Great Britain and includes adjacent island groups, especially the Hebrides and Northern Isles. It borders England to the south, the Atlantic Ocean to the north and west, the North Sea to the east, and the Irish Sea to the southwest.

Scotland’s mainland is broadly divided into three regions: the mountainous Highlands in the north and northwest, the flatter Lowlands across the center, and the hilly Southern Uplands along the southern border, near England.

key_facts.text: Edinburgh is Scotland’s capital, while Glasgow is its largest and most populous city.
The Highlands contain Ben Nevis, the highest peak in the British Isles, rising to 1,345 meters.
In Scotland, “loch” can refer to either a lake or a saltwater inlet, especially along the deeply indented western coast.

overview.text: Frankenstein’s monster is a fictional character in Mary Shelley’s 1818 novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. In this Gothic story, Victor Frankenstein builds the creature in a laboratory through an ambiguous scientific method. The emotional monster tries to fit into human society but is shunned, leading him to seek revenge against Victor. He occupies a boundary between the usual roles of protagonist and antagonist.

key_facts.text: The subtitle connects Victor to Prometheus, the mythological figure who fashioned humans from clay and gave them fire.
Although “Frankenstein” is commonly applied to the creature, the name belongs to his creator, Victor Frankenstein, who later becomes the monster’s namesake.
A widely recognized screen version is Boris Karloff’s portrayal in the 1930s films Frankenstein, Bride of Frankenstein, and Son of Frankenstein; that version differs greatly from Shelley’s creature.

overview.text: Socrates (c. 470–399 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher of Classical Athens who wrote no texts of his own. The main surviving accounts come from Plato and Xenophon, especially Plato’s dialogues; through Plato, Socrates became a major influence on Western philosophy.

Because these accounts are dialogues by later writers and sometimes conflict, reconstructing Socrates’ exact philosophy is difficult. Plato’s Socrates is chiefly associated with examining ethics and knowledge, acknowledging his own ignorance, and searching for truth rather than teaching a settled system.

key_facts.text: The Socratic method, or elenchus, uses question-and-answer exchanges to test definitions and reveal contradictions in an interlocutor’s beliefs.
Socratic moral intellectualism links virtue with knowledge; a related claim is that people do wrong through ignorance rather than knowingly choosing what is bad.
In 399 BC, Socrates was accused of impiety and corrupting the youth, convicted, and sentenced to death. Plato’s account says he died by poison after refusing offers to help him escape.

overview.text: The Fault in Our Stars is a novel by John Green, published in 2012. Hazel Grace Lancaster narrates the story; she is a 16-year-old with thyroid cancer affecting her lungs. At a support group, she meets Augustus Waters, a 17-year-old who survived osteosarcoma, and falls in love with him. Their relationship connects the novel’s central subjects of illness and love.

The title comes from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar. In the play, Cassius tells Brutus that people are responsible for their circumstances rather than the stars, giving the novel’s title a literary connection beyond its plot.

key_facts.text: Green’s experience as a student chaplain in a children’s hospital helped inspire the novel.
The novel is dedicated to Esther Earl, who died of thyroid cancer in 2010 at age 16.
A 2014 American film adaptation was directed by Josh Boone and starred Shailene Woodley and Ansel Elgort.

overview.text: Cambodia, officially the Kingdom of Cambodia, is a country in mainland Southeast Asia. It borders Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam, has a coast on the Gulf of Thailand, and is centered on a low-lying plain linked to the Mekong River and Tonlé Sap. Phnom Penh is its capital and largest city.

Cambodia is strongly associated with the Khmer civilization and Angkor Wat, a famous religious complex built during the Khmer Empire. Its modern history includes independence from France, civil war, and the Khmer Rouge regime, which ruled from 1975 to 1979 and carried out the Cambodian genocide.

key_facts.text: Tonlé Sap is Southeast Asia’s largest lake.
Jayavarman II’s declaration as king in 802 marked the beginning of the Khmer Empire.
Cambodia became independent from France in 1953.
The Khmer Rouge were ousted during the Cambodian–Vietnamese War in 1979.

overview.text: The United States census is the Constitution-mandated federal census conducted every ten years. It includes U.S. territories, and the Census Bureau is responsible for conducting it.

The 2020 census invited every household to respond online, by phone, or on paper. In the years between decennial censuses, the Bureau issues estimates based on surveys and statistical models, especially the Population Estimates Program and American Community Survey.

key_facts.text: The first census after the American Revolution was taken in 1790 under Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson.
There have been 24 federal censuses since 1790.
From 1940 through 2000, a supplemental “long form” went to only some households and asked additional socioeconomic and housing questions.
The population census is separate from the Census of Agriculture, overseen by the USDA since 1997, and from censuses conducted by state or local governments.

overview.text: India, officially the Republic of India, is a large country in South Asia. It borders the Indian Ocean, with the Arabian Sea to the southwest and the Bay of Bengal to the southeast. Its land borders connect it with Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar; Sri Lanka and the Maldives are nearby across the Indian Ocean.

India’s geography is linked to both long human history and environmental diversity. Settled life in the western Indus River basin developed into the Indus Valley Civilisation in the third millennium BCE. The country includes four biodiversity hotspots and protected habitats that support wildlife.

key_facts.text: India’s neighbors are Pakistan to the west; China, Nepal, and Bhutan to the north; and Bangladesh and Myanmar to the east.
In 1956, India reorganized its states largely along linguistic lines, strengthening regional language identity and encouraging regional literature and cinema.
In 1947, British India was partitioned into the independent dominions of India and Pakistan; the partition was accompanied by large-scale loss of life and unprecedented migration.
Buddhism and Jainism arose during India’s early urbanizing period. Islam, Christianity, Judaism, and Zoroastrianism later became established on parts of India’s southern and western coasts.

overview.text: An electron is an elementary subatomic particle with a negative electric charge. Atoms contain electrons along with protons and neutrons, but electrons are far less massive. In an atom, an electron’s matter wave occupies an orbital around the positively charged nucleus; the arrangement and energy of the electrons help determine the atom’s chemical properties.

The outermost, or valence, electrons are least tightly bound and can be shared or transferred to form bonds and facilitate chemical reactions. Electron behavior also connects atomic physics to technology: delocalized electrons carry charge and heat through metals, while controllable charge carriers in semiconductors support modern electronics. Free electrons can be formed into beams for tools such as electron microscopes and particle accelerators.

key_facts.text: Electrons have almost 2,000 times less mass than protons and neutrons.
The inner electron shells form the atomic core, while valence electrons are the least tightly bound.
In semiconductors, the number of mobile electrons and holes can be adjusted through factors such as doping, temperature, voltage, and radiation.
Free-electron beams in a vacuum can be accelerated and focused for applications including electron microscopy, lithography, welding, and particle acceleration.

overview.text: In ancient Greek mythology and religion, Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter who becomes queen of the underworld after Hades abducts her and takes her into marriage. Her descent and cyclical return to the surface connect her with spring and vegetation, especially grain: crops disappear into the earth when sown, then sprout and are harvested.

With Demeter, Persephone was central to the Eleusinian Mysteries, religious rites associated with a promised happy afterlife. In cult, she was often called Kore (“the Girl”), and her Latin name is Proserpina.

key_facts.text: The Eleusinian Mysteries were based on ancient agrarian cults, although their origins are uncertain.
In Epizephyrian Locris, in modern Calabria, Persephone was worshiped as a goddess of marriage and childbirth.
Classical Greek art often shows Persephone being carried away by Hades; other images portray her robed and holding a sheaf of grain.
Roman tradition identified Proserpina with Libera, an Italic goddess.

overview.text: The speed of light in vacuum, written c, is the speed of electromagnetic waves when no material slows them. Its exact value is 299,792,458 meters per second, commonly rounded to 300,000 kilometers per second. Relativity treats c as the same for all observers and as the upper limit for the travel of information, matter, and energy.

The finite travel time of light matters across space: distant starlight shows objects as they were in the past, and signals to spacecraft can take hours. Light and other electromagnetic waves move more slowly through materials such as glass, while the ratio between vacuum speed and material speed is called the refractive index.

key_facts.text: The meter is defined using the distance light travels in vacuum during 1/299,792,458 of a second, making c an exact value rather than a measured approximation.
Visible light, other electromagnetic radiation, massless particles, and gravitational waves travel at c in vacuum; particles with rest mass can approach but not reach it.
A material’s refractive index is n = c/v. Typical visible light travels in glass at about c/1.5, or roughly 200,000 kilometers per second.
Ole Rømer showed that light is not instantaneous by studying Jupiter’s moon Io. Maxwell connected light with electromagnetic waves, and Einstein made c central to relativity and the equation E = mc².

overview.text: Chandragupta Maurya founded and became the first emperor of the Maurya Empire, based in Magadha in the Indian subcontinent. He rose during unrest after Alexander the Great’s Indian campaign, defeated the Nanda dynasty, and expanded his power into the eastern Indus Valley and Punjab. The exact chronology of these conquests remains debated.

His expansion reached parts of the western Indus Valley and possibly eastern Afghanistan; a marriage alliance connected him with Seleucus I Nicator. The play Mudrarakshasa presents Chanakya as Chandragupta’s mentor and later minister. The empire established under Chandragupta reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka.

key_facts.text: Chandragupta’s reign is conventionally dated to about 320–298 BCE.
The Maurya Empire included Gujarat and a broad network of cities and trade routes.
Accounts of his origins are legendary, while surviving descriptions of his reign come mainly from later Greek, Roman, and Indian religious sources.
Mauryan administration was decentralized, involving provinces, local governments, and large autonomous regions.
The Maurya period is associated in the supplied account with economic prosperity, reforms, and infrastructure expansion.

overview.text: To Kill a Mockingbird is a 1960 Southern Gothic novel by American author Harper Lee and a classic of modern American literature. It is widely read in U.S. middle and high schools. The novel treats serious subjects, including racial inequality and rape, while also using warmth and humor. Its primary themes are racial injustice and loss of innocence. It also addresses class, courage, compassion, and gender roles in the Deep South. The book emphasizes tolerance and condemns prejudice, though its use of racial epithets has led to challenges in classrooms.

key_facts.text: The novel won the Pulitzer Prize in the year after its release.
Its plot and characters are loosely based on Lee’s family, neighbors, and a 1936 event near her hometown of Monroeville, Alabama.
A 1962 film adaptation directed by Robert Mulligan, with a screenplay by Horton Foote, won an Oscar.
Lee had no other published book until Go Set a Watchman appeared in 2015; that work was described as an earlier draft of To Kill a Mockingbird.

overview.text: Spartacus was a Thracian gladiator who became one of the leaders of the Third Servile War, a major slave uprising against the Roman Republic. His revolt began in 73 BCE, when he and roughly 70 other gladiators escaped from a training school near Capua.

The rebellion grew into a serious challenge to Roman authority before being defeated in 71 BCE by forces led by Marcus Licinius Crassus. Spartacus is an important but partly obscure historical figure: the main surviving accounts were written long afterward, disagree with one another, and offer no eyewitness or slave perspective.

key_facts.text: The escaped gladiators defeated several Roman military units, and their diverse force later expanded far beyond its original size.
Spartacus was presumed to have died in the final battle, but his body was never identified.
After the revolt, 6,000 captured rebels were crucified along the Appian Way.
Plutarch and Appian provide the fullest surviving narratives, but both wrote more than a century after Spartacus’s death.
Scholars debate Spartacus’s goals; surviving accounts do not specifically say that he intended to end slavery throughout the Roman Republic.

overview.text: Jerusalem is an ancient city in the Southern Levant, situated on a plateau in the Judaean Mountains between the Mediterranean Sea and the Dead Sea. It is sacred to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam, making it a major religious center and a prominent subject in Middle Eastern geography.

Jerusalem remains central to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Both Israel and Palestine claim it as their capital: Israel maintains major governmental institutions there, while Palestine envisions it as its seat of power. Neither claim is widely recognized internationally.

key_facts.text: The Old City’s historic walls were rebuilt under Ottoman ruler Suleiman the Magnificent in 1538; its four quarters are Armenian, Christian, Jewish, and Muslim.
Settlement in the City of David area dates to the 4th millennium BCE; by the 9th century BCE, Jerusalem was a religious and administrative center of the Kingdom of Judah.
In Islam, Jerusalem is regarded as the third-holiest city after Mecca and Medina and is associated with Muhammad’s Night Journey.
The Old City contains major religious sites including the Western Wall, Dome of the Rock, Al-Aqsa Mosque Compound, and Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

overview.text: Islam is a monotheistic Abrahamic religion that originated in Mecca around 610 CE, when Muslims believe Muhammad received his first revelation through Gabriel. Muslims believe God is one and regard the Quran as God’s final revelation; Muhammad is considered the final prophet. Islam recognizes earlier prophetic figures such as Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Its Five Pillars organize major acts of worship, while Islamic law (Sharia) addresses many areas of life. Islam expanded beyond Arabia under the Rashidun and Umayyad Caliphates. Its two main branches are Sunni and Shia, which share Islam’s foundational beliefs despite differences in history, theology, law, and practice.

key_facts.text: The Five Pillars are Shahada (profession of faith), Salah (daily prayers), Zakat (almsgiving), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).
The Sunnah consists of Muhammad’s teachings and normative examples; accounts that document them are called Hadith.
The two major Islamic festivals are Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. The three holiest sites are in Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem.
The Sunni-Shia split began with disagreements over succession to Muhammad and later developed wider differences, although both branches share Islam’s fundamental foundations.

overview.text: Peter I, known as Peter the Great, ruled Russia jointly with his brother Ivan V until 1696, then alone. He was tsar from 1682 to 1721 and Russia’s first emperor from 1721 until his death in 1725. His reign combined long wars with major administrative and cultural reforms.

Victory over Sweden in the Great Northern War gave Russia territory on the eastern Baltic and helped it become an empire. Peter promoted Westernized institutions, industry, education, and government reforms, and founded Saint Petersburg on the Neva River, moving the capital there from Moscow in 1712.

key_facts.text: Peter’s Azov campaigns were followed by the creation of a Russian navy.
He introduced the Julian calendar in 1699 and, in 1703, Russia’s first newspaper and a reformed civil script.
His administrative changes included the Governing Senate in 1711, the Collegium in 1717, and the Table of Ranks in 1722.
The Russian Academy of Sciences and Saint Petersburg State University were founded in 1724 during his reign.

overview.text: Jamaica is an island country in the Caribbean and the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles, after Cuba and Hispaniola. It lies south of Cuba and west of Hispaniola, the island shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic. Kingston is its capital and largest city.

Jamaica was under Spanish rule before England conquered it in 1655, after which it became part of the British West Indies. Its plantation economy depended on enslaved Africans until emancipation in 1838; Jamaica became independent from the United Kingdom on August 6, 1962.

key_facts.text: Jamaica is identified as the birthplace of reggae and the Rastafari religion; related genres include dub, ska, and dancehall.
The country has international prominence in cricket, sprinting, and athletics.
Tourism, including resort tourism, is a major part of Jamaica’s economy.

overview.text: The Little Mermaid (Danish: Den lille havfrue; also translated as The Little Sea Maid) is a literary fairy tale by Danish author Hans Christian Andersen. First published in 1837 in a collection of fairy tales for children, it follows a young mermaid princess willing to give up her life in the sea to gain a human soul. The story has been analyzed for its themes and for combining a tragic narrative with a happy ending.

key_facts.text: The tale’s original Danish title is Den lille havfrue.
It has been adapted into musical theatre, anime, ballet, opera, and film.
A mermaid statue stands in Copenhagen, Denmark, where the story was written and first published.

overview.text: In 1803, the United States acquired the Louisiana territory from the French First Republic for $15 million. The purchase covered most of the Mississippi River’s drainage basin west of the river. Because France controlled only a small part of this region, the transaction largely gave the United States the right to pursue Native American lands through treaties or conquest, excluding other colonial powers.

President Thomas Jefferson wanted control of New Orleans, a crucial Mississippi River port. James Monroe and Robert R. Livingston were sent to negotiate for it, but French officials offered the entire territory instead. The resulting acquisition extended U.S. sovereignty west of the Mississippi and nearly doubled the country’s nominal size.

key_facts.text: Napoleon’s France regained Louisiana from Spain in 1800, but military setbacks in Saint-Domingue and the threat of war with Britain encouraged France to sell it.
The U.S. negotiators dealt with François Barbé-Marbois, France’s treasury minister, during the purchase negotiations.
The acquisition included New Orleans and the areas that now make up all of Arkansas, Missouri, Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas, and Nebraska.
The purchase’s western boundary was later settled with Spain through the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819, while its northern boundary was adjusted by the Treaty of 1818 with Britain.

overview.text: Spanish (español), also called Castilian (castellano), is a Romance language in the Indo-European family. It developed from Vulgar Latin on the Iberian Peninsula and originated in the Kingdom of Castile. Today it is a global language used mainly in Spain and the Americas. Spanish is official in 21 countries and is one of the six official languages of the United Nations. Its international importance is also reflected in its use by organizations such as the UN and European Union and in its widespread teaching as a foreign language.

key_facts.text: Spanish belongs to the Ibero-Romance group, which developed from several Iberian dialects of Vulgar Latin after the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
The oldest Latin texts showing traces of Spanish date to the 9th century; systematic written use began in Toledo in the 13th century.
Spanish colonialism helped carry the language overseas, especially to the Americas.
About three-quarters of modern Spanish vocabulary is Latin in origin, including Latin borrowings from Ancient Greek.
Spanish is one of the world’s most widely taught foreign languages, alongside English and French.

overview.text: Cuneiform is a writing system of the ancient Near East, named for the wedge-shaped impressions that form its signs. It was originally developed to write Sumerian in southern Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), and it is the earliest known writing system.

Cuneiform matters in world history because it preserved written records across several ancient Near Eastern languages. Akkadian texts, attested from the 24th century BC onward, make up most of the cuneiform record, while later adaptations included Hittite and other languages.

key_facts.text: The name comes from the Latin cuneus, meaning “wedge,” referring to the script’s characteristic impressions.
Cuneiform was adapted for languages including Eblaite, Elamite, Hurrian, Luwian, and Urartian.
Modern rediscovery began with the publication of trilingual Achaemenid royal inscriptions at Persepolis; these were first deciphered in the early 19th century.
The modern study of cuneiform is called Assyriology, a field associated with early excavations of cuneiform libraries in ancient Assyria.

overview.text: Claude Debussy (1862–1918) was a French composer whose innovative music helped reshape late-19th- and early-20th-century classical music. He is often associated with musical Impressionism, though he rejected that label. His style developed through unusual harmony and orchestral coloring, influenced partly by Russian and Far Eastern music, Chopin, and Liszt.

Debussy’s major works include the orchestral pieces Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune and La mer, as well as the opera Pelléas et Mélisande. La mer was conceived as an alternative to the traditional symphony, while Pelléas et Mélisande brought him international fame in 1902.

key_facts.text: Pelléas et Mélisande was the only opera Debussy completed.
His piano music includes sets of 24 Préludes and 12 Études.
Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune dates from 1894; Debussy’s other orchestral works include Nocturnes and Images.
Debussy’s music influenced composers including Béla Bartók, Igor Stravinsky, George Gershwin, and Olivier Messiaen.

overview.text: Louis XIV was king of France from 1643 until his death in 1715. He began personal rule in 1661 after Cardinal Mazarin’s death and pursued a centralized state. His concentrated royal authority made him a major symbol of European absolutism, and he was associated with the titles “Sun King” and “Louis the Great.”

His court at the Palace of Versailles helped bring nobles into the royal system, while his patronage supported French Baroque architecture and the arts. France became a leading European power during his reign, but repeated wars placed heavy demands on its resources and left the kingdom war-weary and deeply in debt.

key_facts.text: Louis revoked the Edict of Nantes, removing rights from Huguenot Protestants and causing many to convert or emigrate.
Major conflicts during his personal rule included the Franco-Dutch War, the Nine Years’ War, and the War of the Spanish Succession.
His cultural program supported figures such as Molière, Racine, Lully, and Le Nôtre; his era was called the “Grand Siècle.”
His reign lasted 72 years and 110 days, described in the material as the longest of any sovereign monarch in history.

overview.text: The Sahara is a vast desert covering much of North Africa. At about 9.2 million square kilometers, it is the world’s largest hot desert and the third-largest desert overall, after the deserts of Antarctica and the northern Arctic. It does not include every part of North Africa: fertile Mediterranean coastal areas, the Atlas Mountains, and the Nile Valley are distinct landscapes.

The desert extends from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea and from the Mediterranean southward to the Sahel, a belt of semi-arid tropical savanna. Its varied landscape includes mountain regions and named areas such as the Ténéré and Libyan deserts, rather than being one uniform expanse of sand.

key_facts.text: The Sahel forms the Sahara’s southern boundary, including areas around the Niger River valley and Sudan.
Major regions include the western Sahara, Ahaggar Mountains, Tibesti Mountains, Aïr Mountains, Ténéré, and Libyan Desert.
Over hundreds of thousands of years, the Sahara has repeatedly shifted between desert and savanna grassland.
These long-term changes are linked to Earth’s axial precession and resulting changes in the North African monsoon.

overview.text: Moctezuma Xocoyotzin—often called Montezuma II—was the ninth emperor of the Aztec, or Mexica, Empire. He ruled from about 1502 or 1503 to 1520. During his reign, the empire reached its greatest size, and Indigenous Mesoamerican civilizations first came into contact with Europeans.

His rule ended during the opening stages of the Spanish conquest: Hernán Cortés and his men seized Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, and Moctezuma was killed. His historical image is disputed: Spanish accounts portray him as weak-willed or superstitious, while other portrayals range from great leader to tyrant. Accounts also disagree about who killed him.

key_facts.text: Moctezuma expanded the empire southward to Xoconosco in Chiapas and the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, incorporating Zapotec and Yopi peoples.
He changed the earlier meritocratic social system and widened the divide between nobles and commoners, including by barring commoners from work in royal palaces.
Two rulers succeeded him, but their reigns were brief, and the Aztec Empire quickly collapsed afterward.
Moctezuma’s name appears in European sources as Moctezuma II; “Montezuma” is another common form.

overview.text: The Maya were a Mesoamerican civilization whose history extended from antiquity into the early modern period. They developed across present-day southeastern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize, western Honduras, and El Salvador. Maya society is especially associated with temple architecture, glyphic writing, art, mathematics, calendars, and astronomy.

During the Classic period, Maya civilization consisted of many city-states connected by trade networks. Tikal and Calakmul became powerful rivals, while Chichen Itza later rose in the north. Maya elites recorded history and ritual knowledge in hieroglyphic texts and used interlocking calendars and mathematics that included an early explicit zero.

key_facts.text: The first Maya cities developed around 750 BCE, and hieroglyphic writing was in use in the region by the third century BCE.
The ninth century saw widespread political collapse in the central Maya region, including civil wars, abandoned cities, and a shift of population northward.
Classic-period rule often centered on a “divine king,” believed to mediate between humans and the supernatural; kingship was usually, though not always, patrilineal.
Spanish conquest began in the sixteenth century, and Nojpetén, identified as the last Maya city, fell in 1697.
The Maya remain a living group of peoples whose descendants inhabit much of the same region and speak many surviving Mayan languages.

overview.text: The Red Badge of Courage is Stephen Crane’s 1895 war novel set during the American Civil War. It follows Henry Fleming, a young Union private who flees battle, feels ashamed, and longs for a wound—a “red badge of courage”—to counteract his cowardice. When his regiment faces the enemy again, Henry serves as its flag-bearer.

Crane emphasizes Henry’s inner experience, especially fear, rather than treating war as only an external sequence of events. Realistic battle scenes, recurring color imagery, and an ironic tone support themes of maturation, heroism, cowardice, and nature’s indifference. The novel drew widespread acclaim soon after publication and became a bestseller; it is described as a major American text.

key_facts.text: The novel first appeared in shortened newspaper installments in December 1894; the full book was published in October 1895.
Crane was born after the Civil War and had not experienced battle firsthand; he used contemporary and written accounts as material.
The fictional battle is believed to draw on the Battle of Chancellorsville, though that identification is uncertain.
Crane called the book’s focus a “psychological portrayal of fear,” while critics debate its allegorical and symbolic dimensions.
The novel has been adapted for the screen several times and has never gone out of print.

overview.text: The pedal harp, also called the concert harp, is a large, technologically modern harp designed mainly for art music (formal concert music). It may be performed solo, used in a chamber ensemble, or included in an orchestra.

Its defining feature is a pedal system that alters the pitches of its strings. This allows the instrument to play works in any key, an important capability for harmonically complex music from the Romantic period and later twentieth-century classical music.

key_facts.text: A typical pedal harp has 47 strings.
Its strings are arranged at seven strings per octave, giving it a range of six and a half octaves.
“Concert harp” is another name for the pedal harp.

overview.text: Les Misérables is a French epic historical novel by Victor Hugo. It follows several characters, with particular attention to the struggles of the ex-convict Jean Valjean and his experience of redemption. Against a backdrop of French history, the novel explores law and grace, justice, politics, religion, moral philosophy, and romantic and familial love. Its broad scope places individual lives alongside national history, and the work has been adapted for the stage, film, and television.

key_facts.text: The novel was first published on 31 March 1862.
Its narrative begins in 1815 and culminates in the 1832 June Rebellion in Paris.
In English-speaking contexts, the original French title is usually retained; alternatives include The Miserables, The Wretched, and The Miserable Ones.
The work has been adapted numerous times for film, television, and the stage, including as a musical.

overview.text: A supernova is a powerful, bright explosion of a star. Most arise through one of two broad mechanisms: runaway nuclear fusion in a white dwarf, or the gravitational collapse of a massive star’s core. A white dwarf may be triggered by gaining matter from a companion or by a stellar merger.

Supernovae can briefly shine as brightly as an entire galaxy. Their expelled material drives a shock wave that sweeps up surrounding gas and dust into a supernova remnant; these events also supply elements to interstellar space and can help trigger new star formation.

key_facts.text: A collapsed massive star may leave behind a neutron star or black hole, while a white-dwarf explosion can destroy the star completely.
Core collapse occurs when fusion can no longer produce enough energy to oppose the star’s gravity, especially once iron fusion begins.
SN 1987A occurred in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, in 1987.
Supernovae are a major source of cosmic rays and may also produce gravitational waves.

overview.text: The French Revolution was a period of political and societal change in France that began with the Estates General in 1789 and ended with the Coup of 18 Brumaire on November 9, 1799. It grew from financial crisis, social distress, and political and economic problems that the existing regime could not manage. Many of its ideas are considered fundamental principles of liberal democracy and remain important in French political discourse.
The revolution transformed France’s government: the monarchy gave way to the First Republic, followed by the Reign of Terror, the Directory, and finally the Consulate under Napoleon Bonaparte.

key_facts.text: In June 1789, representatives of the Third Estate broke away from the Estates General and re-formed themselves as a National Assembly.
The Storming of the Bastille on July 14, 1789, was followed by the abolition of feudalism and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.
King Louis XVI’s attempted flight to Varennes in 1791 weakened confidence in the monarchy; the monarchy was replaced by the First Republic in September 1792.
During the Reign of Terror, the Committee of Public Safety was dominated by radical Jacobins led by Maximilien Robespierre; the Terror ended with the Thermidorian Reaction in July 1794.
The unstable Directory was replaced by the Consulate after the 1799 coup of 18 Brumaire, with Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul.

overview.text: Darius III was the thirteenth and final Achaemenid King of Kings of Persia, ruling from 336 to 330 BCE. His brief reign unfolded during the collapse of Achaemenid rule under Alexander the Great’s invasion. Alexander defeated Persian forces in several battles, destroyed Persepolis by fire in 330 BCE, and brought the Persian Empire effectively under his control. Before Alexander could reach him, Darius was killed by his relative Bessus.

key_facts.text: Darius was a distant member of the Achaemenid dynasty rather than a close successor. Before becoming king, he served as satrap of Armenia and oversaw the royal postal service.
He came to the throne after the poisoning of Artaxerxes IV Arses. Darius later forced the court official Bagoas to drink poison after discovering a plan against him.
Alexander began his invasion of the Persian Empire in 334 BCE, leading to several Persian defeats and the destruction of Persepolis in 330 BCE.
Darius was killed by Bessus, his relative and the satrap of Bactria, before Alexander reached him.

overview.text: South Korea, officially the Republic of Korea (ROK), is an East Asian country occupying the southern half of the Korean Peninsula. It borders North Korea along the Korean Demilitarized Zone.

After Japan’s surrender in World War II, Korea was divided into Soviet-occupied northern and U.S.-occupied southern zones. Failed reunification negotiations produced the Republic of Korea in the south in August 1948 and the DPRK in the north the following month. The 1950–53 Korean War ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty.

key_facts.text: The Yellow Sea lies west of South Korea, while the Sea of Japan lies to its east.
About half of South Korea’s population lives in the Seoul metropolitan area; Busan, Daegu, and Incheon are also identified as major cities.
The Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) achieved lasting unification and helped establish the basis of modern Korean identity.

overview.text: Bleeding Kansas, also called Bloody Kansas or the Border War, was a series of violent confrontations in Kansas Territory and nearby Missouri from 1854 to 1859. The central question was whether Kansas would permit slavery and enter the Union as a slave state or a free state. This local struggle reflected the nation’s larger sectional conflict over slavery.

The Kansas–Nebraska Act made the decision an example of popular sovereignty, meaning territorial settlers would vote on slavery rather than leaving the issue to Congress. Proslavery and antislavery settlers competed through elections, rival governments, raids, and violence. Kansas was ultimately admitted as a free state in 1861, and the conflict served as a prelude to the Civil War.

key_facts.text: The issue had national importance because Kansas’s two future senators could affect the closely divided U.S. Senate.
Some Missouri settlers with proslavery views entered Kansas and claimed to be residents in an effort to influence the decision.
Kansas developed rival political structures, including the proslavery Lecompton government and the antislavery governments associated with Lawrence and Topeka.
The struggle involved electoral fraud, raids, assaults, and murders; violence by proslavery forces prompted retaliatory raids by antislavery free-staters.
Kansas’s admission as a free state became effective on January 29, 1861, during the secession crisis.

overview.text: Franz Peter Schubert (1797–1828) was an Austrian composer of the late Classical and early Romantic eras. Although he lived only 31 years, he produced more than 1,000 compositions, including over 600 Lieder—German art songs—as well as symphonies, sacred music, operas, piano music, and chamber music.

Important Schubert associations include the songs “Erlkönig” and “Gretchen am Spinnrade,” the Trout Quintet, the “Unfinished” Symphony, and song cycles such as Winterreise. Interest in his music increased greatly after his death, when composers including Mendelssohn, Schumann, Liszt, and Brahms discovered and championed his works.
