It is especially associated with African American cultural history because Central and West Harlem were the center of the Harlem Renaissance in the 1920s and 1930s, a major African American cultural movement. “Greater Harlem” can refer to a wider area that includes several surrounding neighborhoods.

key_facts.text: The neighborhood’s approximate boundaries are the Hudson River, Harlem River and 155th Street, Fifth Avenue, and 110th Street.
Harlem began as a Dutch village formally organized in 1658 and was named for Haarlem in the Netherlands.
Large numbers of African American residents arrived during the Great Migration in the early 20th century.
The Great Depression and post–World War II deindustrialization brought job losses, while the 21st century saw declining crime rates and gentrification.
Central Harlem is part of Manhattan Community District 10 and is served by the New York City Subway and local buses.

overview.text: Human hair is a protein filament produced by follicles in the dermis, the skin layer where those follicles are found. Across the body, follicles produce different kinds of hair, and hair is made mainly of protein, especially alpha-keratin. Hair matters in everyday life through growth, hair types, and care.

Hair also has cultural meaning. Hairstyles and hair removal differ across cultures and historical periods; hair can indicate personal beliefs or social position, including age, gender, or religion. This makes hair both a biological feature and a visible part of identity and social tradition.

key_facts.text: Hair is one of the distinguishing characteristics of mammals.
Human follicles produce thick terminal hair and fine vellus hair.
Except for areas of glabrous skin, the human body is covered in hair-producing follicles.
Hair is primarily a protein biomaterial, notably alpha-keratin.
Cultural attitudes toward hairstyles and hair removal vary across cultures and historical periods.

overview.text: Christopher Columbus was an Italian explorer and navigator from the Republic of Genoa who completed four transatlantic voyages for the Catholic Monarchs, Isabella I and Ferdinand II. His first voyage left Palos in August 1492 and reached an island in the Bahamas on October 12.

His expeditions inaugurated centuries of European exploration, conquest, and colonization in the Americas. The resulting Columbian Exchange transferred plants, animals, people, technology, diseases, and ideas between the Old World and New World. Columbus’s legacy also includes colonial violence: diseases contributed to the genocide of Hispaniola’s Indigenous peoples, who were subjected to enslavement and other mistreatment.

key_facts.text: Columbus planned to reach the East Indies by sailing west, hoping to profit from the spice trade; he never clearly abandoned his belief that he had reached the Far East.
The 1492 expedition used three ships, visited Cuba and Hispaniola, established a colony in present-day Haiti, and returned to Castile with captured Indigenous people.
His later voyages explored the Lesser Antilles in 1493, Trinidad and northern South America in 1498, and the eastern coast of Central America in 1502.
As colonial governor, Columbus faced accusations of significant brutality and was arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500 after conflicts with the Castilian Crown and colonial officials.

overview.text: Isis is a major goddess in ancient Egyptian religion and a key figure in the Osiris myth. In that story, she resurrects her slain brother and husband, Osiris, and produces and protects his heir, Horus. She was also believed to help the dead enter the afterlife and was regarded as the divine mother of the pharaoh, who was likened to Horus. People invoked her maternal aid in healing spells.

Her reputed magical power accompanied a broadening cult. During the first millennium BCE, Isis absorbed traits from other goddesses, and temples dedicated mainly to her were built in Egypt and Nubia. Greek and Roman worshippers later spread her cult across the Mediterranean, associating her with marriage, protection of ships, festivals, and initiation ceremonies.

key_facts.text: In art, Isis was commonly shown as a woman wearing a throne-like hieroglyph; later depictions sometimes gave her Hathor’s cow-horn-and-sun-disk headdress.
The temple of Philae was a religious center for both Egyptians and Nubians.
Greek devotees associated Isis with the invention of marriage and the protection of ships at sea.
Her worship ended amid the rise of Christianity during the fourth through sixth centuries CE.

overview.text: John Wilkes Booth was an American stage actor from Maryland’s prominent Booth theatrical family. During the Civil War, he became a Confederate sympathizer and spy who opposed President Abraham Lincoln and the abolition of slavery.

On April 14, 1865, Booth shot Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C.; Lincoln died the next morning. The assassination grew out of a broader conspiracy involving attacks planned against other government leaders, and it occurred shortly after Robert E. Lee’s army surrendered.

key_facts.text: Booth and his co-conspirators first planned to kidnap Lincoln, then changed their plan to murder Lincoln, Vice President Andrew Johnson, and Secretary of State William H. Seward.
Seward was severely wounded but recovered; Johnson was never attacked.
After fleeing south, Booth was found twelve days later hiding in a Virginia barn. He refused to surrender, and Union soldier Boston Corbett fatally shot him after the barn was set ablaze.
Four of the eight conspirators later convicted were hanged.

overview.text: Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) was an English philosopher and political theorist whose work helped establish modern political philosophy. His best-known book, Leviathan (1651), presented an influential formulation of social-contract theory. The book is closely associated with Hobbes’s account of the state of nature, described as a “war of all against all,” and with his advocacy of governance by an absolute sovereign as a response to human conflict and societal breakdown.

The destruction and brutality Hobbes observed during the English Civil War (1642–1651) heavily influenced this political outlook. His writings also profoundly influenced understandings of political structure and human nature.

key_facts.text: Hobbes studied at Oxford, graduated from Cambridge in 1608, and later tutored the Cavendish family while traveling in Europe.
His other major works include De Cive, De Corpore, De Homine, and the posthumously published Behemoth.
Alongside social-contract theory, Leviathan popularized ideas about laws of nature.
Hobbes also wrote about history, law, geometry, optics, theology, ethics, and classical translation, making him a polymath.

overview.text: France, officially the French Republic, is a country primarily located in Western Europe. Metropolitan France stretches from the Rhine to the Atlantic Ocean and from the Mediterranean Sea to the English Channel and North Sea. It borders several European countries, while also having a maritime border with the United Kingdom.

France’s geography extends beyond Europe through overseas regions and territories, including French Guiana in South America, Saint Pierre and Miquelon in the North Atlantic, the French West Indies, and islands in Oceania and the Indian Ocean. Paris is the capital and largest city.

key_facts.text: France’s European land neighbors are Belgium, Luxembourg, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Monaco, Andorra, and Spain.
French Guiana is an overseas region of France located in South America.
Saint Pierre and Miquelon is a French territory in the North Atlantic.
France has 18 integral regions, five of them overseas.

overview.text: France, officially the French Republic, is a country primarily in Western Europe whose overseas regions and territories extend to places in South America, the Caribbean, the Atlantic, Oceania, and the Indian Ocean. Paris is its capital and principal cultural and economic center. Its historical foundations include Celtic Gaul, Roman rule, the Frankish kingdom, and the development of West Francia into the Kingdom of France.

France is central to the study of European history through its monarchy, religious conflicts, the reign of Louis XIV, the French Revolution, Napoleon’s empire, and the republics that followed. It is also associated with major artistic, scientific, philosophical, and political developments, including the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the establishment of the Fifth Republic under Charles de Gaulle in 1958.

key_facts.text: Rome annexed the area inhabited by the Gauls in 51 BC, helping produce a distinctive Gallo-Roman culture.
The Treaty of Verdun in 843 divided the Carolingian Empire; West Francia later developed into the Kingdom of France.
During Louis XIV’s reign, France expanded its influence through warfare while experiencing major artistic and scientific flourishing.
The French Revolution began in 1789, overthrew the ancien régime, and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man.
Napoleon Bonaparte established the First French Empire, while the empire’s collapse eventually led through later political changes to the Fifth Republic in 1958.

overview.text: William Shakespeare (c. 1564–1616) was an English playwright, poet, and actor, born and raised in Stratford-upon-Avon. Often called the Bard of Avon, he is associated with plays, 154 sonnets, and long narrative poems; some other verses have uncertain authorship.

His London career included acting, writing, and part-ownership of a theatrical company. His works range from comedies and histories to tragedies such as Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, and Macbeth, followed by tragicomedies including The Winter’s Tale and The Tempest. They remain widely studied, performed, and reinterpreted.

key_facts.text: At 18, Shakespeare married Anne Hathaway; they had Susanna and twins Hamnet and Judith.
The Lord Chamberlain’s Men later became the King’s Men after James VI of Scotland ascended to the English throne.
Most of Shakespeare’s known works were produced between 1589 and 1613.
In 1623, John Heminges and Henry Condell published the First Folio, a collected edition containing 36 plays.

overview.text: Little Women is an American coming-of-age novel by Louisa May Alcott, first published in two volumes in 1868 and 1869. It follows Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy March as they move from childhood toward womanhood. Because the story draws loosely on Alcott’s life and that of her three sisters, it is often classified as autobiographical or semi-autobiographical.

One interpretation identifies domestic life, work, and true love as connected concerns in the sisters’ development and formation of individual identity. Sarah Elbert also describes the novel as combining elements of romantic children’s fiction with sentimental fiction, creating a distinctive literary form.

key_facts.text: The two original volumes were combined into one novel in 1880. In the United Kingdom, the second volume was titled Good Wives, a name supplied by the publisher.
Alcott later wrote two sequels featuring the March sisters: Little Men (1871) and Jo’s Boys (1886).
Little Women has been translated into numerous languages and frequently adapted for stage and screen.

overview.text: Georgia Totto O’Keeffe (1887–1986) was an American modernist painter and draftswoman whose seven-decade career remained largely independent of major art movements. She gained international recognition for paintings of natural forms, especially flowers, hills, and desert-inspired landscapes connected to places where she lived.

O’Keeffe developed an increasingly abstract style through charcoal drawings in 1915. In New York, she painted abstract city scenes and close-up flowers; from 1929 onward, the Southwest inspired landscapes and images of animal skulls. She moved to New Mexico permanently in 1949.

key_facts.text: Art dealer and photographer Alfred Stieglitz exhibited O’Keeffe’s work in 1916; their personal and professional relationship led to marriage in 1924.
O’Keeffe called her New York paintings “My New Yorks.”
Examples of her skull imagery include Cow’s Skull: Red, White, and Blue (1931) and Summer Days (1936).
Although her work has been associated with feminist interpretations, O’Keeffe preferred to be regarded simply as an artist rather than as a “woman artist.”

overview.text: The Milky Way, also called the Galaxy, is the galaxy containing the Solar System. Seen from Earth, it appears as a hazy band of light because many stars in its distant arms cannot be individually distinguished with the naked eye.

It is a barred spiral galaxy: its stars, gas, and dust are arranged in spiral-shaped regions around a central bulge and bar structure. At its center is Sagittarius A*, an intense radio source associated with a supermassive black hole.

key_facts.text: The Solar System lies about 27,000 light-years from the Galactic Center, near the inner edge of the Orion Arm.
The Milky Way has satellite galaxies and belongs to the Local Group, a larger collection of galaxies.
Galileo Galilei first resolved the Milky Way’s glowing band into individual stars using a telescope in 1610.
Observations by Edwin Hubble in 1923 established that the Milky Way is one of many galaxies, rather than the entire universe.

overview.text: Édouard Manet was a French modernist painter who became one of the first 19th-century artists to depict modern life. He is especially associated with The Luncheon on the Grass and Olympia, paintings that helped mark the beginning of modern art.

Manet’s direct, simple style challenged established artistic expectations and connected Realism with the emerging movement of Impressionism. His work was controversial at first but later became influential to younger and future painters.

key_facts.text: The Luncheon on the Grass premiered in 1863, and Olympia premiered in 1865.
Both paintings caused strong controversy among critics and the Academy of Fine Arts.
Manet was born into an upper-class family with strong political connections.
He abandoned a naval career planned for him in order to pursue painting.

overview.text: The Holodomor was a massive, largely human-caused famine in Soviet Ukraine from 1932 to 1933. It formed part of the wider Soviet famine of 1930–1933, which also affected other major grain-producing regions of the USSR.

Scholars link the disaster to agricultural collectivization and policies intended to industrialize the Soviet economy, while debating how far Joseph Stalin’s government deliberately targeted Ukrainians. Ukraine’s unusually high grain quotas made it especially vulnerable.

key_facts.text: Death-toll estimates vary: a 2003 international statement gave 7–10 million, while later scholarship estimated 3.5–5 million victims.
Soviet authorities banned public discussion of the famine until Mikhail Gorbachev’s glasnost reforms in the 1980s.
Since 2006, Ukraine, 33 other UN member states, and the European Parliament have recognized the Holodomor as genocide.
Whether the famine legally and historically constitutes genocide remains disputed because scholars differ over intentionality and the available documentary evidence.

overview.text: Mercury is the Solar System’s innermost and smallest planet, a rocky world with a cratered surface resembling Earth’s Moon. Its 88-Earth-day orbit and 58.65-Earth-day rotation create a 3:2 spin–orbit resonance, so a solar day lasts about 176 Earth days—twice its year. Mercury has an extremely thin exosphere, and its tiny axial tilt leaves polar craters permanently shadowed, where water ice may exist.

key_facts.text: Caloris Planitia is Mercury’s largest crater, measuring about 1,550 kilometers across.
Although it is closest to the Sun, Mercury is the second-hottest planet after Venus because it lacks an atmosphere that can trap heat.
Mariner 10 made the first successful flyby of Mercury; MESSENGER and BepiColombo later explored it as orbiters.
The planet’s English name comes from Mercurius, the Roman god associated with commerce, communication, and the gods’ messenger.

overview.text: The Creeper is a fictional hostile mob—an automated mobile enemy—in Minecraft. It can spawn in dark places, quietly approach a player, and then explode instead of attacking directly. The blast can destroy nearby blocks and hurt or kill players within range; its greenish appearance and near-silent behavior make it a stealth-based threat.

The character originated from a pig-model software bug: the pig’s length and height were accidentally switched. Markus “Notch” Persson chose to keep the odd result as a “creepy creature.” The Creeper later became a widely recognized Minecraft icon, appearing in franchise media, merchandise, advertising, and popular-culture parodies.

key_facts.text: The Creeper model first appeared in a Minecraft pre-alpha update on August 20, 2009; Creepers were introduced in another pre-alpha version on September 1.
Lightning can turn a Creeper into a “Charged Creeper.”
Creepers are hostile mobile non-player characters, often shortened to “mobs.”

overview.text: Edvard Munch (1863–1944) was a Norwegian painter who developed a distinctive style by treating his own emotional and psychological state as a subject. Illness and bereavement shaped his early experience, while travel and contacts with artists in Paris and Berlin influenced his use of color and artistic development.

The Scream (1893) is one of the most iconic and acclaimed images in Western art. Munch also developed The Frieze of Life, a series exploring deeply felt themes such as love, anxiety, jealousy, and betrayal, and produced an extensive body of graphic art and prints.

key_facts.text: Munch said The Scream began during a sunset walk in Kristiania, now Oslo, when he heard what he called an “enormous, infinite scream of nature.”
Between 1893 and 1910, Munch made two painted versions, two pastel versions, and several prints of The Scream.
In Paris, Munch encountered the color use of Paul Gauguin, Vincent van Gogh, and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec; in Berlin, he met August Strindberg.
His printmaking included etching, drypoint, and aquatint on copper plates; beginning in 1894, he also engraved directly onto copper.

overview.text: Natural rubber is a plant-derived elastomer, meaning a polymer that can stretch and recover. It consists mainly of polyisoprene, polymers of isoprene, with minor impurities. The material is associated with latex harvested from the Pará rubber tree (Hevea brasiliensis) and is used extensively in products and applications, either alone or with other materials. Its useful properties include high stretch and resilience, buoyancy, and waterproofness.

key_facts.text: Latex is a sticky, milky-white colloid collected by cutting the tree’s bark and gathering the fluid in vessels; this process is called tapping.
Manufacturers refine latex into rubber suitable for commercial processing.
Demand exceeded natural-rubber supplies by the late 19th century, helping prompt the chemical synthesis of synthetic rubber in 1909.
Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, and Cambodia are identified as leading rubber-producing countries.

overview.text: Harriet Tubman, born Araminta Ross, escaped slavery in 1849 and repeatedly returned to Maryland to help relatives and other enslaved people reach freedom through the Underground Railroad, a network of antislavery activists and safe houses. After the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, she helped guide escapees farther north into British North America (Canada).

During the Civil War, Tubman worked for the Union Army as a cook and nurse, then as an armed scout and spy. She helped guide the Combahee Ferry raid, which liberated more than 700 enslaved people. After the war, she supported women’s suffrage and helped establish a home for elderly African Americans.

key_facts.text: Tubman was also called “Moses,” and she claimed she never lost a person traveling with her.
She met John Brown in 1858 and helped plan and recruit supporters for his 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry.
A childhood head injury caused recurring dizziness, pain, and spells of hypersomnia; she interpreted vivid visions and dreams as premonitions from God.
The source credits Tubman with approximately 13 rescue missions involving about 70 enslaved people, including family and friends.
After the war, Tubman lived on property she had purchased in Auburn, New York, where she cared for her aging parents.

overview.text: Moses is a Hebrew prophet in Abrahamic religions, associated with leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt during the Exodus and with receiving divine law that became part of the Torah. Judaism and Samaritanism regard him as their most important prophet; Christianity and Islam also regard him as an important prophet.

In the Book of Exodus, Moses returns to Egypt after encountering an angel speaking from a burning bush, leads the Israelites out after the Ten Plagues, and receives the Ten Commandments at Mount Sinai. The same account places his death on Mount Nebo after 40 years of desert wandering.

key_facts.text: As an infant, Moses was hidden among Nile bulrushes to evade Pharaoh’s order; Pharaoh’s daughter found and adopted him.
Moses’ elder brother Aaron spoke for him because Moses objected that he could not speak eloquently.
The Exodus account says Moses died at age 120, within sight of the Promised Land.
Most scholars regard the biblical Moses as legendary but leave open the possibility of a Moses-like figure in the 13th century BCE.

overview.text: Great Expectations is Charles Dickens’s bildungsroman—a coming-of-age novel—about Pip, an orphan whose education is presented through his first-person narration. Set in Kent and London in the early-to-mid-19th century, it was first published as a serial in 1860–61.

Its central cast includes the escaped convict Abel Magwitch, eccentric Miss Havisham, cold Estella, and Joe Gargery, a kind blacksmith. Through stark images of poverty, prisons, chains, and violence, the novel examines wealth and poverty, love and rejection, and the eventual triumph of good over evil. Its characters have entered popular culture, and the novel has been translated and adapted widely.

key_facts.text: The novel first appeared in Dickens’s weekly periodical All the Year Round before Chapman & Hall published it in three volumes in October 1861.
Its opening scene is a graveyard encounter in which young Pip is accosted by the escaped convict Abel Magwitch.
The work received strong public response during its serial run and later maintained a favorable reputation among literary critics.

overview.text: Tutankhamun (also called Tutankhamen or King Tut) was a pharaoh of Egypt’s Eighteenth Dynasty who ruled c. 1332–1323 BCE and died at about age 18. Born Tutankhaten, he is associated with restoring traditional polytheistic worship after the earlier Atenist religious shift.

His modern public recognition is closely associated with the discovery of his tomb in 1922 by excavators led by Howard Carter. Although ancient robbers had entered it, the tomb retained much of its original contents, including the mummy, and contained more than 5,000 artifacts; his mask remains a popular symbol of ancient Egypt.

key_facts.text: The royal court moved from Amarna back to Memphis, while the cult of Amun at Thebes regained prominence.
Tutankhamun was succeeded by his vizier Ay, who was later succeeded by Horemheb, Tutankhamun’s former commander-in-chief.
Because his intended royal tomb was unfinished, he was buried in a small non-royal tomb adapted for him.
A 2012 proposal linked his death to malaria and a leg fracture, so the cause should be treated as uncertain.

overview.text: The Firebird (French: L’Oiseau de feu) is a ballet and orchestral concert work by Russian composer Igor Stravinsky, written for Sergei Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes in 1910. Michel Fokine created the original choreography, while Alexandre Benois and others helped develop a scenario drawn from Russian fairy tales about a Firebird whose power can bless or curse its owner.

Set in the castle of the evil immortal Koschei, the ballet follows Prince Ivan as he battles Koschei with help from the magical Firebird. Its music distinguishes mortal and supernatural forces through recurring leitmotifs and specialized orchestral techniques. The Paris premiere succeeded immediately, bringing Stravinsky international fame and leading to further collaborations with Diaghilev.

key_facts.text: Stravinsky later arranged three concert suites: in 1911, 1919, and 1945; the last included major reorchestration and structural changes.
The 1919 suite is identified as the most popular of the three.
The 1911 suite ends with the “Infernal Dance.”
Later choreographers have either preserved Fokine’s original choreography or created new productions using the music, sometimes with different settings or themes.

overview.text: Sam Houston was an American military general and statesman closely associated with the Texas Revolution. He led the Texian Army to victory at San Jacinto in 1836 and then became president of the Republic of Texas.

Houston later supported Texas annexation by the United States, served in the U.S. Senate, and became governor of Texas. His political career also included opposition to secession, although he was a slaveholder and was forced from office in 1861.

key_facts.text: Houston served as both the first and third president of the Republic of Texas.
Before moving to Texas, he served under Andrew Jackson in the War of 1812 and was elected governor of Tennessee in 1827.
He was the only person elected governor of two different U.S. states: Tennessee and Texas.
As a U.S. senator, Houston opposed the Kansas–Nebraska Act and later left the Democratic Party over it.
Houston opposed Southern secession and unsuccessfully tried to keep Texas out of the Confederacy at the beginning of the Civil War.

overview.text: George Walker Bush was the 43rd president of the United States, serving from 2001 to 2009. A Republican and former governor of Texas, he was the eldest son of George H. W. Bush, the 41st president. His 2000 victory over Al Gore followed a narrow, contested Electoral College result involving a Florida recount and the Supreme Court case Bush v. Gore.

The September 11 attacks reshaped Bush’s presidency. His administration began the War on Terror, invaded Afghanistan in an effort to overthrow the Taliban and destroy al-Qaeda, and invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein’s regime, citing claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction and ties to al-Qaeda. Domestic initiatives included No Child Left Behind and expanded surveillance powers under the Patriot Act.

key_facts.text: Bush won reelection in 2004, defeating Democrat John Kerry and winning the popular vote.
Bush initiated the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief in 2003 and later signed legislation creating Medicare Part D.
Bush launched a troop “surge” in Iraq in 2007; his administration was also criticized over Hurricane Katrina and detainee abuse at Abu Ghraib prison.
Near the end of his presidency, a financial crisis led Bush and Congress to support emergency measures including the Troubled Asset Relief Program.

overview.text: Edgar Allan Poe’s “The Tell-Tale Heart” is a 1843 American short story commonly associated with Gothic fiction. Its unnamed narrator tries to convince the reader of the narrator’s sanity while describing a murder. The victim is an old man whose filmy, pale-blue “vulture-eye” becomes the narrator’s stated focus.

The narrator presents the killing as carefully calculated, dismembers the body, and hides it under the floorboards. A resulting thumping sound is interpreted as the dead man’s beating heart. The story leaves the narrator’s motive, gender, and relationship with the old man unclear, while critics’ proposed explanations remain speculation.

key_facts.text: The story first appeared in January 1843 in James Russell Lowell’s The Pioneer.
The narrator insists that the old man had never wronged them and denies killing for greed, leaving the exact motive uncertain.
Suggested identities for the old man include a father figure or landlord, but these interpretations are not established by the story.

overview.text: A mitochondrion is a double-membraned organelle found in most eukaryotic cells, including those of animals, plants, and fungi. It uses aerobic respiration to produce ATP, a chemical-energy molecule used throughout the cell, explaining its familiar “powerhouse of the cell” nickname. Its specialized regions include an outer membrane, inner membrane, intermembrane space, cristae, and matrix.

Mitochondria also participate in cell signaling, differentiation, cell death, cell-cycle control, and growth. They possess a genome resembling bacterial genomes, supporting endosymbiotic theory: ancestral free-living prokaryotes are thought to have become permanent partners inside eukaryotic cells.

key_facts.text: Mitochondrial abundance varies by cell type: mature red blood cells have none, while a liver cell can contain more than 2,000.
The singular is mitochondrion; mitochondria is the plural.
Mitochondria have been implicated in conditions including mitochondrial diseases, cardiac dysfunction, and heart failure.

overview.text: F. Scott Fitzgerald (Francis Scott Key Fitzgerald) was an American novelist, essayist, and short-story writer. His novels portray the flamboyance and excess associated with the Jazz Age, a term he helped popularize through the collection Tales of the Jazz Age.

His novels include This Side of Paradise, The Beautiful and Damned, The Great Gatsby, and Tender Is the Night. The Great Gatsby appeared in 1925 and initially sold poorly despite generally favorable reviews; Fitzgerald did not receive critical acclaim until after his death.

key_facts.text: Born in 1896 in Saint Paul, Minnesota, Fitzgerald attended Princeton before leaving to join the Army during World War I.
During periods in Europe, he associated with the expatriate “Lost Generation” literary community and befriended Ernest Hemingway.
He wrote numerous stories for popular magazines, including The Saturday Evening Post, Collier’s Weekly, and Esquire.
A later move to Hollywood led to an unsuccessful screenwriting career; his unfinished novel The Last Tycoon was published after his death in 1941.

overview.text: Mexico City (Ciudad de México, or CDMX) is Mexico’s capital, located in the Valley of Mexico on the high Mexican Central Plateau. At an elevation of 2,240 meters, it is organized into 16 boroughs, or alcaldías, which contain neighborhoods called colonias.

Its history begins with Tenochtitlan, a Mexica city built around 1325 on islands in Lake Texcoco. Following the Spanish siege of 1521, Tenochtitlan was nearly destroyed and the city was rebuilt according to Spanish urban standards. During the colonial period, it became a major political, administrative, and financial center; after independence, the surrounding territory became a federal district in 1824.

key_facts.text: The municipality was established in 1524 as México Tenochtitlán; from 1585, its official name was Ciudad de México.
In 1997, residents gained the right to elect the city’s head of government and members of its unicameral Legislative Assembly.
On January 29, 2016, the Federal District was officially renamed Ciudad de México, or CDMX, as part of changes granting the city greater autonomy.

overview.text: Tyrian purple is a reddish-purple natural dye associated with royal and imperial purple. It came from predatory sea snails, and its costly production gave clothing bearing the color high social value in ancient times. The subject connects dye chemistry with clothing, wealth, and status.

key_facts.text: The dye’s colored compound is 6,6′-dibromoindigo.
“Tyrian” refers to Tyre, a city in ancient Phoenicia, in modern-day Lebanon.
Extracting the dye required tens of thousands of snails and substantial labor, making it costly to use.

overview.text: Amplitude describes how much a variable changes. For a periodic variable, it measures the change within one period, which may be a time period or a spatial period. For a non-periodic signal, amplitude instead describes its magnitude compared with a reference value. The term has multiple definitions, but these definitions relate to the size of differences between the variable’s extreme values.

key_facts.text: A period can refer to time or to distance in space.
A non-periodic signal’s amplitude is evaluated relative to a reference value.
Some older texts used “amplitude” to mean the phase of a periodic function.

overview.text: The Popol Vuh is a foundational sacred narrative of the K’iche’ people, one of the Maya peoples of Guatemala. It combines a creation myth with the adventures of the Hero Twins, Hunahpú and Xbalanqué, and a chronicle of K’iche’ history. The work thus connects religious mythology with the remembered history of a specific Maya community.
It is especially important for studying Mesoamerican mythology because early accounts are scarce, partly because missionaries and colonists destroyed many documents during the Spanish conquest.

key_facts.text: The title is translated as “Book of the Community” or “Book of Counsel.” Its name refers to a woven mat that served as a royal throne and symbolized communal unity in ancient K’iche’ society.
The narrative was preserved through oral tradition until about 1550, when it was recorded in writing.
The 18th-century Spanish Dominican friar Francisco Ximénez is credited with documenting it through a K’iche’ transcription alongside Spanish translations.

overview.text: Sun Tzu was a Chinese general, strategist, philosopher, and writer associated with the Eastern Zhou period. He is traditionally credited with The Art of War, a Classical Chinese text on military strategy connected with the Warring States period. However, the work’s earliest parts may date to at least a century after him.

Traditional historical accounts associate Sun Tzu with service as a minister to King Helü of Wu. His identity is also connected to Sun Bin: classical Chinese texts used “Sun Tzu” for both figures, and some historians once considered them the same person until Sun Bin’s treatise was rediscovered.

key_facts.text: “Sun Tzu” is an honorific meaning “Master Sun”; Sun Wu is his traditionally reported birth name, and Changqing is his courtesy name.
Sima Qian and other traditional historians placed Sun Tzu’s lifetime around 544–496 BC.
Sun Bin, traditionally described as Sun Wu’s descendant, also wrote a military-tactics treatise titled The Art of War.
Before Sun Bin’s treatise was rediscovered in 1972, some historians had considered Sun Wu and Sun Bin the same person.

overview.text: Drake, born Aubrey Drake Graham, is a Canadian rapper and singer who first gained recognition as Jimmy Brooks on the teen drama Degrassi: The Next Generation. He later moved from independently released mixtapes into a major music career. His style helped bring R&B-influenced singing into hip-hop, making rap-singing a central association with his work.

His major albums include Thank Me Later, Take Care, Nothing Was the Same, Views, and Scorpion. Songs associated with this period include “One Dance,” “God’s Plan,” “Nice for What,” and “In My Feelings.” Beyond recording, Drake founded OVO Sound and became a global ambassador for the Toronto Raptors.

key_facts.text: Before signing with Young Money Entertainment, Drake independently released the mixtapes Room for Improvement, Comeback Season, and So Far Gone.
“One Dance,” from Views, became the first song to surpass one billion streams on Spotify.
Drake’s business activities include the production company DreamCrew, the OVO fashion label, and the Nocta collaboration with Nike.
His awards include five Grammys, six American Music Awards, and three Juno Awards.

overview.text: Known by its Japanese title Oku no Hosomichi, The Narrow Road to the Deep North is a haibun work by the Japanese poet Matsuo Bashō. It is regarded as one of the major texts of Edo-period Japanese literature, linking Bashō’s name with an important Japanese literary form and period.

key_facts.text: The work is also translated as The Narrow Road to the Interior.
Its literary form is haibun.
The first edition appeared posthumously in 1702.

overview.text: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was a German writer and polymath whose literary work includes poetry, plays, novels, and aesthetic criticism. His broad influence made him a central figure in German-language literature; he also wrote on science and served as a statesman and theater director.

Goethe was an early participant in Sturm und Drang, a literary movement, and his years in Weimar helped establish the cultural setting known as Weimar Classicism. His major literary associations include The Sorrows of Young Werther, Wilhelm Meister’s Apprenticeship, Hermann and Dorothea, and Faust.

key_facts.text: The Sorrows of Young Werther was published in 1774; its success preceded Goethe’s move to Weimar in 1775.
The first part of Faust appeared in 1808; the source describes Faust as Goethe’s most celebrated drama.
Goethe managed the Weimar theater from 1791 and began a friendship with Friedrich Schiller in 1794, premiering Schiller’s plays until Schiller’s death in 1805.
Goethe’s poems were set to music by composers including Mozart, Beethoven, Schubert, Berlioz, Liszt, Wagner, and Mahler.

overview.text: The Book of Psalms, also called the Psalter or Tehillim, is an anthology of Hebrew religious hymns. It is the first book of Ketuvim (“Writings”), the third section of the Tanakh, and is also part of the Old Testament. In Jewish and Western Christian traditions, it contains 150 psalms.

The collection includes praise, communal and individual lament, royal songs, thanksgiving, wisdom, pilgrimage, and other forms. The English title comes through Greek from a term associated with instrumental music and its accompanying words, while Tehillim means “praises,” reflecting the book’s praise and supplication to God.

key_facts.text: The Psalter is arranged in five sections, each ending with a doxology, or hymn of praise.
Many psalms are attributed to David and other biblical figures, including Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses, and Solomon; modern scholars do not treat Davidic authorship as established historical fact.
Jewish and Western Christian traditions recognize 150 psalms, while Eastern Christian churches include several additional ones.
The collection’s dating is difficult to establish: some psalms are considered preexilic and others postexilic.

overview.text: Nepal’s national flag is a red, white, and blue concave pentagon made by joining two pennants, or a double-pennon. It serves as both the state and civil flag. Its unusual geometry makes it the world’s only nonrectangular national flag and the only one taller than it is wide. The blue border represents peace, while the red field is associated with bravery and Nepal’s national flower, the rhododendron.

The modern form was adopted on December 16, 1962, and standardized by civil engineer Shankar Nath Rimal at the request of King Mahendra. It developed from traditional pennants associated with rival branches of the ruling dynasty. Before 1962, the sun and crescent moon on the flag had human faces; these were removed as part of its modernization.

key_facts.text: One popular interpretation identifies the moon with peace and the sun with hard work.
Historically similar triangular pennants, including Hindu religious banners called dhvaja, helped inspire the design.
The sun and moon can symbolize Nepal’s hoped-for permanence and longevity.
Other interpretations connect the moon with the cool Himalayas and the sun with the heat of the southern Terai lowlands.

overview.text: An athlete competes in sporting activities involving strength, speed, power, or endurance. The term can refer broadly to participants in sports or more narrowly to competitors in athletics, such as track-and-field events and marathons.

key_facts.text: Athletes may compete professionally or as amateurs.
The broad use of athlete for participants in any sport occurs especially in the United States; sportsperson is another term for this meaning.
Athlete is also sometimes used for a physically fit person, whether or not that person competes in sports.

overview.text: The Toyota Production System (TPS) is Toyota’s integrated socio-technical management system: it combines management philosophy with practices for manufacturing and logistics, including relationships with suppliers and customers. It became a major precursor of lean manufacturing. Japanese industrial engineers Taiichi Ohno and Eiji Toyoda developed it between 1948 and 1975.

Its central logic is to make what is needed when it is needed, use a pull system to avoid overproduction, and expose problems through continuous flow and visual controls. TPS also calls for stopping to correct problems, standardizing work, developing people and partners, and continuously removing waste—anything that does not advance a process or add value. These practices connect production control with quality, employee development, and organizational learning.

key_facts.text: Jidoka, or “automation with a human touch,” calls for stopping production when problems occur.
Heijunka means leveling out the workload, favoring a steady pace over bursts of activity.
Genchi genbutsu means going to the source or seeing for oneself to find facts and understand a situation before deciding.
Nemawashi emphasizes slow, consensus-based consideration of options followed by rapid implementation; Hansei is reflection paired with ongoing kaizen, or continuous improvement.
TPS extends beyond the factory: it asks leaders to develop people and challenges suppliers and other partners while helping them improve.

overview.text: Extraterrestrial life is life originating beyond Earth; none has yet been detected. It could range from microbes to intelligent beings. Astrobiology combines astronomy, biology, chemistry, geology, oceanography, and atmospheric science to study how life begins, evolves, persists, and what evidence scientists should seek elsewhere.

Earth’s extreme ecosystems—including hydrothermal vents, acidic hot springs, volcanic lakes, salt-loving organisms, and the deep biosphere—help frame questions about habitability. Searches examine worlds such as Mars, Venus, Europa, and Titan through telescopes, specimens, biosignatures, and possible technosignatures; SETI also seeks artificial radio and laser signals.

key_facts.text: The Drake equation speculates about the existence of sapient life elsewhere.
NASA’s Curiosity rover landed at Mars’s Gale Crater in 2012 and was designed to assess Mars’s past and present habitability.
SETI searches for radio waves and laser pulses, but natural signals can resemble artificial ones, and a distant civilization might not transmit toward Earth.

overview.text: Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC), also called the Dewey Decimal System, is a library classification system first published in the United States by Melvil Dewey in 1876. It organizes library materials by discipline and subject, using decimal notation to place items relative to other books on library shelves. This helps users locate materials and return them to their proper positions.

DDC is hierarchical: it has ten classes, each divided into ten divisions and then ten sections. Three-digit numbers identify broad levels, while decimals add detail. Its Relative Index gives alphabetical access to class numbers by topic. The system became widely used internationally; as of 2009, it was used in 200,000 libraries in at least 135 countries.

key_facts.text: DDC began as a 44-page pamphlet and has been revised through 23 major editions; the latest printed edition was published in 2011.
Its notation can be constructed by combining a topic number with elements for geography, time, language, or bibliographic form; this is called a synthetic or faceted approach.
Fiction is assigned numbers in the 800s, although many libraries shelve fiction separately by the author’s surname.
A complete assigned number includes a Dewey class number and a book number; a common book-number form, the Cutter number, represents the author.
The 000 class covers computer science, information, and general works.

overview.text: Navy pilots work in naval aviation: military air power operated by a navy from ships or coastal air stations. Carrier-based aircraft are designed for short flight decks, demanding landings, and limited storage space. Naval aviation also uses helicopters, which can operate from a wider range of ships than fixed-wing aircraft.

key_facts.text: Naval aircraft carry out missions including combat, anti-submarine warfare, reconnaissance, transport, and search and rescue.
Many carrier aircraft have folding wings to reduce the space needed to store them aboard ship.
Aircraft carriers and their planes changed warfare at sea during World War II, reducing the dominance of battleships.

overview.text: Bön (Bon), also called Yungdrung Bön (“Eternal Bön”), is an indigenous Tibetan religion practiced as a significant minority tradition in Tibet and surrounding Himalayan regions. It resembles Tibetan Buddhism in many ways but retains elements from earlier Tibetan religious traditions.

Bön’s history is layered and debated. Early “bon” may have meant a ritual, a priest, or a local religion, while scholars have limited knowledge of pre-Buddhist Tibetan religion. The living Yungdrung tradition developed in the 10th and 11th centuries amid the later spread of Buddhism; Bön and Buddhism both came into conflict and sometimes collaborated. Bonpos traditionally trace their religion to Zhangzhung and Tonpa Shenrab, whose historicity is not established.

key_facts.text: Practitioners are called Bonpos. Traditional accounts locate Bön’s origins in Zhangzhung, around Mount Kailash, and identify Tonpa Shenrab as its founder; available sources do not establish his historicity.
Bön developed a monastic tradition with celibate monks called trangsong, while also maintaining a strong tradition of lay yogis.
Bön monks study scripture, train in philosophical debate, and perform rituals.

Bön tradition includes terma: teachings said to have been hidden and later revealed by tertons, or treasure revealers. The Bon Kanjur and Tenjur were compiled during the Tibetan religious renaissance.
Bön received official recognition as a religious group with the same rights as Tibetan Buddhist schools in 1979; this status was reaffirmed in 1987.

overview.text: In Louisiana geography, a parish is the state’s primary civil subdivision—the equivalent of a county. Louisiana has 64 parishes and is the only state besides Alaska whose primary subdivisions are not called counties. The term comes from the French paroisses and reflects Louisiana’s French colonial heritage.

The civil usage grew from Louisiana’s colonial history: French and Spanish rule was officially Roman Catholic, and local government was based on ecclesiastical parishes. Thus, “parish” links Louisiana’s distinctive political geography with its religious and French colonial past.

key_facts.text: After the Louisiana Purchase, the territory used counties in 1805; parishes were created in 1807, while the old county units continued until 1845.
Louisiana’s parishes have different local-government systems: 38 are governed by police juries, while 26 use other arrangements such as council-president or council-manager governments.
Four parishes created from former Spanish West Florida in 1810 became part of the region now known as the Florida Parishes.

overview.text: In visual art, Théodore Géricault’s The Raft of the Medusa (1818–1819) is a monumental oil painting centered on a raft and an icon of French Romanticism. It shows the aftermath of the 1816 wreck of the French naval frigate Méduse, when at least 150 people were set adrift on a hastily built raft; only 15 survived the 13 days before rescue. The disaster became an international scandal, partly because the captain was widely blamed for incompetence. Géricault’s dramatic subject and presentation broke with the calm and order of prevailing Neoclassicism. The work established his international reputation and influenced artists including Delacroix, Turner, Courbet, and Manet.

key_facts.text: The painting originally had the title Scène de Naufrage, or “Shipwreck Scene.”
To prepare the work, Géricault interviewed two survivors, built a scale model of the raft, and studied bodies in hospitals and morgues.
Its pyramidal composition rises from dead and dying figures in the foreground toward survivors signaling to a distant rescue ship.
Pallid flesh tones, murky colors, dark brown pigments, and strong light-dark contrasts intensify the painting’s tragic mood.

overview.text: In She-Ra and the Princesses of Power, Etheria is the planet where the story’s central conflict unfolds. Adora and Catra, orphans raised as soldiers in Hordak’s Horde, end up on opposing sides: after finding a magic sword that transforms her into She-Ra, Adora learns that the Horde is harming Etheria’s inhabitants and joins the Rebellion. She helps rebuild the Princess Alliance, a league of kingdoms ruled by magical princesses, while Catra becomes her enemy.

key_facts.text: Hordak is a tyrannical leader whose goal is to conquer Etheria.
The Princess Alliance successfully defends its rebel stronghold, Bright Moon, against a Horde assault in the first season.
Hordak’s interdimensional portal project threatens to tear Etheria apart and is intended to contact the warlord Horde Prime.

source.title: She-Ra and the Princesses of Power

overview.text: Jake from State Farm is a recurring character in State Farm television commercials. The character became associated with the 2011 “State of Unrest” ad, in which a man’s wife interrupts a 3 a.m. call to a State Farm representative and asks what he is wearing; Jake replies, “Uh, khakis.” Jake Stone, an actual State Farm employee, played the original version. In 2020, Kevin Miles took over the role in a reimagining of that commercial. Miles’s Jake appears in varied settings and in ads with celebrities, including Aaron Rodgers and Paul Rudd.

key_facts.text: The original Jake commercial was part of State Farm’s 2011 “State of...” advertising campaign.
Miles’s version of Jake is identified by a red shirt and khakis.
Drake appeared as Jake’s stand-in in a commercial shown during Super Bowl LV.
State Farm’s 2011 “Get to a Better State” campaign used humorous unfortunate situations, often followed by an agent appearing after someone sang the company jingle.

overview.text: Sir Ernest Henry Shackleton (1874–1922) was an Anglo-Irish explorer who led three British expeditions to Antarctica. He took part in Robert Falcon Scott’s Discovery expedition before the Nimrod expedition of 1907–1909. His later Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition aimed to cross the continent via the South Pole. When Endurance became trapped in pack ice and sank in 1915, the expedition became a struggle for survival. Shackleton’s party reached Elephant Island; he then traveled to South Georgia to seek help and returned to rescue the stranded men. He later became a role model for leadership in extreme circumstances.

key_facts.text: During the Nimrod Expedition, Shackleton and three companions reached 88°23′ south latitude—about 180 kilometers from the South Pole—and members of the team climbed Mount Erebus.
Endurance became frozen into the Weddell Sea ice on 19 January 1915 and sank on 21 November after the crew had abandoned it.

In 1916, Shackleton and five companions sailed the small lifeboat James Caird from Elephant Island to South Georgia; Shackleton, Frank Worsley, and Tom Crean then crossed the island’s mountains to reach a whaling station.
The Chilean Navy tug Yelcho reached Elephant Island on 30 August 1916 and rescued all 22 men stranded there.

overview.text: Umuofia is the fictional Igbo clan in Chinua Achebe’s 1958 novel Things Fall Apart. It is associated with Okonkwo, a famous wrestler, warrior, and influential leader, and with the elders, oracle, customs, and religious practices that organize communal decisions.

The plot traces Umuofia’s disruption by Christian missionaries and a colonial government. While Okonkwo is exiled, missionaries gain converts and a new government is introduced; after his return, the community must decide how to respond to foreign rule and religious change.

key_facts.text: Umuofia’s elders choose Okonkwo as guardian of Ikemefuna, a boy taken as a peace settlement after a conflict with another clan.
Okonkwo’s seven-year exile follows his accidental killing of Ezeudu’s son. This is separate from Ikemefuna’s death, which Okonkwo carries out earlier.
Nwoye becomes curious about the missionaries, leaves his family after being beaten by Okonkwo, and is introduced to Christianity by the Igbo missionary Mr. Kiaga.
After a Christian convert unmasks an elder embodying an ancestral spirit, Umuofia destroys a church; colonial authorities then imprison local leaders and demand fines.
Okonkwo kills a government messenger when officials try to stop a village meeting, then dies by suicide. This violates Igbo teachings and damages his standing among his people.

overview.text: The Roswell incident concerns debris found by a rancher near Roswell, New Mexico, in 1947. Roswell Army Air Field personnel recovered metallic and rubber material, and the Army Air Forces briefly announced that it had a “flying disc.” The material is identified as part of Project Mogul, a secret, uncrewed balloon train intended to detect Soviet nuclear tests; a weather-balloon explanation obscured that purpose.

The episode became historically important as a durable UFO conspiracy narrative, not as a confirmed extraterrestrial crash. Later claims expanded the story beyond the recovered debris, and it became a trope in science fiction; Roswell also promotes itself as a destination for UFO-associated tourism.

key_facts.text: The initial “flying disc” announcement made international headlines before being retracted within a day.
Project Mogul operated from nearby Alamogordo Army Air Field and used linked balloons and assorted equipment.
In 1978, retired Air Force officer Jesse Marcel said the weather-balloon explanation was a cover story; the 1980 book The Roswell Incident popularized the extraterrestrial speculation.
Air Force reports published in the 1990s linked the incident to Project Mogul rather than debris from a UFO.
Expanded claims about hidden alien evidence, gray aliens, corpses, autopsies, and reverse-engineered technology have no factual basis.

overview.text: Theranos was an American health-technology company founded in 2003 by Elizabeth Holmes. It promoted compact devices that supposedly could perform many blood tests rapidly and accurately from very small samples. The company raised more than $700 million from investors and reached a reported $9 billion valuation at its peak.

In 2015, researchers and journalist John Carreyrou questioned whether Theranos’s technology worked as advertised. Reporting and regulatory inspections found serious problems involving its testing practices and devices, leading to commercial and legal challenges. The company eventually dissolved in September 2018.

key_facts.text: John Carreyrou’s reporting for The Wall Street Journal helped expose that Theranos was using conventional laboratory machines and that its Edison devices might give inaccurate results.
FDA inspections identified problems with Theranos’s blood-collection devices, while CMS warned that testing at one laboratory posed an immediate danger to patient health and safety.
Walgreens ended its partnership with Theranos in 2016 after Theranos voided or corrected test results.

Holmes and former company president Sunny Balwani were charged with fraud and wire fraud. Holmes was convicted in 2022 and sentenced to 11 years and 3 months in prison; Balwani was also convicted and sentenced to prison.
